questions.q: Which of the following is a safety hazard of a 12-volt storage battery that lacks internal protection circuitry?
a: Touching both terminals with your hands can cause electrical shock
Shorting the terminals can cause burns, fire, or an explosion
RF emissions from a nearby transmitter can cause the electrolyte to emit poison gas
questions.x: A lead-acid battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a dead short. A dropped wrench across the terminals will glow red, spray molten metal, and can rupture the case. Lead-acid also vents hydrogen, so an arc near a charging battery risks an explosion.

questions.q: What health hazard is posed by electrical current flowing through the body?
a: It may cause injury by heating body tissue
It may disrupt the electrical functions of cells
It may cause involuntary muscle contractions
questions.x: Current through the body can burn tissue, disrupt breathing, and stop the heart through ventricular fibrillation. All three are real, so the inclusive answer is right. Current is what injures you, which is why fairly low voltages can still kill.
questions.xs: IEC 60479 (effects of current on the human body)

questions.q: In the United States, what circuit does black wire insulation indicate in a three-wire 120 V AC cable?
questions.x: In US practice black insulation marks the hot conductor. White is neutral and green or bare is ground. Treat any black or red wire as live until you have proven otherwise with a meter.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a fuse in an electrical circuit?
a: To prevent power supply ripple from damaging a component
To remove power in case of an overload
To limit current and prevent shocks
questions.x: A fuse is a deliberate weak point that opens when current climbs past its rating, cutting power before the wiring overheats. It protects the circuit and the building, not the equipment plugged into it.

questions.q: Why should a 5-ampere fuse never be replaced with a 20-ampere fuse?
a: The larger fuse would be likely to blow because it is rated for higher current
The power supply ripple would greatly increase
Excessive current could cause a fire
Voltage drop in the higher current fuse could result in excessively low voltage to the device
questions.x: The fuse rating is chosen for the wire behind it. Fit a 20-amp fuse to wiring sized for 5 amps and the fuse will happily pass current that overheats the conductors, so the wiring becomes the fuse. That is how electrical fires start.

questions.q: What is a good way to guard against electrical shock at your station?
a: Use three-wire cords and plugs for all AC powered equipment
Connect all AC powered station equipment to a common safety ground
Ensure all capacitors used for high-voltage DC are fully discharged before working inside equipment
questions.x: Good practice stacks up: bond equipment to a common ground, use three-wire cords, and disconnect power before working inside a chassis. All the listed measures are sound, so the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: Where should a lightning arrester be installed in a coaxial feed line?
a: At the output connector of a transceiver
At the AC power service panel
On a grounded panel near where feed lines enter the building
questions.x: Mount the arrester on a grounded panel where the feed lines enter the building. Bleeding the surge to ground at the entry point keeps it out of the shack. An arrester deep inside the house has already let the strike travel past everything you wanted to protect.

questions.q: Where should a fuse or circuit breaker be installed in a 120V AC power circuit?
a: In series with the hot conductor only
In series with the hot and neutral conductors
In parallel with the hot conductor only
In parallel with the hot and neutral conductors
questions.x: In series with the hot conductor only. Interrupting the hot line stops current and leaves the equipment at ground potential. Fusing the neutral instead could open it while the chassis stays connected to a live hot wire, which is worse than no fuse.

questions.q: What should be done to all external ground rods or earth connections?
a: Waterproof them with silicone caulk or electrical tape
Keep them as far apart as possible
Bond them together with heavy wire or conductive strap
Tune them for resonance on the lowest frequency of operation
questions.x: Bond every ground rod and earth connection together with heavy wire or strap. Separate grounds sitting at different potentials during a surge will push current through your equipment as it equalizes. One bonded system, not several isolated ones.

questions.q: What hazard exists when rapidly charging or discharging an unprotected battery?
questions.x: Fast charging or discharging generates heat and drives the chemistry harder than it is meant to go, producing gas inside the cell. Lead-acid vents hydrogen; lithium cells can go into thermal runaway. Overheating and out-gassing are the hazards.

questions.q: What hazard exists in a power supply immediately after turning it off?
a: Circulating currents in the dc filter
Leakage flux in the power transformer
questions.x: Filter capacitors hold their charge after the power is off, sometimes at lethal voltage for a long time. Switching off is not the same as being safe. Verify with a meter and discharge through a resistor before reaching inside.

questions.q: Which of the following precautions should be taken when measuring high voltages with a voltmeter?
a: Ensure that the voltmeter has very low impedance
Ensure that the voltmeter and its leads are rated for use at the voltages being measured
Ensure that the circuit is grounded through the voltmeter
Ensure that the voltmeter is set to the correct frequency
questions.x: Both the meter and its leads have voltage ratings, and the leads are usually the weak link. Using probes rated below the voltage you are measuring risks flashover to your hands. Confirm the rating covers the circuit before you touch anything.

questions.q: Which of the following is good practice when installing ground wires on a tower for lightning protection?
a: Put a drip loop in the ground connection to prevent water damage to the ground system
Make sure all ground wire bends are right angles
Ensure that connections are short and direct
questions.x: Keep ground conductors short and direct. A lightning surge rises so fast that the conductor's inductance dominates, and every extra foot or bend adds impedance that pushes the surge to find another route, possibly through your equipment.

questions.q: What is required when climbing an antenna tower?
a: Have sufficient training on safe tower climbing techniques
Use appropriate tie-off to the tower at all times
Always wear an approved climbing harness
questions.x: Climbing requires a proper climbing harness, a helper or observer on the ground, and gear inspected before use. All the listed requirements are genuine, so the inclusive answer is right.
questions.xs: OSHA 1926 Subpart M; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: Under what circumstances is it safe to climb a tower without a helper or observer?
a: When no electrical work is being performed
When no mechanical work is being performed
When the work being done is not more than 20 feet above the ground
questions.x: Never. There is no tower short enough or job quick enough to make solo climbing acceptable. If something goes wrong up there, an observer on the ground is the only thing standing between an accident and a fatality.

questions.q: Which of the following is an important safety precaution to observe when putting up an antenna tower?
a: Wear a ground strap connected to your wrist at all times
Insulate the base of the tower to avoid lightning strikes
Look for and stay clear of any overhead electrical wires
questions.x: Look for overhead power lines and stay clear of them. A tower section or antenna being raised is a long conductor swinging through the air, and contact with a distribution line is usually fatal. Survey the site before anything goes up.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a safety wire through a turnbuckle used to tension guy lines?
a: Secure the guy line if the turnbuckle breaks
Prevent loosening of the turnbuckle from vibration
Provide a ground path for lightning strikes
Provide an ability to measure for proper tensioning
questions.x: Wire through the turnbuckle body stops it from unwinding as wind vibration works it loose over months. Guy tension slowly slackens otherwise, and a loose guy lets the tower move in ways it was never designed to.

questions.q: What is the minimum safe distance from a power line to allow when installing an antenna?
a: Add the height of the antenna to the height of the power line and multiply by a factor of 1.5
The height of the power line above ground
Enough so that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires
questions.x: Site the antenna so that if the whole thing falls, no part reaches within 10 feet of the power wires. Plan for the failure, not just the installation. Height plus guy radius decides how far away that has to be.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; OSHA clearance guidance

questions.q: Which of the following is an important safety rule to remember when using a crank-up tower?
a: This type of tower must never be painted
This type of tower must never be grounded
This type of tower must not be climbed unless it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed
questions.x: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it is fully retracted or mechanical locks are in place. The cable is the only thing holding the sections apart, and a cable failure with a climber aboard turns the tower into a guillotine.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; manufacturer safety guidance

questions.q: Which is a proper grounding method for a tower?
a: A single four-foot ground rod, driven into the ground no more than 12 inches from the base
A ferrite-core RF choke connected between the tower and ground
A connection between the tower base and a cold-water pipe
Separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and each other
questions.x: Give each tower leg its own eight-foot ground rod, then bond the rods to the tower and to each other. Multiple paths share the surge current, and bonding keeps every part of the system at the same potential while it happens.

questions.q: Why should you avoid attaching an antenna to a utility pole?
a: The antenna will not work properly because of induced voltages
The antenna may unbalance the power transformer, causing power fluctuations
The antenna could contact high-voltage power lines
questions.x: Utility poles carry high-voltage lines, and the pole is the utility's property besides. Climbing one or attaching hardware puts you within reach of conductors that will kill you long before you touch them.

questions.q: Which of the following is true when installing grounding conductors used for lightning protection?
a: Wires must be carefully routed with precise right-angle bends
questions.x: Avoid sharp bends. A fast surge does not follow a tight corner well, and the added inductance can make it jump the bend to something nearby. Sweeping curves keep the current on the conductor you chose for it.

questions.q: Which of the following establishes grounding requirements for an amateur radio tower or antenna?
questions.x: Local electrical codes govern grounding, generally adopting the National Electrical Code. The FCC regulates your transmissions, not your wiring, so grounding requirements come from the locality rather than Part 97.

questions.q: What type of radiation are radio signals?
questions.x: Radio waves are non-ionizing. Their photons lack the energy to strip electrons from atoms, so RF cannot ionize tissue the way X-rays or gamma rays do. Its effect at high levels is heating, which is what the exposure rules are written around.

questions.q: Which of the following bands has the lowest maximum permissible exposure for RF safety?
questions.x: The 30 to 300 MHz range has the most restrictive limits, so of these bands 50 MHz is the answer. The human body is roughly resonant at those frequencies, absorbing energy most efficiently, so the allowable exposure is set lowest there.

questions.q: How does the allowable power density for RF safety change if duty cycle changes from 100 percent to 50 percent?
a: It increases by a factor of 3
It increases by a factor of 2
There is no adjustment allowed for lower duty cycle
questions.x: Exposure limits are averaged over time, so transmitting half as much doubles the power density you may produce. Drop from 100 percent to 50 percent duty cycle and the allowable density goes up by a factor of two.

questions.q: What factors affect the RF exposure of people near an amateur station antenna?
a: Frequency and power level of the RF field
Distance from the antenna to a person
questions.x: Power, frequency, antenna gain and pattern, and how close people get all feed into the exposure calculation, along with duty cycle. Every listed factor genuinely matters, so the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: Why do exposure limits vary with frequency?
a: Lower frequency RF fields have more energy than higher frequency fields
Lower frequency RF fields do not penetrate the human body
Higher frequency RF fields are transient in nature
The human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others
questions.x: The body absorbs RF more efficiently at some frequencies than others, peaking where a person is about a half wavelength tall. Limits are tightened where absorption is greatest, which is why the VHF range is the most restrictive.

questions.q: Which of the following is an acceptable method to determine whether your station complies with FCC RF exposure regulations?
a: By calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65
By calculation based on computer modeling
By measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment
questions.x: You may use the FCC's calculation tables, run the equations yourself, or measure with calibrated field-strength equipment. All are acceptable, so the inclusive answer applies. OET Bulletin 65 is the document that lays out the methods.

questions.q: What hazard is created by touching an antenna during a transmission?
questions.x: Touching a radiating antenna concentrates RF current at the contact point and produces a burn that is deep and slow to heal. It happens at surprisingly modest power. Mount antennas where nobody can reach them while you transmit.

questions.q: Which of the following actions can reduce exposure to RF radiation?
questions.x: Move the antennas. Exposure falls steeply with distance, so relocating an antenna farther from people is usually more effective than cutting power, and it costs you nothing on the air.

questions.q: How can you make sure your station stays in compliance with RF safety regulations?
a: By informing the FCC of any changes made in your station
By re-evaluating the station whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed
By making sure your antennas have low SWR
By using only Underwriter Laboratories approved transmitting equipment
questions.x: Re-evaluate whenever anything in the transmitter or antenna system changes. A new amplifier, a different antenna, or a relocated feed point all alter the exposure picture, so the original evaluation no longer describes your station.

questions.q: Why is duty cycle one of the factors used to determine safe RF radiation exposure levels?
a: It affects the average exposure to radiation
It affects the peak exposure to radiation
It takes into account the antenna feed line loss
It takes into account the thermal effects of the final amplifier
questions.x: The limits are based on average exposure over a period, not on peak power. A transmitter sending half the time delivers half the average energy, so duty cycle scales the exposure directly.

questions.q: What is the definition of duty cycle during the averaging time for RF exposure?
a: The difference between the lowest and highest power output of a transmitter
The difference between the PEP and the average power output of a transmitter
The percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting
The percentage of time that a transmitter is not transmitting
questions.x: Duty cycle is the percentage of the averaging period during which the transmitter is actually transmitting. SSB and CW have low duty cycles because you are receiving much of the time; FM and digital modes run far higher.

questions.q: How does RF radiation differ from ionizing radiation (radioactivity)?
a: RF radiation does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA
RF radiation can only be detected with an RF dosimeter
RF radiation is limited in range to a few feet
questions.x: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy per photon to break chemical bonds and damage DNA directly. RF does not come close, so its only established hazard at high levels is heating. Different mechanism entirely, not simply a weaker version.

questions.q: Who is responsible for ensuring that no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC exposure limits?
a: Anyone who is near an antenna
questions.x: The station licensee. Section 97.13(c) puts the duty on the licensee before allowing the station to transmit, and §97.103(a) makes the licensee responsible for proper operation generally. It does not shift to the control operator or the equipment maker.

questions.q: Which of the following is part of the Basis and Purpose of the Amateur Radio Service?
a: Providing personal radio communications for as many citizens as possible
Advancing skills in the technical and communication phases of the radio art
questions.x: Section 97.1 lists five principles behind the amateur service. Paragraph (c) is the one tested here: the rules provide for "advancing skills in both the communication and technical phases of the art." On the exam, look for the choice that names skills and covers both sides of the hobby, operating and technical. That pairing is the giveaway.

questions.q: Which agency regulates and enforces the rules for the Amateur Radio Service in the United States?
questions.x: The FCC writes Part 97 and enforces it. Every rule on this exam traces back to the Commission. Any question asking who regulates, licenses, or enforces amateur radio in the United States has the same answer.

questions.q: What do the FCC rules state regarding the use of a phonetic alphabet for station identification in the Amateur Radio Service?
a: It is required when transmitting emergency messages
It is encouraged when using phone emissions
It is required when in contact with foreign stations
questions.x: Voice identification must be in English, and the rule adds that "use of a phonetic alphabet as an aid for correct station identification is encouraged." Encouraged is the word to spot. Pair "encouraged" with "phone emissions" and you have the answer.

questions.q: How do you receive official notification of your new license and call sign after passing the exam?
a: Email from the FCC with a link to download the license grant
USPS First-Class Mail from the FCC
Email from the lead volunteer examiner
USPS First-Class Mail from the lead volunteer examiner
questions.x: Section 97.23 requires your license grant to carry an email address where you can receive electronic correspondence. That is the channel the FCC uses: an email with a link to download your grant. Two things to hold onto for the exam. It comes from the FCC, and it arrives electronically.

questions.q: What proves that the FCC has issued an operator/primary license grant?
a: A printed copy of the certificate of successful completion of examination
An email notification from the NCVEC granting the license
The license appears in the FCC ULS database
questions.x: A control operator must be a person "for whom an amateur operator/primary station license grant appears on the ULS consolidated licensee database." The ULS entry is the proof. Until your grant posts there you are not licensed to transmit, whatever paperwork you are holding.

questions.q: On which of the following HF frequencies can automatically controlled amateur propagation beacons be found?
a: Anywhere in the Technician portion of 10 meters
Anywhere, if they are registered with the FCC
In a specific portion of each of the HF Technician bands
On ten meters, between 28.200 MHz and 28.300 MHz
questions.x: Section 97.203(d) lists the segments where a beacon may run under automatic control. The only HF one is 28.200 to 28.300 MHz on ten meters. Memorize that range. Worth carrying alongside it: §97.203(c) caps beacon power at 100 watts.

questions.q: What is the FCC Part 97 definition of a space station?
a: An amateur station located more than 50 km above Earth's surface
An amateur station using amateur radio satellites for relay of signals
questions.x: Straight from the definitions: "Space station. An amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface." Altitude is the entire definition. Fifty kilometers is the number to remember, and how the station got up there does not enter into it.

questions.q: Who recommends transmit/receive channels for repeater and auxiliary stations?
a: A Frequency Spectrum Manager appointed by the FCC
A Volunteer Frequency Coordinator recognized by local amateurs
questions.x: A frequency coordinator is an entity recognized by local amateurs "that recommends transmit/receive channels and associated operating and technical parameters" for repeater and auxiliary stations. Recommends, not assigns. The answer you want is the one built around recommending channels.

questions.q: Who selects a Frequency Coordinator?
a: The FCC Office of Spectrum Management and Coordination Policy
The local chapter of the Office of National Council of Independent Frequency Coordinators
Amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations
questions.x: Same definition, other half of the sentence. A coordinator is one "recognized in a local or regional area by amateur operators whose stations are eligible to be auxiliary or repeater stations." When the question asks who selects a coordinator, look for the choice describing local amateurs rather than any national organization.

questions.q: Besides an FCC-issued amateur operator license, what is required to be the control operator of a Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service (RACES) Station?
a: A written recommendation by the local ARRL Emergency Coordinator
Membership in the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)
Certification of current enrollment by a civil defense organization
questions.x: No station may transmit in RACES unless it "is certified by a civil defense organization as registered with that organization." Your operator license alone is not enough. The exam is testing that second piece: enrollment with the served civil defense organization, in place beforehand.

questions.q: Which of the following is prohibited?
a: International communications on VHF bands and higher frequencies
questions.x: One sentence: "No amateur operator shall willfully or maliciously interfere with or cause interference to any radio communication or signal." Willful or malicious is the exam language and it matches the answer nearly word for word.

questions.q: Which of the following frequency ranges are available for phone operation by Technician licensees?
questions.x: Technicians get one slice of HF phone: 28.300 to 28.500 MHz on ten meters. The rest of the Technician HF allocation is CW and data only. Learn the pair 28.300 and 28.500 as your phone window and this question and T1B06 both fall out of it.

questions.q: Which of the following U.S. amateur radio operators are allowed to contact the International Space Station (ISS) on VHF bands?
a: Only amateurs with a General class or higher license
Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license
Only amateurs with a General class or higher license, and NASA approval
Any amateurs with a Technician class or higher license, and NASA approval
questions.x: Working the ISS happens on 2 meters and 70 centimeters, and Technicians hold full privileges on both. Section 97.207(a) adds that any class of operator may work a space station within the privileges they hold. No upgrade required.

questions.q: Which frequency is in the 6-meter amateur band?
questions.x: The 6-meter band runs 50.0 to 54.0 MHz, so 52.525 MHz sits inside it. That frequency is also the national FM simplex calling channel on 6 meters, which makes it easy to remember.

questions.q: Which amateur band includes 146.52 MHz?
questions.x: The 2-meter band is 144 to 148 MHz, so 146.52 MHz falls in it. You will meet 146.52 constantly: it is the national FM simplex calling frequency. Knowing that one number answers this question without doing any band math.

questions.q: Which of the following bands include frequencies where Technicians are authorized to use digital modes such as FT8?
questions.x: Technicians may run digital modes on all of their HF, VHF and UHF allocations, subject to the emission types §97.305 authorizes for each segment. When a question lists several Technician bands and asks where digital is allowed, the answer is usually all of them.

questions.q: On which HF bands does a Technician class operator have phone privileges?
questions.x: Ten meters is the only HF band where a Technician may use phone, in the 28.300 to 28.500 MHz segment. The Technician allocations on 80, 40 and 15 meters are CW and data only. One HF band for voice, and it is 10 meters.

questions.q: Which of the following VHF/UHF band segments are limited to CW only?
a: 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz
219 MHz to 220 MHz and 420.0 MHz to 420.1 MHz
questions.x: The bottom 100 kHz of both 6 meters and 2 meters is reserved for CW: 50.0 to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 to 144.1 MHz. These are the weak-signal segments where operators work long-haul contacts, and voice would swamp them. Remember it as the first 100 kHz of each band.

questions.q: How are US amateurs restricted in segments of bands where the Amateur Radio Service is secondary?
a: U.S. amateurs may find non-amateur stations in those segments, and must avoid interfering with them
U.S. amateurs must give foreign amateur stations priority in those segments
International communications are not permitted in those segments
Digital transmissions are not permitted in those segments
questions.x: Where amateur radio is secondary, another service holds the primary allocation. You may transmit there, but you must not interfere with the primary users and you have to accept interference from them. Secondary means you yield, not that the segment is off limits.

questions.q: Why should you not set your transmit frequency to be exactly at the edge of an amateur band or sub-band?
a: To allow for calibration error in the transmitter frequency display
So that modulation sidebands do not extend beyond the band edge
To allow for transmitter frequency drift
questions.x: Your emitted signal occupies bandwidth on both sides of the dial reading, and neither your display nor the far end is perfectly calibrated. Sitting right on the edge can push sidebands outside the band. Section 97.101(a) requires good engineering and good amateur practice, so leave yourself margin.

questions.q: Where may SSB phone be used in amateur bands above 50 MHz?
a: Only in sub-bands allocated to General class or higher licensees
In at least some segment of all these bands
On any band if the power is limited to 25 watts
questions.x: Every amateur band above 50 MHz has at least some segment where SSB phone is authorized. The emission table in §97.305(c) is the source. If a question asks where SSB may be used above 50 MHz, the answer covers all those bands rather than any single one.

questions.q: What is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators in their HF band segments?
questions.x: Technician HF work is capped at 200 watts PEP on the 80, 40, 15 and 10 meter segments. That number is written directly into §97.313(c)(2). Two numbers carry most of the power questions: 200 watts on Technician HF, 1500 watts nearly everywhere else.

questions.q: Except for some specific restrictions, what is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators using frequencies above 30 MHz?
questions.x: The blanket limit for any amateur station is 1.5 kW PEP, which is 1500 watts, and that is what applies to a Technician above 30 MHz. Section 97.313(a) still requires you to use the minimum power needed, but 1500 watts is the ceiling the exam is asking for.

questions.q: For which classes of amateur radio licenses does the FCC currently issue new licenses?
a: Technician, Technician Plus, General, Amateur Extra
questions.x: Section 97.17(a) states that no new license grant will be issued for Novice or Advanced Class. Five classes still exist on paper and existing holders keep theirs, but the FCC issues only three today: Technician, General, Amateur Extra.

questions.q: Who may select a desired call sign under the vanity call sign rules?
a: Only a licensed amateur with a General or Amateur Extra Class license
Only a licensed amateur with an Amateur Extra Class license
Only a licensed amateur who has been licensed continuously for more than 10 years
questions.x: Any licensed amateur named in an operator or club station grant may apply for a vanity call sign. There is no license class requirement to request one, though which call signs are available to you does depend on your class.

questions.q: What types of international communications are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations permitted to make?
a: Communications incidental to the purposes of the Amateur Radio Service and remarks of a personal character
Communications incidental to conducting business or remarks of a personal nature
Only communications incidental to contest exchanges; all other communications are prohibited
Any communications that would be permitted by an international broadcast station
questions.x: The rule is a single sentence, and the answer quotes it nearly verbatim: transmissions to a different country are "limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and to remarks of a personal character." Look for that phrasing and pick it.

questions.q: What may happen if the FCC is unable to reach you by email?
a: Fine and suspension of operator license
Revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license
Revocation of access to the license record in the FCC system
Nothing; there is no such requirement
questions.x: Your grant has to show an email address the FCC can actually reach you at. Section 97.23 states plainly that undeliverable correspondence may result in revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license. Keep the address current after any move or provider change.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid Group D call sign format for Technician class?
questions.x: Group D covers Novice and Technician licensees and uses the 1x3 format: one letter, one numeral, three letters. KF1XXX fits. Count the characters on each choice and take the one shaped 1x3.
questions.xs: FCC sequential call sign system; 47 CFR §97.19

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true about using your amateur radio license when operating aboard a vessel or craft in international waters?
a: Amateur operation is prohibited in international waters
You may only operate during maritime emergencies
You need special FCC authorization for maritime mobile operation
You may operate from a US-documented vessel with the master's permission
questions.x: Section 97.5(a)(2) extends your authority to a vessel documented or registered in the United States, and §97.11(a) requires that installing and operating the station be approved by the master of the ship. Both conditions apply: a US-documented vessel, and the master's permission.

questions.q: How long before the expiration date may an amateur radio license renewal be requested?
questions.x: Renewal may be filed starting 90 days before the expiration date. Do not confuse this with the grace period, which is a separate two-year window that only opens after expiration. Ninety days before, two years after.

questions.q: What is the normal term for an FCC-issued amateur radio license?
questions.x: The rule is one line: "An amateur service license is normally granted for a 10-year term." Ten years, every class, with no exam to renew.

questions.q: What is the grace period for renewal if an amateur license expires?
questions.x: Once a license expires you get a two-year filing grace period to apply for renewal. Miss that window and you retake the exams. Pair it with the 90-day figure from T1C07: file 90 days early, or salvage it within 2 years.

questions.q: How soon after passing the examination for your first amateur radio license may you transmit on the amateur radio bands?
a: Immediately on receiving your Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE)
As soon as your operator/station license grant appears on the ARRL website
As soon as your operator/station license grant appears in the FCC’s license database
As soon as you receive your license in the mail from the FCC
questions.x: Passing the exam does not put you on the air. Your authority begins when the operator and station license grant appears in the FCC database. Check ULS, and once your call sign is there, transmit.

questions.q: If your license has expired and is still within the allowable grace period, may you continue to transmit on the amateur radio bands?
a: Yes, for up to two years
Yes, as soon as you apply for renewal
Yes, for up to one year
No, you must wait until the license has been renewed
questions.x: The grace period protects your call sign and lets you renew without retesting. It does not authorize transmitting. An expired license is an expired license, so you stay off the air until the renewal grant appears.

questions.q: With which countries are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations prohibited from exchanging communications?
a: Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications
Any country whose administration has notified the American Radio Relay League (ARRL) that it objects to such communications
Any country banned from such communications by the International Amateur Radio Union (IARU)
Any country banned from making such communications by the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
questions.x: You may work any country except one whose administration has told the ITU it objects to amateur communications with the United States. The objection has to be filed with the ITU, and the FCC publishes the list. Very few countries are on it, but that ITU notification is the test the question is after.

questions.q: Under which of the following circumstances are one-way transmissions by an amateur station prohibited?
a: Announcements of upcoming ham radio operating events
questions.x: Section 97.113(b) is blunt: an amateur station "shall not engage in any form of broadcasting." Other one-way transmissions such as beacons, telecommand and brief tuning are allowed where the rules name them. Broadcasting is the one that is always out.

questions.q: When is it permissible to transmit messages encoded to obscure their meaning?
a: Only when using a remote station during a contest
Only when transmitting certain approved digital codes
Only when transmitting control commands to space stations or model craft
questions.x: Encoding to hide meaning is prohibited, with two narrow exceptions. Section 97.211(b) lets a telecommand station send codes to a space station, and §97.215(b) says model craft control signals do not count as obscuring codes. Space stations and model craft: those are the only two.

questions.q: Under what conditions is an amateur station authorized to transmit music using a phone emission?
a: When incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications
When the music produces no spurious emissions
When transmissions are limited to less than three minutes per hour
When the music is transmitted above 1280 MHz
questions.x: Music by phone emission is prohibited except where this section allows it, and the one opening is in §97.113(c): retransmitting manned spacecraft communications, "including incidental music," with prior NASA approval. Music is only ever legal here as a byproduct of that retransmission.

questions.q: When may amateur radio operators use their stations to notify other amateurs of the availability of equipment for sale or trade?
a: When the equipment is not the personal property of either the station licensee, or the control operator, or their close relatives
When no profit is made on the sale
When selling amateur radio equipment and not on a regular basis
questions.x: You may tell other amateurs that gear is available for sale or trade, "provided that such activity is not conducted on a regular basis." Two conditions ride on this answer: it has to be equipment normally used in an amateur station, and it cannot become a routine business.

questions.q: What, if any, are the restrictions concerning transmission of language that may be considered indecent or obscene?
a: The FCC maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
questions.x: Obscene or indecent words or language appear on the prohibited list in §97.113(a)(4) with no exception, no time-of-day allowance, and no band where it becomes acceptable. When a question offers a conditional answer here, the flat prohibition is the right one.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an auxiliary station?
a: A station sending one-way transmissions between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter
A backup radio for emergency use in case the main station radio fails
A station used in the Military Auxiliary Radio System for linking government and amateur stations in a digital network
A second station utilized in multi-operator contest stations
questions.x: An auxiliary station carries communications point to point inside a system of cooperating amateur stations. A link feeding a remote receiver back to the main repeater transmitter is the textbook case. Section 97.201(b) restricts auxiliary stations to 2 meters and shorter.

questions.q: In which of the following circumstances may the control operator of an amateur station receive compensation for operating that station?
a: When the communication is related to the sale of amateur equipment by the control operator's employer
When the communication is a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution
When the communication is made to obtain emergency information for a local broadcast station
questions.x: Pay for operating is barred except in a few listed cases. The one here: a control operator may accept compensation "as an incident of a teaching position" when the station is used as part of classroom instruction at an educational institution. Teacher, classroom, part of instruction.

questions.q: When may amateur stations transmit information in support of broadcasting, program production, or news gathering, assuming no other means is available?
a: When such communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
When broadcasting communications to or from the space shuttle
Where non-commercial programming is gathered and supplied exclusively to the National Public Radio network
questions.x: Amateurs may not support program production or news gathering, with one carve-out: communications "directly related to the immediate safety of human life or the protection of property" where no other means is reasonably available at the time. Safety of life or property is the phrase to match.

questions.q: How does the FCC define broadcasting for the Amateur Radio Service?
a: Any transmission made by the licensed station
Transmission of messages directed only to amateur operators
Transmissions intended for reception by the general public
questions.x: The definition is short: "Broadcasting. Transmissions intended for reception by the general public, either direct or relayed." Intent and audience decide it. Whether anyone actually listens does not matter, and neither does the mode.

questions.q: When may an amateur station transmit without identifying on the air?
a: When the transmissions are of a brief nature to make station adjustments
When the transmitted power level is below 0.1 watt
When transmitting signals to control model craft
questions.x: Telecommand of model craft is the exception to identifying. Section 97.215(a) drops the identification requirement for transmissions directed only to the model, provided a label with your call sign and address is fixed to the transmitter. Note also §97.215(c): 1 watt maximum.

questions.q: Which of the following is required when making on-the-air test transmissions?
a: Conduct tests only between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. local time
Notify the FCC of the transmissions
questions.x: There is no such thing as an anonymous test transmission. Section 97.119(a) applies to everything you put on the air, so identify with your assigned call sign even when you are only checking an antenna or setting drive level.

questions.q: When may an amateur station transmit without a control operator?
a: When using automatic control, such as in the case of a repeater
When the station licensee is away and another licensed amateur is using the station
When the transmitting station is an auxiliary station
questions.x: Section 97.7 opens with it: "When transmitting, each amateur station must have a control operator." There is no exception anywhere in Part 97, including automatic control, where the control operator simply does not have to be at the control point. The answer is never.

questions.q: Who may be the control operator of a station communicating through an amateur satellite or space station?
a: Only an Amateur Extra Class operator
A General class or higher licensee with a satellite operator certification
Only an Amateur Extra Class operator who is also an AMSAT member
Any amateur allowed to transmit on the satellite uplink frequency
questions.x: Satellite work follows the same rule as everything else. If your license class authorizes the uplink frequency, you may be the control operator; if it does not, you may not. Check the uplink against your privileges and the question answers itself.

questions.q: Who must designate the station control operator?
questions.x: The station licensee designates the control operator. The FCC presumes the licensee is also the control operator unless station records document otherwise, which is why that presumption is worth remembering alongside this answer.

questions.q: What determines the transmitting frequency privileges of an amateur station?
a: The frequency authorized by the frequency coordinator
The frequencies printed on the license grant
The highest class of operator license held by anyone on the premises
The class of operator license held by the control operator
questions.x: Privileges follow the control operator's license class, not the station owner's and not the equipment's. An Extra may operate a Technician's station across Extra segments, and a Technician at an Extra's station is still held to Technician limits.

questions.q: What is an amateur station’s control point?
a: The location of the station’s transmitting antenna
The location of the station’s transmitting apparatus
The location at which the control operator function is performed
The mailing address of the station licensee
questions.x: Definition, word for word: "Control point. The location at which the control operator function is performed." It is where the operator does the controlling, which may be nowhere near the transmitter.

questions.q: When, other than during an emergency, may a Technician class licensee be the control operator of a station operating in an Amateur Extra Class band segment?
a: When designated as the control operator by an Amateur Extra Class licensee
As part of a multi-operator contest team
When using a club station whose trustee holds an Amateur Extra Class license
questions.x: Frequency privileges come from the control operator's license class, and no provision lets a Technician work an Extra-only segment. Not with an Extra present, not with permission, not for a special event. The answer is at no time.

questions.q: When the control operator is not the station licensee, who is responsible for the proper operation of the station?
a: All licensed amateurs who are present at the operation
The control operator and the station licensee
questions.x: When the two are different people, §97.103(a) makes "both persons equally responsible" for proper operation. Responsibility is shared rather than transferred, so the answer naming both the control operator and the station licensee is the one.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of automatic control?
a: Controlling a station over the internet
Using a computer or other device to send CW automatically
Using a computer or other device to identify automatically
questions.x: Automatic control means the station complies with the rules without a control operator present at the control point. A repeater is the everyday example, and §97.205(d) specifically authorizes repeaters to be automatically controlled.

questions.q: Which amateur stations may be remotely controlled?
questions.x: Section 97.109(c) is one line: "When a station is being remotely controlled, the control operator must be at the control point. Any station may be remotely controlled." Any station. Remote control carries no eligibility restriction, unlike automatic control.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of remote control as defined in Part 97?
a: Operating the station over the internet
Controlling a model aircraft, boat, or car by amateur radio
questions.x: Remote control is defined as a control operator who "indirectly manipulates the operating adjustments in the station through a control link." The internet is simply one kind of control link. You are still operating the radio yourself, just from somewhere else.

questions.q: What is a control operator as defined in Part 97?
a: The person speaking or otherwise communicating messages over an amateur station
The person who is the licensee of an amateur station
An amateur operator identified in the FCC database as responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at a station license location
An amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at that station
questions.x: Straight from the definitions: a control operator is "an amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for the transmissions from that station to assure compliance with the FCC Rules." Designated by the licensee, responsible for compliance.

questions.q: When must the station licensee make the station and the station records available for inspection?
a: At any time ten days after notification by the FCC of such an inspection
At any time upon request by an FCC representative
At any time after a written notification by the FCC of such inspection
Only when presented with a valid warrant by an FCC official or government agent
questions.x: The station licensee "must make the station and the station records available for inspection upon request by an FCC representative." No warrant, no advance notice, and no set hours in the rule. Upon request is the standard.

questions.q: How often must you identify with your FCC-assigned call sign when using tactical call signs such as “Race Headquarters”?
a: Never, the tactical call is sufficient
At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
At the end of every transmission
questions.x: Tactical calls like Race Headquarters or Net Control are fine for traffic handling, but they satisfy nothing legally. Your FCC-assigned call sign still has to go out at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it.

questions.q: When are you required to transmit your assigned call sign?
a: At the beginning of each contact, and every 10 minutes thereafter
At least once during each transmission
At least every 15 minutes during and at the end of a communication
At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
questions.x: The identification requirement is at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of each one. Note what is not required: you do not have to identify at the beginning. Ten minutes and at the end.

questions.q: What language must you use for identification when using a phone emission?
a: Any language recognized by the United Nations
Any language recognized by the ITU
questions.x: Identification by phone must be "by a phone emission in the English language." You may hold the entire rest of the contact in any language you like. The call sign itself goes out in English.

questions.q: What method of call sign identification is required for a station transmitting phone signals?
a: Send the call sign followed by the indicator RPT
Send the call sign using a CW or phone emission
Send the call sign followed by the indicator R
Send the call sign using only a phone emission
questions.x: A station running phone may identify by voice or by sending CW. Both are authorized under §97.119(b), and CW is permitted on any frequency the control operator may use. Look for the answer that allows either one.

questions.q: Which of the following self-assigned indicators are acceptable when using a phone transmission?
questions.x: Self-assigned indicators are allowed as long as they do not conflict with an indicator specified elsewhere in the rules or with a prefix assigned to another country. Common ones like /M, /P and /AG all qualify, which is why the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: Which of the following restrictions apply when a non-licensed person speaks to a foreign amateur radio station via a station under the control of an FCC-licensed amateur radio operator?
a: The person must be a U.S. citizen
The foreign station must be in a country with which the U.S. has a third-party agreement
The licensed control operator must do the station identification
questions.x: Third-party traffic with a foreign station requires a third-party agreement between the United States and that country, with an exception for emergency and disaster relief. Absent an agreement or an emergency, the unlicensed person cannot speak.

questions.q: What is the definition of third-party communications?
a: A message from a control operator to another amateur station control operator on behalf of another person
Amateur radio communications where three stations are in communications with one another
Operation when the transmitting equipment is licensed to a person other than the control operator
Temporary authorization for an unlicensed person to transmit on the amateur bands for technical experiments
questions.x: The definition names all three parties: a message from the control operator of one amateur station (first party) to the control operator of another (second party) on behalf of another person (third party). Count the parties in each choice and pick the one with all three.

questions.q: What type of amateur station simultaneously retransmits the signal of another amateur station on a different channel or channels?
questions.x: Definition: "Repeater. An amateur station that simultaneously retransmits the transmission of another amateur station on a different channel or channels." Simultaneously and on a different channel are what separate a repeater from a store-and-forward digipeater.

questions.q: Who is accountable if a repeater inadvertently retransmits communications that violate the FCC rules?
a: The control operator of the originating station
The control operator of the repeater
Both the originating station and the repeater owner
questions.x: Section 97.205(g) protects the repeater operator: the control operator of a repeater that inadvertently retransmits violative communications "is not accountable" for them. Accountability stays with whoever put the signal into the input, which is the originating station.

questions.q: Which of the following is a requirement for the issuance of a club station license grant?
a: The trustee must have an Amateur Extra Class operator license grant
The club must have at least four members
The club must be registered with the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
questions.x: A club station license needs at least four members and a trustee who holds an operator license. Four is the number the exam wants. The trustee is designated by a club officer and must be a licensed amateur.

questions.q: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 2-meter band?
questions.x: Standard 2-meter repeater offset is 600 kHz, plus or minus depending on where in the band the output sits. Your radio usually picks the direction automatically. Pair it with the 70 cm figure: 600 kHz on 2 meters, 5 MHz on 70 centimeters.

questions.q: What is the national calling frequency for FM simplex operations in the 2-meter band?
questions.x: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency, the channel to try when you want a direct contact without a repeater. It shows up on the Technician exam more than once, so commit the number.

questions.q: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 70-centimeter band?
questions.x: On 70 centimeters the standard offset is 5 MHz. The band is far wider than 2 meters, so a larger split is practical and keeps the repeater's own transmitter from desensing its receiver.

questions.q: What is an appropriate way to call another station on a repeater if you know the other station's call sign?
a: Say "break, break," then the other station’s call sign, followed by your call sign
Say the station's call sign, then identify with your call sign
Say "CQ" three times, then the other station's call sign, followed by your call sign
Wait for the station to call CQ, then answer with your call sign
questions.x: Give the other station's call sign, then your own. That is all a repeater contact needs. Long CQ calls are for HF; on a repeater people are monitoring and a short directed call gets answered faster.

questions.q: How should you respond to a station calling CQ?
a: Transmit "CQ" followed by the other station’s call sign
Transmit your call sign followed by the other station’s call sign
Transmit the other station’s call sign followed by your call sign
Transmit a signal report followed by your call sign
questions.x: Answer with their call sign first, then yours. Their call tells them you are replying to them rather than to someone else who called at the same moment, and your call tells them who you are.

questions.q: What is an effective way to seek a call from any phone station when not using a repeater?
a: Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call;” if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
Say “QTC,” followed by “this is” and your call sign; if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
Transmit an unmodulated carrier for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen; repeat as necessary
Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” and your call sign, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary
questions.x: Repeat CQ a few times, say "this is," give your call sign, then stop and listen. The rhythm matters: calling too long means you are transmitting while someone is trying to answer you.

questions.q: What does the term "repeater offset" mean?
a: The difference between a repeater’s transmit and receive frequencies
The repeater has a time delay to prevent interference
The approximately half-second delay to allow for the “squelch tail” to be removed
The fee charged by the repeater owner or club to provide for maintenance
questions.x: Offset is the difference between the repeater's transmit and receive frequencies. The repeater listens on one and talks on the other, and your radio shifts by the same amount in the opposite direction so the pair line up.

questions.q: What is the meaning of the procedural signal “CQ”?
a: A shortened form of the term “Contest QSO”
“Communication Quality,” used to indicate transmitted audio clarity
Only the called station should transmit
questions.x: CQ means calling any station. It is a general invitation to anyone listening rather than a call to a particular operator. When you want one specific station, use their call sign instead.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual

questions.q: Which of the following is a customary way to indicate a station is listening on a repeater and looking for a contact?
a: “CQ CQ” followed by the repeater’s call sign
The station’s call sign followed by the word “listening”
The repeater’s call sign followed by the station’s call sign
questions.x: Give your call sign followed by "listening." It tells the repeater's users that you are there and available without committing them to answer. Shorter and less intrusive than calling CQ, which is why it is the convention on FM.

questions.q: What is a band plan, beyond the privileges established by the FCC?
a: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band
A list of available net frequencies
A plan devised by a club to indicate frequency band usage
questions.x: A band plan is voluntary. It divides a band by mode and activity so weak-signal work, FM, satellites and digital modes stay out of each other's way. The FCC does not enforce it, but ignoring it counts against good amateur practice under §97.101(a).

questions.q: What term describes an amateur station that is transmitting and receiving on the same frequency?
questions.x: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on one frequency, talking directly to the other station with no repeater in between. Duplex is the opposite, with separate transmit and receive frequencies.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the reverse function on a VHF/UHF transceiver?
a: To listen on a repeater’s input frequency
To listen on a repeater’s output frequency
questions.x: Reverse swaps your transmit and receive frequencies so you hear the repeater's input instead of its output. Use it to find out whether you can hear the other station directly. If you can, you both might move to simplex and leave the repeater free.

questions.q: What term describes the use of a sub-audible tone transmitted along with normal voice audio to open the squelch of a receiver?
questions.x: CTCSS stands for Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System, a low-frequency tone sent under your voice that tells the repeater the signal is meant for it. Motorola's trade name PL is the same thing. The tone sits below the audio passband, so you never hear it.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a linked repeater network?
a: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network
A single repeater with more than one receiver
Multiple repeaters with the same control operator
A system of repeaters linked by APRS
questions.x: In a linked network, whatever one repeater receives goes out on all of them. That extends coverage across a region, so a handheld in one city can reach someone hundreds of miles away through the chain.

questions.q: Which of the following could be the reason you are unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear?
a: You are using the wrong CTCSS tone
You are using the wrong DCS code
questions.x: Hearing a repeater does not mean it can hear you. The usual causes are a wrong or missing CTCSS tone, an incorrect offset, or simply being too far away for your low-power signal to reach the input. All three are common, so the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: Which of the following would cause your FM transmission audio to drop out on voice peaks?
a: Your FM deviation is too low
Your transmit power is too high
questions.x: FM deviation follows your audio level, so talking too loudly drives deviation past what the system allows. The transmitter's limiter clamps the peaks and the receiver loses them, which sounds like your audio cutting out exactly when you get emphatic. Back off the mic.
questions.xs: TIA-603 deviation limits; FM modulation theory

questions.q: What type of signaling to a repeater uses two simultaneous audio tones?
questions.x: DTMF is Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency, the same tones a telephone keypad produces. Each button sends two tones at once, one from a row group and one from a column group, and the pair identifies the digit unambiguously.

questions.q: How can you join a digital repeater’s “talkgroup”?
a: Register with the local Frequency Coordinator
Register with the digital repeater control operator
Program your radio with the group’s ID or code
Program your radio with the DTMF tone used by the talkgroup
questions.x: Program the group's ID into your radio. A talkgroup is a numeric identifier rather than a frequency, so joining one is a configuration change, not a tuning change. You stay on the same repeater channel either way.

questions.q: Which of the following applies when two stations transmitting on the same frequency interfere with each other?
a: The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency
Both stations should choose another frequency to avoid conflict
Whichever station was on the frequency first has preemptive rights to the frequency
Use subaudible tones so both stations can share the frequency
questions.x: Part 97 settles this: licensees and control operators "must cooperate in selecting transmitting channels," and "no frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station." Nobody owns a frequency, so the two stations work it out between themselves.

questions.q: Why are simplex channels designated in the VHF/UHF band plans?
a: So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater
So stations with simple transmitters can access the repeater without automated offset
questions.x: Simplex channels give stations close enough to hear each other directly a place to go. A repeater covers a wide area, so two people a mile apart holding a long conversation through one blocks everybody else for no benefit.

questions.q: Which Q signal indicates that you are receiving interference from other stations?
questions.x: QRM is interference from other stations. Its partner QRN is natural noise such as static from lightning. Keep them straight: QRM is people, QRN is nature.

questions.q: Which Q signal indicates that you are changing frequency?
questions.x: QSY means changing frequency. As a question it asks whether you should change; as a statement it announces that you are. Do not confuse it with QSL, which is acknowledgment of receipt.

questions.q: What is the digital color code used on DMR repeater systems?
a: An access code which must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater
A code which automatically programs the repeater offset to a frequency chosen by the user
A code which identifies the specific CODEC being used so that the repeater can properly decode the audio
A code transmitted by the repeater to indicate health and status of the equipment
questions.x: The color code is a 4-bit access value carried in every DMR burst. Your radio's programmed code must match the repeater's or it will be ignored. It performs the same job for DMR that a CTCSS tone does for FM, keeping nearby systems on the same frequency from triggering each other.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a squelch function?
a: Reduce a CW transmitter's key clicks
Mute the receiver audio when a signal is not present
Eliminate parasitic oscillations in an RF amplifier
questions.x: Squelch mutes the receiver audio until a signal appears, sparing you a constant hiss between transmissions. Set it just past the point where the noise stops. Crank it higher than that and weak stations will not break through.
questions.xs: ARRL Operating Manual; FM receiver design

questions.q: Which of the following is a “talkgroup”?
a: A group of amateur radio operators who share email on a specific amateur radio topic
An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group aren’t bothered by other radio traffic
The members of a net organized for amateur radio operators with a specific common interest
A method of automatically alerting all group members to the frequency where any member is transmitting
questions.x: A talkgroup is a numeric identifier that sorts traffic on a shared digital system. Your radio only unmutes for the groups you have selected, so a single repeater carries many conversations while each user hears only the ones they signed up for.

questions.q: When do the FCC Part 97 Amateur Radio Service rules NOT apply to the operation of an amateur station?
questions.x: Part 97 applies at all times, with no exception for emergencies, drills or field operations. Sections 97.403 and 97.405 do not suspend the rules; they permit any means of radiocommunication when life or property is in immediate danger. Everything else still stands.

questions.q: Which of the following are typical duties of a Net Control Station?
a: Choose the regular net meeting time and frequency
Ensure that all stations checking into the net are properly licensed for operation on the net frequency
Call the net to order and direct communications between stations checking in
questions.x: Net control calls the net to order and directs who transmits and when. On a busy net a dozen stations may need to pass traffic, and without one station deciding the order, everyone doubles and nothing moves.

questions.q: What technique is used to ensure that voice messages containing unusual words are received correctly?
a: Send the words by voice and Morse code
Use the Q-code “QSR” to ask the receiving station to repeat the words back
Spell the words using a standard phonetic alphabet
questions.x: Spell the word using the standard phonetic alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie. Unusual names and street addresses are exactly where a listener's brain fills in the wrong word, and phonetics remove the guess.

questions.q: What is RACES?
a: An emergency organization combining amateur radio and citizens band operators and frequencies
A radio contest held in a short period, sometimes called a “sprint”
An FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies
questions.x: RACES is the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service, defined in Part 97 subpart E for civil defense communications during a national, regional or local emergency. It runs on amateur frequencies but under the direction of a civil defense organization.

questions.q: What does the term “traffic” refer to in net operation?
a: Formal messages exchanged by net stations
The number of stations checking in and out of a net
Operation by mobile or portable stations
A count of the number of activations of the net each month
questions.x: Traffic means formal messages passed between stations, typically radiograms with a set format. It is the business the net exists to move, as distinct from the conversation around it.

questions.q: What is the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)?
a: A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service
A group of licensed amateurs who are members of the military and who voluntarily agreed to provide message handling services in the case of an emergency
A training program that provides licensing courses for those interested in obtaining an amateur license to use during emergencies
A training program that certifies amateur operators for membership in the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service
questions.x: ARES is made up of licensed amateurs who have registered their skills and equipment with the ARRL for public service work. Membership is voluntary and open to any licensee willing to serve, with no government certification involved.

questions.q: Which of the following is standard practice when you participate in a net?
a: When first responding to the net control station, transmit your call sign, name, and address as in the FCC database
Record the time of each of your transmissions
Unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station
questions.x: Transmit only when net control directs you to, unless you have an emergency. That single discipline is what separates a net from a pile-up. A genuine emergency always overrides the order of business.

questions.q: Which of the following relays messages using email addresses based on amateur callsigns?
questions.x: Winlink moves email over radio using addresses built from amateur call signs. It lets stations exchange messages with the regular internet when local connectivity is gone, which is why it turns up in emergency work.

questions.q: Are amateur station control operators ever permitted to operate outside the frequency privileges of their license class?
a: Yes, but only when part of a FEMA emergency plan
Yes, but only when part of a RACES emergency plan
Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
questions.x: Yes, but only when human life or property is in immediate danger. Section 97.403 permits "any means of radiocommunication at its disposal" in that situation. It is a genuine emergency provision, not a convenience, and it does not cover drills.

questions.q: What information is contained in the preamble of a formal traffic message?
a: The email address of the originating station
The address of the intended recipient
The telephone number of the addressee
Information needed to track the message
questions.x: The preamble carries the handling data: message number, precedence, station of origin, check, place of origin, and time and date filed. None of it is the message itself. It is what lets any station in the chain track and account for the traffic.
questions.xs: ARRL National Traffic System radiogram format

questions.q: What is meant by “check” in a radiogram header?
a: The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message
The call sign of the originating station
A list of stations that have relayed the message
A box on the message form that indicates that the message was received and/or relayed
questions.x: Check is the count of words or word equivalents in the text. The receiving operator counts what they wrote down and compares. If the numbers disagree, something was lost or added and the message gets repeated.
questions.xs: ARRL National Traffic System radiogram format

questions.q: Which of the following requires certification by a civil defense agency?
questions.x: RACES is the one requiring certification. No station may transmit in RACES unless it is certified by a civil defense organization as registered with that organization. ARES asks only that you volunteer; RACES needs the served agency to enroll you first.

questions.q: Why do VHF signal strengths sometimes vary greatly when the antenna is moved only a few feet?
a: The signal path encounters different concentrations of water vapor
VHF ionospheric propagation is very sensitive to path length
Multipath propagation cancels or reinforces signals
The Doppler effect causes slight frequency shifts which result in changes in signal strength
questions.x: Your signal arrives by several paths at once, direct plus reflections off buildings and terrain. Those copies add or cancel depending on how their phases line up. At 2 meters a half wavelength is about a foot, so moving the antenna a few feet swings you from a null into a peak.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. P.1406; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: How does vegetation affect UHF and microwave signals?
a: Causes knife-edge diffraction, distorting voice peaks
Absorbs signals, leading to poor reception of weak signals
Amplifies signals, improving reception of weak signals
questions.x: Leaves and wet wood absorb RF, and the effect climbs sharply with frequency. At UHF and microwave a stand of trees can eat enough signal to drop a marginal path entirely. Strong signals survive; weak ones do not.

questions.q: What antenna polarization is normally used for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
questions.x: Weak-signal CW and SSB work above 50 MHz is horizontally polarized by convention. FM and repeaters use vertical. Mixing the two costs you signal, so match whatever the activity you are joining uses.

questions.q: What is the effect of antenna cross-polarization over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path?
questions.x: An antenna responds to the component of the field aligned with it. Cross-polarize the two ends of a line-of-sight path and much of the energy is simply not coupled, typically costing 20 dB or more. The signal weakens rather than disappearing.

questions.q: When using a directional antenna, how might your station be able to communicate with a distant repeater if buildings or obstructions are blocking the direct line of sight path?
a: Change from vertical to horizontal polarization
Try to find a path that reflects signals to the repeater
questions.x: VHF and UHF reflect well off buildings, water towers and hillsides. If the direct path is blocked, swing the beam off-axis and hunt for a surface that bounces you in. Aiming away from the repeater to work it feels wrong and often works.

questions.q: What is the meaning of the term “picket fencing”?
a: Alternating transmissions during a net operation
Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation
A type of ground system used with vertical antennas
Interference from cable TV in the form of carriers at fixed intervals across the band
questions.x: Picket fencing is the rapid flutter you hear from a moving vehicle. The car passes through multipath peaks and nulls in quick succession, chopping the signal at a rate that sounds like running a stick along a fence.

questions.q: What weather condition might decrease range at microwave frequencies?
questions.x: Above roughly 10 GHz, raindrops are a meaningful fraction of a wavelength and scatter and absorb the signal. Heavy precipitation can cut a microwave path badly. The same rain does essentially nothing at HF or VHF.

questions.q: What is a likely cause of irregular fading of signals propagated by the ionosphere?
a: Frequency shift due to Faraday rotation
Random combining of signals arriving via different paths
questions.x: Ionospheric signals reach you by more than one route, often with slightly different path lengths that shift as the layers move. Those copies drift in and out of phase, so the sum rises and falls irregularly. Same physics as VHF multipath, just on a far larger scale.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; ITU-R Rec. P.533

questions.q: Which of the following results from the fact that signals propagated by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized?
a: Either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception
Both the transmitting and receiving antennas must be of the same polarization
questions.x: The ionosphere twists the polarization of a passing wave, and what comes out is elliptical with a component in nearly every orientation. Because some energy is always available to either orientation, vertical or horizontal antennas both work on HF skip.

questions.q: What effect does multi-path propagation have on data transmissions?
a: Transmission rates must be increased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
Transmission rates must be decreased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
No significant changes will occur if the signals are transmitted using FM
Error rates are likely to increase
questions.x: Delayed copies of the signal smear one symbol into the next, which is intersymbol interference. The receiver starts misreading bits and the error rate climbs. It is why data modes struggle on paths that voice tolerates.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. P.1406; digital communications theory

questions.q: Which region of the atmosphere can reflect HF radio waves?
questions.x: The ionosphere, roughly 50 to 400 km up, where solar radiation strips electrons from gas atoms. Those free electrons bend HF waves back toward Earth. Strictly it is refraction rather than reflection, though the exam and everyday usage both say reflect.

questions.q: What effect does fog or rain have on 10-meter and 6-meter band signals?
questions.x: Little effect. At 28 and 50 MHz the wavelength is meters long while raindrops are millimeters, far too small to scatter the wave meaningfully. Weather only starts mattering to signal strength up in the microwave bands.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave?
questions.x: The electric and magnetic fields sit at right angles to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel. That geometry falls straight out of Maxwell's equations and holds for every electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: What property of a radio wave defines its polarization?
a: The orientation of the electric field
The orientation of the magnetic field
The ratio of the energy in the magnetic field to the energy in the electric field
The ratio of the velocity to the wavelength
questions.x: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric field. Vertical electric field means a vertically polarized wave. The magnetic field is always perpendicular to it, so naming one fixes the other.

questions.q: What are the two components of a radio wave?
questions.x: An electric field and a magnetic field, each regenerating the other as the wave travels. Neither exists alone in a propagating wave, which is exactly why it is called electromagnetic.

questions.q: What is the velocity of a radio wave traveling through free space?
questions.x: Radio waves are light, so they travel at c, about 300,000,000 meters per second in free space. Nothing about being invisible makes them slower. In coaxial cable the speed drops, which is what velocity factor accounts for.

questions.q: What is the relationship between wavelength and frequency?
a: Wavelength gets longer as frequency increases
Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases
Wavelength is constant at all frequencies
Wavelength and frequency increase as path length increases
questions.x: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related through c = f times lambda. Since c is fixed, raising frequency shortens wavelength. That is why 2 meters is a much higher frequency than 80 meters.

questions.q: What is the formula for converting frequency to approximate wavelength in meters?
a: Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz multiplied by 300
Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz divided by 300
Wavelength in meters equals frequency in megahertz divided by 300
Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz
questions.x: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in MHz. The 300 comes from the speed of light expressed as 300 million meters per second divided by a million. Check it: 300 over 146 MHz is about 2 meters.

questions.q: In addition to frequency, which of the following is used to identify amateur radio bands?
