questions.x: Amateur bands carry a wavelength nickname alongside their frequency range. The 146 MHz band is 2 meters, 28 MHz is 10 meters, and so on. Run 300 divided by the frequency and the band name appears.

questions.q: What frequency range is referred to as VHF?
questions.x: Part 97 defines it outright: "VHF (very high frequency). The frequency range 30-300 MHz." The 2-meter and 6-meter bands both live here. Each band above it starts where the last one ends, at ten times the frequency.

questions.q: What frequency range is referred to as UHF?
questions.x: From the same definitions list: "UHF (ultra high frequency). The frequency range 300-3000 MHz." That covers the 70-centimeter band. Note the decade pattern: HF 3 to 30 MHz, VHF 30 to 300, UHF 300 to 3000.

questions.q: What frequency range is referred to as HF?
questions.x: "HF (high frequency). The frequency range 3-30 MHz." This is the skip territory, holding 80 through 10 meters. Learn the three ranges as one chain and all three questions come free.

questions.q: What is the approximate velocity of a radio wave in free space?
questions.x: About 300,000,000 meters per second, which is 3 times 10 to the eighth. The precise figure is 299,792,458 m/s, and rounding to 300 million is what makes the 300 divided by frequency shortcut work.

questions.q: Which of these frequencies travels at the highest velocity in free space?
a: All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity
questions.x: They all travel at the same speed. In free space c does not depend on frequency, so a 1.8 MHz signal and a 10 GHz signal arrive together. Frequency changes wavelength, never velocity.

questions.q: Why are simplex UHF signals rarely heard beyond their radio horizon?
a: They are too weak to go very far
FCC regulations prohibit them from going more than 50 miles
UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere
UHF signals are absorbed by the ionospheric D region
questions.x: UHF passes straight through the ionosphere instead of bending back down. Without that return path you are limited to what the horizon allows, so a simplex UHF contact ends where line of sight does.

questions.q: What is a characteristic of HF communication compared with communications on VHF and higher frequencies?
a: Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF
There is less atmospheric interference (static) on HF
questions.x: HF signals refract off the ionosphere and come back to Earth hundreds or thousands of miles away. That skip is routine on HF and rare above it, which is the main practical difference between the two.

questions.q: What is one characteristic of VHF signals received via auroral backscatter?
a: They are often received from 10,000 miles or more
They are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound
They occur only during winter nighttime hours
They are generally strongest when your antenna is aimed west
questions.x: Aurora scatters VHF signals off rapidly moving, uneven curtains of ionized gas. The constant motion Doppler-smears the signal, leaving CW with a rough buzz and SSB barely intelligible. That raspy sound is the giveaway.

questions.q: Which of the following types of propagation is most commonly associated with occasional strong signals on the 10-, 6-, and 2-meter bands from beyond the radio horizon?
questions.x: Sporadic E is the usual explanation for sudden strong openings on 10, 6 and 2 meters. Dense patches form in the E region around 60 miles up and reflect signals well above the frequencies the ionosphere normally returns. They come and go without warning.

questions.q: Which of the following effects may allow radio signals to travel beyond obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations?
questions.x: A wave passing a sharp edge such as a ridgeline or a building corner bends slightly around it and re-radiates into the shadow behind. Knife-edge diffraction is why a station tucked behind a hill can still be workable.

questions.q: What type of propagation is responsible for allowing over-the-horizon VHF and UHF communications to ranges of approximately 300 miles on a regular basis?
questions.x: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals in a layer of the lower atmosphere that guides them like a waveguide. Paths of 300 miles or more open up, most often over water and in stable weather.

questions.q: What band is best suited for communicating via meteor scatter?
questions.x: Six meters is the sweet spot for meteor scatter. Lower frequencies suffer too much ordinary ionospheric interference, higher ones reflect poorly off the brief ionized trails. Bursts last from a fraction of a second to a few seconds.

questions.q: What causes tropospheric ducting?
a: Discharges of lightning during electrical storms
questions.x: A temperature inversion puts warm air above cool air, reversing the normal gradient. The sharp change in refractive index at that boundary bends signals back down instead of letting them escape, forming the duct.

questions.q: What is generally the best time for long-distance 10-meter band propagation via the F region?
a: From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of high sunspot activity
From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of high sunspot activity
From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of low sunspot activity
From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of low sunspot activity
questions.x: Ten meters via the F region works from dawn until shortly after sunset, and only when sunspot numbers are high. The band depends on solar ultraviolet to ionize the F layer enough to bend 28 MHz, so it usually closes after dark.
questions.xs: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ARRL Handbook

questions.q: Which of the following bands may provide long-distance communications via the ionosphere’s F region during the peak of the sunspot cycle?
questions.x: At solar maximum the F region ionizes strongly enough to return 10 meters and sometimes even 6. Both bands go quiet at the bottom of the cycle. The sunspot count is what decides whether they open.
questions.xs: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ARRL Handbook

questions.q: Why is the radio horizon for VHF and UHF signals more distant than the visual horizon?
a: Radio signals move somewhat faster than the speed of light
Radio waves are not blocked by dust particles
The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly
Radio waves are blocked by dust particles
questions.x: Air density falls with altitude, so a radio wave bends gently downward as it travels, following the curve of the Earth a little way past where light would leave. Engineers model it as a 4/3 Earth radius, putting the radio horizon roughly 15 percent farther out.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. P.834 (4/3 Earth radius model)

questions.q: Which of the following is an appropriate power supply rating for a typical 50-watt output mobile FM transceiver?
questions.x: Mobile gear runs on a nominal 13.8 volts, matching a car's charging system rather than the 12 V battery label. A 50-watt final is only about half efficient, so it pulls near 150 watts from the supply. Divide by 13.8 and you land around 11 amps, which is why 12 A is the sensible rating.

questions.q: Which of the following should be considered when selecting an accessory SWR meter?
a: The frequency and power level at which the measurements will be made
The distance that the meter will be located from the antenna
The maximum SWR anticipated on the transmission line
The ability of the meter to compensate for a poor transmission line match to the antenna
questions.x: An SWR meter is built for a frequency range and a power range, and it reads wrong outside either. A meter made for HF will not measure 440 MHz, and a QRP meter reading 100 watts may be damaged. Match both to your station.

questions.q: Why are short, heavy-gauge wires used for a transceiver’s DC power connection?
a: To minimize voltage drop when transmitting
To provide a close match to the power supply output impedance
To minimize radiative losses in the power cable
questions.x: At 12 amps even a small wire resistance costs real voltage, because the drop is current times resistance. Long or thin wire starves the radio on transmit peaks, which shows up as low power or a reset. Short and thick keeps the resistance negligible.

questions.q: How are the audio input and output of a transceiver connected in a station configured to operate using FT8?
a: To a computer running a terminal program and connected to a terminal node controller unit
To the audio output and input of a computer running FT8 software
To an FT8 conversion unit, a keyboard, and a computer monitor
To a computer connected to the FT8converter.com website
questions.x: FT8 is generated and decoded in software, so the radio's audio output feeds the computer's input and the computer's output feeds the radio's mic input. The sound card does the modulating and demodulating; the radio just moves the audio to and from RF.

questions.q: Where should an RF power meter be installed?
a: In the feed line, between the transmitter and antenna
In parallel with the push-to-talk line and the antenna
In the power supply cable, as close as possible to the radio
questions.x: Put it in the feed line between transmitter and antenna, because that is the only place the forward and reflected power actually exist. A meter anywhere else is not measuring what reaches the antenna.

questions.q: What signals are used in a computer-radio interface for digital mode operation?
a: Receive and transmit mode, status, and location
Receive audio, transmit audio, and transmitter keying
NMEA GPS location and DC power
questions.x: Three signals: audio out of the radio into the computer, audio out of the computer into the radio, and a keying line to switch the transmitter on. Two audio paths and one control line. Modern USB interfaces bundle all three into one cable.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the connections required between a computer and a transceiver to operate digital modes?
a: Computer “line in” to transceiver speaker connector
Computer “line out” to transceiver speaker connector
questions.x: Receive audio flows from the transceiver's speaker or headphone jack into the computer's line input. That is the path the decoding software listens on. The return path runs the other way, computer output into the radio's microphone or accessory input.

questions.q: Which of the following conductors is preferred for bonding at RF?
a: Copper braid removed from coaxial cable
questions.x: RF current rides on the surface of a conductor rather than through its middle, so what matters is surface area and low inductance, not cross-sectional area. Flat strap gives you far more perimeter and less inductance per foot than round wire of the same weight.

questions.q: How can you determine the length of time that equipment can be powered from a battery?
a: Divide the watt-hour rating of the battery by the peak power consumption of the equipment
Divide the battery ampere-hour rating by the average current draw of the equipment
Multiply the watts per hour consumed by the equipment by the battery power rating
Multiply the square of the current rating of the battery by the input resistance of the equipment
questions.x: Ampere-hours divided by amps leaves hours. A 20 Ah battery feeding a 2 A load runs about 10 hours on paper. Real batteries deliver less under heavy load and in the cold, so treat the figure as an upper bound.

questions.q: What function does a digital mode hotspot perform for nearby transceivers?
a: Communication with a digital voice or data network
FT8 digital communications via AFSK using a smartphone connected to the internet
RTTY encoding and decoding without a computer
High-speed digital communications for meteor scatter
questions.x: A hotspot is a low-power digital transceiver that bridges your handheld to a digital voice network over your internet connection. It covers your house, not your county. The reach comes from the network, not from RF.

questions.q: Where should the negative power return of a mobile transceiver be connected in a vehicle?
a: To the shell of the power connector
To any metal part of the vehicle
questions.x: Run the negative lead back to the battery's chassis ground rather than picking up a convenient sheet metal screw. Body panels are joined by welds and bolts that make poor, noisy RF connections, and the resulting voltage drop shows up as alternator whine in your audio.

questions.q: What is an electronic keyer?
a: A device for switching antennas from transmit to receive
A device for voice activated switching from receive to transmit
A device that assists in manual sending of Morse code
An interlock to prevent unauthorized use of a radio
questions.x: An electronic keyer turns paddle movements into properly timed dots and dashes at a set speed. You still send the code yourself; the keyer handles the timing so the character spacing stays even.

questions.q: What is the effect of excessive microphone gain on SSB transmissions?
questions.x: Too much microphone gain drives the transmitter past its linear range, so the output no longer follows the input. The result is distorted audio and splatter onto neighboring frequencies. Set gain by ALC indication rather than by ear.

questions.q: Which of the following can be used to enter a transceiver’s operating frequency?
questions.x: Either the keypad or the VFO knob will do it. Direct entry gets you to a known frequency instantly; the knob is for tuning around and finding what is there. Most radios offer both because the two tasks are different.

questions.q: How is squelch adjusted so that a weak FM signal can be heard?
a: Set the squelch threshold so that receiver output audio is on all the time
Turn up the audio level until it overcomes the squelch threshold
questions.x: Squelch mutes audio below a threshold, so a weak signal that fails to cross it never reaches the speaker. Back the control off until the receiver hisses continuously and the weak station comes through. You trade quiet for sensitivity.

questions.q: What does an FM signal sound like when received slightly off frequency?
a: There is no effect except for reduction in amplitude
questions.x: An FM detector converts frequency shifts to audio using a response curve centered on the carrier. Tune slightly off and the signal sits on a nonlinear part of that curve, so the recovered audio comes out distorted.

questions.q: What does the scanning function of an FM transceiver do?
a: Tunes through a range of frequencies to check for activity
Tunes through a range of frequencies to determine the antenna’s resonant frequency
questions.x: Scanning steps the receiver through a range of frequencies or memory channels, pausing when it finds a signal that breaks squelch. It is how you find activity without turning the knob yourself.

questions.q: Which of the following controls could be used if the voice pitch of a single-sideband signal returning to your CQ call seems too high or low?
questions.x: RIT, also labeled Clarifier, shifts your receive frequency slightly without moving your transmit frequency. Voice pitch on SSB depends on how closely the two stations are tuned, so a small nudge brings a high or low sounding voice back to natural.

questions.q: What is a DMR “code plug”?
a: An adapter cable used to connect a DMR radio to a computer for internet access
Configuration data loaded onto your radio to access repeaters and talkgroups
An upgrade to DMR programming software provided by the radio manufacturer to accommodate new radio models
A Coder-Decoder (CODEC) that converts analog voice data to DMR digital data and vice versa
questions.x: A code plug is the configuration file loaded into a DMR radio: channels, frequencies, color codes, talkgroups and contacts. Nothing works until it is programmed, which is why DMR users trade code plugs for their local systems.

questions.q: What is the advantage of having a choice of receiver filter bandwidths in a multimode transceiver?
a: Permits monitoring several modes simultaneously by selecting a separate filter for each mode
Permits noise or interference reduction by selecting a bandwidth matching the mode
Increases the number of frequencies that can be stored in memory
Increases the amount of offset between receive and transmit frequencies
questions.x: Noise arrives across the whole passband while the signal occupies only part of it, so a filter matched to the mode admits the signal and rejects the rest. CW needs a few hundred hertz, SSB a couple of kilohertz. Using the right one is often worth more than more antenna.

questions.q: How is a specific group of stations selected on a DMR digital voice transceiver?
a: By retrieving the frequencies from transceiver memory
By enabling the group’s CTCSS tone
By entering the group’s identification code
By inserting a five-pin, pre-programmed code plug
questions.x: Enter the group's identification code. A DMR talkgroup is a number rather than a frequency, so selecting one is a matter of telling the radio which ID to unmute for. Everyone stays on the same channel.

questions.q: Which of the following receiver filter bandwidths provides the best signal-to-noise ratio for SSB reception?
questions.x: Communications-quality SSB voice occupies roughly 2.4 kHz, so a 2400 Hz filter passes the intelligence and rejects everything else. Go wider and you let in noise you do not need; go much narrower and the voice starts sounding muffled.

questions.q: Which of the following must be programmed into a D-STAR digital transceiver before transmitting?
questions.x: D-STAR sends your call sign as digital data in every transmission, so the radio must be programmed with it before it will transmit properly. The network uses that call sign for routing, which is why it is not optional the way a memory label is.

questions.q: Electrical current is measured in which of the following units?
questions.x: Current is measured in amperes, usually shortened to amps. One ampere is a specific number of electrons flowing past a point each second. In Ohm's law it is the letter I, which trips people up until you have seen it a few times.

questions.q: Electrical power is measured in which of the following units?
questions.x: Power is measured in watts. One watt is one joule of energy per second, which is why power always describes a rate rather than an amount. Volts times amps gives you watts in a DC circuit.

questions.q: What is the term for the flow of electrons in an electric circuit?
questions.x: Electron flow through a circuit is called current. Think of the three basics as a set: voltage pushes, current flows, resistance opposes.

questions.q: What term describes the number of times per second that an alternating current makes a complete cycle?
questions.x: Frequency is the count of complete cycles per second. One cycle takes the waveform positive, back through zero, negative, and back to the start. Sixty cycles per second is 60 hertz.

questions.q: A difference in which of the following causes electron flow?
questions.x: A difference in voltage, also called potential difference, is what makes electrons move. No difference means no flow, no matter how good the conductor. Voltage is the push behind the current.

questions.q: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.x: The hertz, named for Heinrich Hertz, who first demonstrated radio waves. One hertz is one cycle per second, so 7 MHz means seven million cycles every second.

questions.q: Why are metals generally good conductors of electricity?
a: They have relatively high Young’s modulus values
questions.x: Metal atoms hold their outermost electrons loosely, leaving a sea of free electrons that drift when voltage is applied. Insulators bind their electrons tightly, so nothing moves. Free electrons are what conduction requires.

questions.q: Which of the following is a good electrical insulator?
questions.x: Glass holds its electrons tightly and conducts essentially nothing, which is why it appears in antenna standoffs and high-voltage insulators. Metals do the opposite.

questions.q: Which of the following describes alternating current?
a: Current that alternates between a positive direction and zero
Current that alternates between a negative direction and zero
Current that alternates between positive and negative directions
questions.x: Alternating current reverses direction repeatedly, flowing one way then the other. Direct current keeps going the same way. House wiring and radio signals are AC; a battery supplies DC.

questions.q: Which term describes the rate at which electrical energy is used?
questions.x: Power is the rate at which energy gets used, measured in watts. Energy is the total consumed over time. Your radio draws 100 watts of power; running it an hour consumes 100 watt-hours of energy.

questions.q: What type of current flow is opposed by resistance?
questions.x: Resistance opposes both AC and DC alike. A 50-ohm resistor is 50 ohms either way. Reactance, from capacitors and inductors, is the property that behaves differently with AC, and it is not the same thing as resistance.

questions.q: How many milliamperes is 1.5 amperes?
questions.x: Milli means one thousandth, so multiply by 1000 going from amperes to milliamperes: 1.5 A is 1500 mA. Moving to a smaller unit always makes the number bigger.

questions.q: Which is equal to 1,500,000 hertz?
questions.x: Kilo means a thousand, so divide by 1000: 1,500,000 Hz becomes 1500 kHz. Divide again and you get 1.5 MHz, which is the same frequency written a third way.

questions.q: Which is equal to one kilovolt?
questions.x: Kilo is a thousand, so a kilovolt is 1000 volts. The same prefix works everywhere: kilohertz, kilowatt, kilometer all mean a thousand of the base unit.

questions.q: Which is equal to one microvolt?
questions.x: Micro means one millionth, so a microvolt is one millionth of a volt. That is the scale of signals arriving at your receiver's antenna terminals, which is why receiver sensitivity is quoted in microvolts.

questions.q: Which is equal to 500 milliwatts?
questions.x: Milli is one thousandth, so divide by 1000: 500 mW is 0.5 watts. Handheld radios on low power and QRP rigs live in this range.

questions.q: Which is equal to 3000 milliamperes?
questions.x: Divide milliamperes by 1000 to reach amperes: 3000 mA is 3 A. Same conversion as T5B01, run the other direction.

questions.q: Which is equal to 3.525 MHz?
questions.x: Multiply MHz by 1000 to get kHz: 3.525 MHz is 3525 kHz. This one is worth knowing cold, since 3.525 MHz is the bottom of the Technician CW segment on 80 meters.

questions.q: Which is equal to 1,000,000 picofarads?
questions.x: Pico is a trillionth and micro is a millionth, six decimal places apart. So a million picofarads makes 1 microfarad. Capacitor values run small enough that pF and uF are the units you actually see.

questions.q: Which decibel value most closely represents a power increase from 5 watts to 10 watts?
questions.x: Doubling power is always 3 dB, whatever the starting point. 5 to 10 watts is a doubling, so 3 dB. Worth memorizing alongside its opposite: halving power is minus 3 dB.

questions.q: Which decibel value most closely represents a power decrease from 12 watts to 3 watts?
questions.x: From 12 to 3 watts is one quarter the power, which is two halvings. Each halving costs 3 dB, so the total is minus 6 dB. The minus sign matters, since power went down.

questions.q: Which decibel value represents a power increase from 20 watts to 200 watts?
questions.x: A ten times change is 10 dB, so 20 to 200 watts is 10 dB. Two rules cover nearly every decibel question on this exam: doubling is 3 dB, ten times is 10 dB.

questions.q: Which is equal to 28400 kHz?
questions.x: Divide kHz by 1000 to reach MHz: 28400 kHz is 28.400 MHz. That frequency sits in the Technician phone segment on 10 meters, between 28.300 and 28.500.

questions.q: Which is equal to 2425 MHz?
questions.x: Giga is a billion, so divide MHz by 1000: 2425 MHz is 2.425 GHz. This lands in the 13-centimeter band, shared with Wi-Fi and microwave ovens.

questions.q: What describes the ability to store energy in an electric field?
questions.x: Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field, which a capacitor does between two plates separated by an insulator. Its partner is inductance, which stores energy in a magnetic field instead.

questions.q: What is the unit of capacitance?
questions.x: The farad, named for Michael Faraday. A full farad is enormous, so practical parts are marked in microfarads or picofarads.

questions.q: What describes the ability to store energy in a magnetic field?
questions.x: Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field, which is what a coil of wire does when current flows through it. Electric field means capacitance; magnetic field means inductance.

questions.q: What is the unit of inductance?
questions.x: The henry, named for Joseph Henry. Like the farad it is a large unit, so you will see millihenries and microhenries on real components.

questions.q: What is the unit of impedance?
questions.x: Impedance is measured in ohms, the same unit as resistance, because both describe opposition to current. That shared unit is why a 50-ohm feed line matches a 50-ohm antenna.

questions.q: What is the abbreviation for kilohertz?
questions.x: kHz, with a lowercase k and a capital H. The capital H honors Hertz as a person's name, and SI uses a small k for kilo. Case is not decorative here.

questions.q: What is the abbreviation for megahertz?
questions.x: MHz, capital M and capital H. The capital M distinguishes mega from milli, which uses a lowercase m. Mixing them up changes the value by a factor of a billion.

questions.q: What formula is used to calculate electrical power (P) in a DC circuit?
questions.x: Power equals current times voltage, P = I x E. The PIE memory wheel holds all three arrangements: cover P and you get I times E, cover I and you get P over E.

questions.q: How much power is delivered by a voltage of 13.8 volts DC and a current of 10 amperes?
questions.x: Multiply volts by amps: 13.8 x 10 = 138 watts. This is the everyday case of a mobile radio on a 13.8-volt supply, so the numbers are worth recognizing.

questions.q: How much power is delivered by a voltage of 12 volts DC and a current of 2.5 amperes?
questions.x: 12 volts times 2.5 amperes gives 30 watts. Straight multiplication, no rearranging needed when the question hands you both volts and amps.

questions.q: How much current is required to deliver 120 watts at a voltage of 12 volts DC?
questions.x: Rearrange P = I x E into I = P / E, then divide: 120 watts over 12 volts is 10 amperes. When the question gives you power and asks for current, divide by the voltage.

questions.q: What is impedance?
a: The opposition to AC current flow
The power handling capability of a component
questions.x: Impedance is the total opposition to alternating current, combining plain resistance with reactance from capacitance and inductance. Reactance varies with frequency, which is why impedance does too.

questions.q: What formula is used to calculate current in a circuit?
questions.x: I = E / R. Current equals voltage divided by resistance. The Ohm's law triangle has E on top with I and R below, so covering the quantity you want shows the arithmetic.

questions.q: What formula is used to calculate voltage in a circuit?
questions.x: E = I x R. Voltage equals current times resistance. With E on top of the triangle, the two below multiply together.

questions.q: What formula is used to calculate resistance in a circuit?
questions.x: R = E / I. Resistance equals voltage divided by current. All three forms are the same equation rearranged, so learning the triangle once covers every version.

questions.q: What is the resistance of a circuit in which a current of 3 amperes flows when connected to 90 volts?
questions.x: Resistance wanted, so divide voltage by current: 90 volts over 3 amperes is 30 ohms. Sanity check by working backward, since 3 amps through 30 ohms does give 90 volts.

questions.q: What is the resistance of a circuit for which the applied voltage is 12 volts and the current flow is 1.5 amperes?
questions.x: 12 volts divided by 1.5 amperes gives 8 ohms. Fractional currents make people reach for a calculator, but 12 over 1.5 is the same as 24 over 3.

questions.q: What is the resistance of a circuit that draws 4 amperes from a 12-volt source?
questions.x: Divide 12 volts by 4 amperes for 3 ohms. Note the phrasing: drawing 4 amperes from a 12-volt source is the same information as 12 volts across the circuit.

questions.q: What is the current in a circuit with an applied voltage of 120 volts and a resistance of 80 ohms?
questions.x: Current wanted, so divide voltage by resistance: 120 over 80 is 1.5 amperes. When the answer lands between whole numbers, that is usually a sign you divided in the right order.

questions.q: What is the current through a 100-ohm resistor connected across 200 volts?
questions.x: 200 volts across 100 ohms gives 2 amperes. Connected across simply means the full voltage appears at the resistor's terminals.

questions.q: What is the current through a 24-ohm resistor connected across 240 volts?
questions.x: 240 volts over 24 ohms is 10 amperes. The tidy numbers here make it a good place to check that you are dividing volts by ohms rather than the reverse.

questions.q: What is the voltage across a 2-ohm resistor if a current of 0.5 amperes flows through it?
questions.x: Voltage wanted, so multiply: 0.5 amperes times 2 ohms is 1 volt. Small currents through small resistances produce small voltages, which is the sanity check on this one.

questions.q: What is the voltage across a 10-ohm resistor if a current of 1 ampere flows through it?
questions.x: 1 ampere through 10 ohms gives 10 volts. Multiplying by one keeps this simple, and it makes the pattern for the next question obvious.

questions.q: What is the voltage across a 10-ohm resistor if a current of 2 amperes flows through it?
questions.x: 2 amperes through 10 ohms is 20 volts. Same resistor as T5D11 with twice the current, so twice the voltage. That proportionality is Ohm's law in one line.

questions.q: In which type of circuit is the current always the same through all components?
questions.x: Series. One path means every electron passes through every component, so the current is identical everywhere. What differs in a series circuit is the voltage across each part.

questions.q: In which type of circuit is the voltage always the same across all components?
questions.x: Parallel. Each branch connects to the same two points, so each sees the same voltage. Current divides among the branches according to their resistances. Series shares current, parallel shares voltage.

questions.q: What electrical component opposes the flow of current in a DC circuit?
questions.x: A resistor opposes current, and how strongly is its resistance in ohms. It is the component you add when a circuit would otherwise pass more current than something downstream can survive.

questions.q: What type of component is often used as an adjustable volume control?
questions.x: A potentiometer is a resistor with a movable contact that taps somewhere along its element. Turning the shaft moves that tap, which is why it works as a volume control. Same part, different name: a variable resistor.

questions.q: What electrical parameter is controlled by a potentiometer?
questions.x: Resistance. The wiper slides along a resistive track, changing how much of that track sits in the circuit. Everything else follows from that, since changing resistance is what changes the voltage or current you are adjusting.

questions.q: What electrical component stores energy in an electric field?
questions.x: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between two plates. Its partner is the inductor, which stores energy magnetically. Electric field means capacitor, every time.

questions.q: What type of electrical component consists of conductive surfaces separated by an insulator?
questions.x: Two conductive surfaces separated by an insulator is the physical description of a capacitor. The insulator is called the dielectric, and no current flows through it. Energy is held in the field across the gap.

questions.q: What type of electrical component stores energy in a magnetic field?
questions.x: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field. Current through a wire creates that field, and winding the wire into a coil concentrates it. Magnetic field means inductor.

questions.q: What electrical component is typically constructed as a coil of wire?
questions.x: An inductor is literally a coil of wire, sometimes wound on a core to strengthen the field. That coiled shape is exactly how it is drawn on a schematic, which makes it one of the easier symbols to recognize.

questions.q: What is the function of an SPDT switch?
a: A single circuit is opened or closed
Two circuits are opened or closed
A single circuit is switched between one of two other circuits
Two circuits are each switched between one of two other circuits
questions.x: Read the name as a description. Single-pole means one common input; double-throw means it can connect to either of two outputs. So one circuit gets routed to one of two destinations.

questions.q: What type of switch is represented by component 3 in figure T-2?
questions.x: Component 3 shows two terminals with a single hinged lever between them. One contact in, one contact out, one moving arm, so single-pole single-throw. A double-throw switch would show a second contact for the lever to reach.

questions.q: Which of the following battery chemistries is rechargeable?
questions.x: Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion and lead-acid are all rechargeable, so the inclusive answer is right. These are the chemistries in handhelds, battery packs and station backup supplies precisely because they can be cycled.

questions.q: Which of the following battery chemistries is not rechargeable?
questions.x: Carbon-zinc is the classic disposable cell, and its chemical reaction does not usefully reverse. Trying to charge one risks leaking or rupturing it. It is the odd one out among the chemistries this pool asks about.

questions.q: Which is true about forward voltage drop in a diode?
a: It is lower in some diode types than in others
It is proportional to peak inverse voltage
It indicates that the diode is defective
It has no impact on the voltage delivered to the load
questions.x: Forward voltage depends on the semiconductor material. Ordinary silicon diodes drop about 0.7 volts, germanium closer to 0.3, and Schottky types lower still. Since it varies by type, the answer that says so is correct.

questions.q: What electronic component allows current to flow in only one direction?
questions.x: A diode conducts in one direction and blocks the other. That one-way behavior is what makes rectifiers possible, turning alternating current into current that flows only one way.

questions.q: Which of these components can be used as an electronic switch?
questions.x: A transistor works as a switch when driven hard between fully off and fully on. A small base or gate current controls a much larger current, with no moving parts and switching speeds no mechanical switch can touch.

questions.q: Which of the following components can consist of three regions of semiconductor material?
questions.x: A bipolar transistor is three regions of doped semiconductor, either NPN or PNP. The three regions give it its three leads, and the thin middle region is what lets a small current control a large one.

questions.q: What type of transistor has a gate, drain, and source?
questions.x: Gate, drain and source belong to the field-effect transistor. A bipolar transistor uses emitter, base and collector instead. Learn the two sets as pairs and either question gives you the other.

questions.q: How is the cathode lead of a semiconductor diode often marked on the package?
questions.x: A stripe on the body marks the cathode end. On the schematic symbol the cathode is the bar the triangle points into, so the painted stripe matches the drawn bar. Conventional current flows into the triangle and out past the stripe.

questions.q: What causes a light-emitting diode (LED) to emit light?
questions.x: Forward current makes an LED light. Electrons crossing the junction release their energy as photons instead of heat, and the semiconductor material sets the color. Reverse the polarity and it simply stays dark.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation FET stand for?
questions.x: Field Effect Transistor. The name describes how it works: voltage on the gate creates an electric field that widens or pinches the channel current flows through. The gate draws almost no current, unlike a bipolar transistor's base.

questions.q: What are the names for the electrodes of a diode?
questions.x: Anode and cathode. Current enters at the anode and leaves at the cathode when the diode is forward biased. The cathode is the striped end on the part and the bar on the symbol.

questions.q: Which of the following can provide power gain?
questions.x: A transistor provides power gain, using a small input signal to control a much larger output drawn from the power supply. Transformers can raise voltage but never add power. Only an active device with a supply behind it can.

questions.q: What does the term gain mean in amplifiers?
a: The output signal voltage relative to the input signal voltage
The output signal current relative to the input signal current
The output signal power relative to the input signal power
questions.x: Gain describes any increase the amplifier produces, whether in voltage, current or power. All three are legitimate ways to express it, so the inclusive answer is correct. Which one matters depends on the job the stage is doing.

questions.q: What are the names of the electrodes of a bipolar junction transistor?
questions.x: Emitter, base and collector. The base is the thin control region in the middle; current flows between emitter and collector under its command. Pair this with the FET set of gate, drain and source.

questions.q: What is an electrical diagram using standard component symbols called?
questions.x: A schematic uses standard symbols to show what is connected to what. It is not a picture of the physical layout, which is why the same schematic can describe boards that look nothing alike.

questions.q: What is component 1 in figure T-1?
questions.x: Component 1 is drawn as a sharp zigzag in the signal path, which is the standard resistor symbol. Here it sits between the input terminals and the transistor's base, limiting the current that reaches it.

questions.q: What is component 2 in figure T-1?
questions.x: Component 2 is a circle containing a vertical bar with two angled leads, one carrying an arrowhead. That is a bipolar transistor. The bar is the base, and the arrow marks the emitter and tells you it is an NPN.

questions.q: What is component 3 in figure T-1?
questions.x: Component 3 is the small dome or loop shape at the top of the drawing, the standard symbol for a lamp. It sits in the transistor's collector circuit, so the transistor switching on is what lights it.

questions.q: What is component 4 in figure T-1?
questions.x: Component 4 is the stack of alternating long and short parallel lines, which is the battery symbol. The long line is positive and the short one negative. More pairs of lines simply suggest more cells.

questions.q: What is component 6 in figure T-2?
questions.x: Component 6 is two parallel plates with one side curved, the symbol for a capacitor. It sits from the rectifier output to ground, which is the classic filter position where it smooths the pulsating DC.

questions.q: What is component 8 in figure T-2?
questions.x: Component 8 is a diode triangle with two small arrows pointing away from it. Those arrows mean the junction emits light, making it a light emitting diode. Arrows pointing toward the symbol instead would mean a photodiode.

questions.q: What is component 9 in figure T-2?
questions.x: Component 9 is a resistor zigzag with an arrow touching it, which marks an adjustable tap along the element. That makes it a variable resistor. The same symbol with three connected terminals is a potentiometer.

questions.q: What is component 4 in figure T-2?
questions.x: Component 4 is two coils drawn facing each other with lines between them representing the core. That is a transformer, and here it takes the AC input down to a lower voltage before the rectifier.

questions.q: What is component 3 in figure T-3?
questions.x: Component 3 is a coil with an arrow tapping it. Coil means inductor, and the arrow means adjustable, so it is a variable inductor. The same arrow convention marks the variable capacitors elsewhere in this figure.

questions.q: What is component 4 in figure T-3?
questions.x: Component 4 is the triangle at the top right, the standard antenna symbol. It sits at the output end of the tuned network, which is exactly where the antenna belongs in a matching circuit.

questions.q: Which of the following is accurately represented in electrical schematics?
questions.x: A schematic accurately shows component connections and nothing more. It does not tell you where parts sit on the board, how long the wires are, or what anything physically looks like. Connections are the whole point.

questions.q: Which of the following devices or circuits changes an alternating current into a varying direct current signal?
questions.x: A rectifier passes current in one direction only, so an AC input comes out as DC that varies but never reverses. Adding a filter capacitor after it smooths that pulsating output into something steady.

questions.q: What is a relay?
questions.x: A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet rather than by hand. A small control current pulls the contacts closed, letting a low-power circuit switch a much larger one while keeping the two electrically separate.

questions.q: Which of the following is a reason to use shielded wire?
a: To decrease the resistance of DC power connections
To increase the current carrying capability of the wire
To prevent coupling of unwanted signals to or from the wire
questions.x: Shielding wraps a grounded conductor around the signal wire so stray fields terminate on the shield instead of the conductor inside. It blocks interference in both directions, keeping noise out and your signal in.

questions.q: Which of the following displays an electrical quantity as a numeric value?
questions.x: A meter displays an electrical quantity as a number, whether on a digital readout or a moving pointer against a scale. The quantity depends on what you set it to measure.

questions.q: What type of circuit controls the amount of voltage from a power supply?
questions.x: A regulator holds output voltage steady as the input voltage or the load current changes. Without one, your radio would see the supply sag every time the transmitter keyed up.

questions.q: What component changes 120 V AC power to a lower AC voltage for other uses?
questions.x: A transformer changes AC voltage using two coils sharing a magnetic field. The turns ratio sets the change, so fewer turns on the secondary gives a lower voltage. It only works on AC, since a changing field is what couples the coils.

questions.q: Which of the following is commonly used as a visual indicator?
questions.x: LEDs are the standard visual indicator: low current, long life, and no filament to burn out. That is why the front panel of every modern radio is covered in them.

questions.q: Which of the following is combined with an inductor to make a resonant circuit?
questions.x: A capacitor combined with an inductor forms a resonant circuit. Their opposing reactances cancel at one frequency, and that frequency is where the circuit responds most strongly. It is the basis of every filter and tuned stage in your radio.

questions.q: What is the name of a device that combines several semiconductors and other components into one package?
questions.x: An integrated circuit packs many semiconductors and other components onto one chip. It is how a function that once filled a chassis now fits in a package smaller than your fingernail.

questions.q: What is the function of component 2 in figure T-1?
a: Give off light when current flows through it
Convert electrical energy into radio waves
questions.x: Component 2 is the transistor, and its job in this circuit is controlling current. A small current into the base governs the much larger current flowing through the lamp, so the transistor acts as the switch or amplifier.

questions.q: Which of the following is a resonant or tuned circuit?
a: An inductor and a capacitor in series or parallel
A resistor circuit used for reducing standing wave ratio
A circuit designed to provide high-fidelity audio
questions.x: An inductor and a capacitor together, wired in series or in parallel. Either arrangement resonates, though they behave oppositely at that frequency: series presents minimum impedance, parallel presents maximum.

questions.q: Which term describes the ability of a receiver to detect the presence of a signal?
questions.x: Sensitivity is how weak a signal the receiver can still detect, usually quoted in microvolts. Its partner term is selectivity, which is about separating signals rather than hearing faint ones. Detect means sensitivity.

questions.q: What is a transceiver?
a: A device that combines a receiver and transmitter
A device for matching feed line impedance to 50 ohms
A device for automatically sending and decoding Morse code
A device for converting receiver and transmitter frequencies to another band
questions.x: A transceiver is a receiver and transmitter in one box, sharing circuitry such as the VFO and often the filters. The word itself is the two terms fused together.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to convert a signal from one frequency to another?
questions.x: A mixer combines two frequencies and produces their sum and difference, which is how a signal gets shifted to another frequency. It is the heart of every superheterodyne receiver, converting incoming signals down to a fixed intermediate frequency.

questions.q: Which term describes the ability of a receiver to discriminate between multiple signals?
questions.x: Selectivity is the ability to separate a wanted signal from others nearby, and it comes mostly from the receiver's filters. Sensitivity hears the weak one; selectivity ignores the loud neighbor.

questions.q: What is the name of a circuit that generates a signal at a specific frequency?
questions.x: An oscillator generates a signal at a chosen frequency, converting DC from the supply into AC at radio frequency. Every transmitter and receiver contains at least one, since without a generated reference there is nothing to mix against.

questions.q: What device converts the RF input and output of a transceiver to another band?
questions.x: A transverter shifts a transceiver's whole operating range onto another band, converting both transmit and receive. It lets an HF radio work a microwave band without replacing the radio, which is common practice on the higher bands.

questions.q: What is the function of a transceiver’s PTT input?
a: Input for a key used to send CW
Switches transceiver from receive to transmit when grounded
Provides a transmit tuning tone when grounded
Input for a preamplifier tuning tone
questions.x: PTT means push to talk, and grounding that input switches the radio from receive to transmit. A foot switch, a microphone button, or a computer interface all work the same way: connect the line to ground and the transmitter keys.

questions.q: Which of the following describes combining speech with an RF carrier signal?
questions.x: Modulation is impressing information onto a carrier by varying one of its properties. Change the amplitude and you get AM, the frequency and you get FM. Speech plus carrier equals modulation.

questions.q: What is the function of the switch which selects either SSB or CW-FM on some VHF power amplifiers?
a: Change the mode of the transmitted signal
Set the amplifier for proper operation in the selected mode
Change the frequency range of the amplifier to operate in the proper segment of the band
questions.x: SSB and CW-FM place different demands on an amplifier. SSB is a varying envelope needing linear amplification, while FM and CW have constant amplitude and can tolerate more efficient nonlinear operation. The switch sets the amplifier up correctly for the mode you picked.

questions.q: What can be added to the output of a transceiver to increase the transmitted output power?
questions.x: An RF power amplifier raises the transmitter's output, taking a few watts in and producing many more using energy from its own supply. Remember §97.313(a) still applies: use the minimum power needed.

questions.q: What is the function of the Variable Frequency Oscillator (VFO) circuit in a transceiver?
a: Set the receive and transmit frequency
Inject a variable frequency to allow CW reception
Generate and demodulate single sideband signals
questions.x: The VFO sets the frequency you transmit and receive on, and it is what moves when you turn the tuning knob. Variable is the operative word, distinguishing it from a crystal oscillator locked to one frequency.

questions.q: What can you do if you are told your FM handheld or mobile transceiver is over-deviating?
a: Change to a higher power level
Talk farther away from the microphone
questions.x: Over-deviation means your audio is driving the transmitter past its allowed frequency swing, which splatters into adjacent channels and sounds distorted. Backing away from the microphone lowers the audio level and brings deviation back in range.

questions.q: What would cause a broadcast AM or FM radio to receive an amateur radio transmission unintentionally?
a: The receiver is unable to reject strong signals outside the AM or FM band
The microphone gain of the transmitter is turned up too high
The audio amplifier of the transmitter is overloaded
The deviation of an FM transmitter is set too low
questions.x: The fault is usually in the consumer receiver, not your transmitter. Broadcast sets are built cheaply with poor front-end filtering, so a strong nearby signal on any frequency can overload the input stage. Your signal is legal and on frequency; their radio simply cannot reject it.

questions.q: Which of the following can cause radio frequency interference?
questions.x: Interference comes from many directions: arcing power lines, switching supplies, LED lighting, and consumer electronics of every kind. Since all the listed sources genuinely cause it, the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: Which of the following might be the cause of low RF power output from a solid-state transceiver?
questions.x: High SWR means power is reflecting back into the transmitter, and solid-state finals protect themselves by folding back output. Low power with everything else normal usually points at the antenna system rather than the radio.

questions.q: Which of the following might reduce interference by an amateur station to a non-amateur over-the-air radio receiver?
a: Block the amateur signal with a filter at the antenna input of the affected receiver
Block the interfering signal with a filter on the amateur transmitter
Switch the transmitter from FM to SSB
Switch the transmitter to a narrow-band mode
questions.x: When a receiver cannot reject your signal, the fix belongs at that receiver. A filter at its antenna input blocks your frequency before it reaches the overloaded front end. Filtering your own transmitter does nothing if your signal is already clean.

questions.q: Which of the following actions should you take if a neighbor tells you that your station’s transmissions are interfering with their radio or TV reception?
a: Make sure that your station is functioning properly and that it does not cause interference to your own radio or television when it is tuned to the same channel
Immediately turn off your transmitter and contact the nearest FCC office for assistance
Install a harmonic doubler on the output of your transmitter and tune it until the interference is eliminated
questions.x: Start by proving your own station is clean. Check that it is working properly and that it does not interfere with your own equipment on the same channel. That tells you whether the problem is yours to fix or theirs, and it is the answer any FCC inquiry would expect.

questions.q: Which of the following can reduce interference to a 2-meter band transceiver from a nearby commercial FM station?
a: Installing bypass capacitors on the microphone cable
questions.x: A band-reject filter, also called a notch or trap, attenuates the commercial FM broadcast band while passing 2 meters. The broadcast station is legal and strong, so the practical fix is keeping its energy out of your receiver's front end.

questions.q: What should you do if something in a neighbor’s home is causing harmful interference to your amateur station?
a: Work with your neighbor to identify the offending device
Politely inform your neighbor that FCC rules prohibit the use of devices that cause interference
Make sure your station meets the standards of good amateur practice
questions.x: Work through it cooperatively: make sure your own station is clean, then help the neighbor identify the offending device, since consumer gear must accept interference under Part 15. All the listed steps are reasonable, so the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: What should be the first step to resolve non-fiber optic cable TV interference caused by your amateur radio transmission?
a: Add a low-pass filter to the TV antenna input
Add a high-pass filter to the TV antenna input
Add a preamplifier to the TV antenna input
Be sure all TV feed line coaxial connectors are installed properly
questions.x: Start with the connectors. Loose or improperly installed coax fittings let signal leak in and out, and they are by far the most common cause of cable TV interference. It costs nothing to check and usually solves it.

questions.q: What might be a problem if you receive a report that your audio signal through an FM repeater is distorted or unintelligible?
a: Your transmitter is slightly off frequency
You are speaking too loudly or too close to the microphone
You are in a bad location
questions.x: Distorted repeater audio has several likely causes: over-deviation from talking too loudly, RF getting back into the microphone circuit, or simply operating too far from the repeater. All are genuine, so the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: Which of the following can eliminate distorted voice transmissions?
a: Adding extra feedline to the antenna to lower SWR
Turning the radio on and off to reset the computer-controlled circuitry
Adding a clip-on ferrite “choke” to the microphone cable to prevent the transmitted signal from feeding back into the transmitter
Turning the squelch control fully clockwise to prevent the transmitted signal from triggering the squelch circuit
questions.x: A clip-on ferrite choke adds impedance to common-mode RF riding on the microphone cable, stopping your own transmitted signal from feeding back into the audio stages. That feedback is a classic cause of distorted transmit audio in a high-RF shack.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a dummy load?
a: To prevent transmitting signals over the air when making tests
To prevent over-modulation of a transmitter
To improve the efficiency of an antenna
To improve the signal-to-noise ratio of a receiver
questions.x: A dummy load absorbs your output so you can test and tune without radiating. It lets you key up, check power and adjust settings without occupying a frequency or interfering with anyone.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to determine if an antenna is resonant at the desired operating frequency?
questions.x: An antenna analyzer sweeps a range of frequencies and shows SWR or impedance across it, so you can see where the antenna is actually resonant. An SWR meter tells you the situation at one frequency while transmitting; the analyzer maps the whole picture without transmitting.

questions.q: What does a typical RF dummy load consist of?
a: A low-voltage power supply and an AC relay
A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor mounted on a heat sink
A low-voltage power supply and a DC relay
A 50-ohm inductive reactance mounted in a shielded enclosure
questions.x: A 50-ohm non-inductive resistor on a heat sink. Fifty ohms matches normal feed line, non-inductive keeps the impedance flat across frequency, and the heat sink handles the power, since every watt you send becomes heat.

questions.q: What reading on an SWR meter indicates a perfect impedance match between the antenna and the feed line?
questions.x: A 1:1 reading means no reflected power, so the load impedance matches the line exactly. SWR is a ratio and 1:1 is the ideal floor. It can never read below that.

questions.q: Why do most solid-state transmitters reduce output power as SWR increases beyond a certain level?
a: To protect the RF output amplifier transistors
To comply with FCC rules on spectral purity
Because power supplies cannot supply enough current at high SWR
To lower the SWR on the transmission line
questions.x: Reflected power from a mismatch stresses the output transistors with voltage and current they were not designed for. Solid-state finals have no tolerance for it, so the radio reduces power to protect them. Tube amplifiers were far more forgiving, which is why this behavior surprises older operators.

questions.q: What does an SWR reading of 4:1 indicate?
questions.x: Any SWR above 1:1 indicates a mismatch between feed line and antenna, and 4:1 is a substantial one. The number tells you the degree of mismatch, not what caused it, so it could be the antenna, the feed line, or a connector.

questions.q: What happens to power lost in a feed line?
questions.x: Lost power becomes heat in the conductors and the dielectric. It does not radiate and it does not come back. That is why a long run of lossy cable at UHF can waste more power than the radio delivers to the antenna.

questions.q: Which instrument can be used to determine SWR?
questions.x: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately, and SWR follows directly from their ratio. Many meters do that calculation for you and show SWR on the scale.

questions.q: Which of the following causes failure of coaxial cables?
a: Rapid fluctuation in transmitter output power
Operation at 100% duty cycle for an extended period
questions.x: Moisture is the usual killer. Water wicks into the braid and dielectric, raising loss and corroding the shield, and the damage travels well beyond the entry point. Sealing connectors properly is the cheapest maintenance you can do.

questions.q: Why should the outer jacket of coaxial cable be resistant to ultraviolet light?
a: Ultraviolet light can increase the resistance of the conductors
Ultraviolet light can increase losses in the cable’s jacket
Ultraviolet and RF signals can mix, causing interference
Ultraviolet light can damage the jacket and allow water to enter the cable
questions.x: Sunlight breaks down the polymer jacket over time, leaving it cracked and brittle. Once cracked it admits water, and moisture is what actually ruins the cable. UV resistance protects the jacket so the jacket can protect the coax.

questions.q: What is an advantage of foam-dielectric versus solid-dielectric coaxial cable?
a: It is more resistant to moisture contamination
It has less loss per foot
It has a better impedance match to 50 ohms
questions.x: Foam dielectric has less loss per foot because much of the insulation is air, which absorbs far less RF energy than solid polyethylene. The tradeoff is that foam is easier to crush and lets moisture migrate more readily if the jacket is breached.
questions.xs: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: Which instrument would you use to measure electric potential?
questions.x: A voltmeter measures electric potential, or the difference in potential between two points. Potential is the formal name for what everyone calls voltage.

questions.q: How is a voltmeter connected to a component to measure applied voltage?
questions.x: In parallel, across the component. Voltage is a difference between two points, so you need probes on both sides of the part you are measuring. A voltmeter has very high resistance so it barely disturbs the circuit while connected.

questions.q: When configured to measure current, how is a multimeter connected to a component?
questions.x: In series, so the current you want to measure actually flows through the meter. That means breaking the circuit to insert it. An ammeter has very low resistance, which is why connecting one across a voltage source is a good way to destroy it.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure electric current?
questions.x: An ammeter measures current, and it goes in series with the circuit. The name comes from ampere, the unit it reads.

questions.q: How does an ohmmeter measure the resistance of a circuit or component?
a: By applying a small current and measuring the resulting voltage
By placing a variable resistor in parallel with the circuit
By placing a variable resistor in series with the circuit
By applying a variable voltage and measuring the resulting current change
questions.x: An ohmmeter supplies a small known current from its own battery, measures the voltage that results, and applies Ohm's law to report resistance. That is why it needs power of its own and why the circuit under test must be unpowered.

questions.q: Which of the following can damage a multimeter?
a: Attempting to measure resistance using the voltage setting
Failing to connect one of the probes to ground
Attempting to measure voltage when using the resistance setting
Not allowing it to warm up properly
questions.x: The resistance setting expects the meter to supply the current, not receive it. Apply an external voltage in that mode and you push current through circuitry never designed for it, often taking out the meter or its fuse.

questions.q: Which of the following measurements are made using a multimeter?
questions.x: A multimeter reads voltage and resistance, and nearly all of them read current too. The name says it: multiple measurements in one instrument.

questions.q: Which of the following types of solder should not be used for radio and electronic applications?
questions.x: Acid-core solder is made for plumbing. Its flux is corrosive and stays active after the joint cools, quietly eating the connection and nearby traces. Electronics work uses rosin-core solder instead.

questions.q: What is the characteristic appearance of a cold tin-lead solder joint?
questions.x: A cold joint looks dull, rough or lumpy rather than smooth and shiny. It formed without enough heat for the solder to flow and wet the metal properly, so it may test fine today and fail intermittently later. Reheat it until it flows.

questions.q: What reading indicates that an ohmmeter is connected across a large, discharged capacitor?
a: Alternating between open and short circuit
questions.x: The ohmmeter's own small current charges the capacitor. As charge builds, the voltage across it rises and the meter interprets that as rising resistance, climbing toward infinity. Watching that behavior is a rough way to check whether a large capacitor is healthy.

questions.q: Which of the following precautions should be taken when measuring in-circuit resistance with an ohmmeter?
a: Ensure that the applied voltages are correct
Ensure that the circuit is not powered
Ensure that the circuit is grounded
Ensure that the circuit is operating at the correct frequency
questions.x: Power the circuit down first. An ohmmeter works by injecting its own current, so any external voltage corrupts the reading and can damage the meter. Discharge any large capacitors before probing, too.

questions.q: Which of the following is a form of amplitude modulation?
questions.x: SSB is amplitude modulation with the carrier and one sideband removed. All the information rode in the sidebands anyway, so stripping the rest saves bandwidth and power without losing anything. It remains AM at heart.

questions.q: What type of modulation is commonly used for VHF packet radio transmissions?
questions.x: VHF packet feeds its tones through an ordinary FM radio, so the modulation is FM or PM. The packet gear generates audio tones and the radio treats them like any other audio, which is why a standard 2-meter rig works unmodified.

questions.q: Which type of voice mode is often used for long-distance (weak signal) contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
questions.x: SSB is the weak-signal voice mode above 50 MHz. Its narrow bandwidth concentrates your power and lets the receiver use a tight filter, so contacts stay workable at signal levels where FM would deliver nothing but hiss.

questions.q: Which type of modulation is commonly used for VHF and UHF voice repeaters?
questions.x: Repeaters use FM or PM. FM's constant amplitude survives multipath and noise well, and its capture effect means the strongest signal takes the channel cleanly instead of two stations garbling each other.

questions.q: Which of the following signal types has the narrowest bandwidth?
questions.x: CW is the narrowest of these, needing only about 150 Hz. There is no voice content to carry, just a carrier switched on and off, so the occupied bandwidth comes down to the keying speed.

questions.q: Which sideband is normally used for 10-meter HF, VHF, and UHF single-sideband communications?
questions.x: Upper sideband is the convention on 10 meters and everything above. Lower sideband is used on 160, 80 and 40 meters. The dividing line falls at 10 meters, so remember 20 meters and up is USB along with all of VHF and UHF.

questions.q: What is one characteristic of single sideband (SSB) compared to FM?
a: SSB signals are easier to tune in correctly
SSB signals are less susceptible to interference
SSB signals are less susceptible to high SWR
questions.x: SSB occupies roughly 3 kHz against 10 to 15 kHz for FM voice. Narrower bandwidth means your transmitter power is concentrated and the receiver can filter more tightly, which is why SSB reaches farther on the same watts.

questions.q: What is the approximate bandwidth of a typical single sideband (SSB) voice signal?
questions.x: About 3 kHz, which is roughly the range of frequencies that carry intelligible speech. That figure anchors several others worth knowing: the 2.8 kHz limit on 60 meters and the 2400 Hz receiver filter that gives the best signal-to-noise ratio.

questions.q: What is the approximate bandwidth of an FM voice signal on VHF repeaters?
questions.x: Between 10 and 15 kHz. FM spreads energy across a band several times wider than the audio it carries, which is the price of its noise immunity. That is also why repeater channels are spaced 15 or 20 kHz apart.

questions.q: What is the approximate bandwidth of AM fast-scan TV transmissions?
questions.x: About 6 MHz, the same width as a broadcast television channel. Moving full-motion video in real time takes roughly two thousand times the bandwidth of an SSB voice signal.

questions.q: What is the approximate bandwidth required to transmit a CW signal?
questions.x: Roughly 150 Hz. Keying a carrier on and off creates sidebands proportional to the keying speed, so at normal code speeds the signal stays very narrow. That narrowness is why CW gets through when nothing else will.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of FM compared with single sideband?
a: Only one signal can be received at a time
FM signals are harder to tune
FM signals are more susceptible to high SWR
questions.x: FM's capture effect means the receiver locks onto the strongest signal and suppresses everything else, so you hear one station at a time. On SSB two stations on nearly the same frequency both come through, which is sometimes an advantage and sometimes a mess.

questions.q: What telemetry information is typically transmitted by satellite beacons?
a: The signal strength of received signals
Time of day accurate to plus or minus 1/10 second
Health and status of the satellite
questions.x: Beacons carry telemetry about the satellite itself: battery voltage, temperatures, and the state of its systems. Ground stations track that data to know whether the spacecraft is healthy and which transponder is active.

questions.q: What is the impact of using excessive effective radiated power on a satellite uplink?
a: Possibility of commanding the satellite to an improper mode
Possibility of rebooting the satellite control computer
questions.x: A linear transponder shares its limited output power among every signal passing through it. Running too much uplink power captures a disproportionate share and pushes everyone else down into the noise. It is the satellite equivalent of shouting over a conversation.

questions.q: Which of the following are provided by satellite tracking programs?
a: Maps showing the real-time position of the satellite track over Earth
The time, azimuth, and elevation of the start, maximum altitude, and end of a pass
The apparent frequency of the satellite transmission, including effects of Doppler shift
questions.x: Tracking software gives you when the satellite rises and sets, where to point the antenna in azimuth and elevation, and how much Doppler shift to expect. All of the listed outputs are standard, so the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: What mode of transmission is commonly used by amateur radio satellites?
questions.x: Amateur satellites carry FM, SSB, CW and digital modes depending on the spacecraft. There is no single satellite mode, so the inclusive answer is right. FM birds are the easiest starting point with a handheld and a small beam.

questions.q: What is a satellite beacon?
a: The primary transmit antenna on the satellite
An indicator light that shows where to point your antenna
A reflective surface on the satellite
A transmission from a satellite that contains status information
questions.x: A beacon is a steady transmission carrying the satellite's status information. It also gives you a reference signal for aiming your antenna and gauging Doppler before you try to work the transponder.

questions.q: Which of the following are inputs to a satellite tracking program?
a: The last observed time of zero Doppler shift
questions.x: Keplerian elements are the numbers describing the orbit's size, shape and orientation, distributed as two-line element sets. Feed current elements into tracking software and it computes where the satellite will be. They go stale, so refresh them.

questions.q: What is Doppler shift in reference to satellite communications?
a: A change in the satellite orbit
A mode where the satellite receives signals on one band and transmits on another
An observed change in signal frequency caused by relative motion between the satellite and Earth station
A special digital communications mode for some satellites
questions.x: Relative motion between satellite and ground station shifts the received frequency, high as it approaches and low as it recedes. On a fast low orbit the shift is large enough that you retune continuously through a pass.

questions.q: What does it mean if a satellite is operating in U/V mode?
a: The satellite uplink is in the 15-meter band and the downlink is in the 10-meter band
The satellite uplink is in the 70-centimeter band and the downlink is in the 2-meter band
The satellite operates using ultraviolet frequencies
The satellite frequencies are usually variable
questions.x: The letters name the bands in order, uplink first. U is 70 centimeters and V is 2 meters, so U/V means you transmit on 70 centimeters and listen on 2 meters. Getting the order backwards is the classic beginner error.

questions.q: What causes spin fading of satellite signals?
a: Circular polarized noise interference radiated from the sun
Rotation of the satellite and its antennas
Doppler shift of the received signal
Interfering signals within the satellite uplink band
questions.x: The satellite tumbles or spins, so its antennas keep changing orientation relative to yours. As the polarization rotates in and out of alignment with your antenna, the signal rises and falls in a regular rhythm.

questions.q: What does the term LEO mean in reference to communication satellites?
a: Low Energy Orbit, which conserves battery power
Low Elevation Orbit, which appears close to the horizon from the earth station
Low Equilibrium Orbit, which has a slightly unstable period
Low Earth Orbit, which has a period of around 100 minutes
questions.x: Low Earth Orbit, a few hundred kilometers up with a period near 100 minutes. That means fast passes lasting only ten or fifteen minutes, plenty of Doppler, and the need to track the satellite as it crosses.

questions.q: Who is permitted to receive telemetry from an amateur radio satellite?
a: Only the control operator or a licensed radio amateur who has received the encryption key from the control operator
Only a licensed radio amateur who has received the encryption key from AMSAT
questions.x: Anyone may receive it. Satellite telemetry is transmitted in the clear precisely so that anyone can decode it, and encoding to obscure meaning would run against Part 97 anyway. Listening has never required a license.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way to determine whether your satellite uplink power into a linear transponder satellite is neither too low nor too high?
a: Check your signal strength report in the telemetry data
Listen for distortion on your downlink signal
Your signal strength on the downlink should be about the same as the beacon
Compare your signal to others on the downlink using an internet SDR receiver
questions.x: Compare your downlink signal to the satellite's beacon. Matching the beacon means you are using a fair share of the transponder. Louder than the beacon means you are taking more than your share and squeezing out other stations.

questions.q: Which of the following methods is used to locate sources of noise interference or jamming?
questions.x: Radio direction finding locates a transmitter by taking bearings from several positions and seeing where they cross. It is the standard method for tracking down noise sources, stuck transmitters and deliberate interference.

questions.q: Which of these items would be useful for a hidden transmitter hunt?
questions.x: A directional antenna, since the hunt depends on knowing which way the signal is coming from. An omnidirectional antenna hears the transmitter equally from everywhere, which tells you nothing about where to walk.

questions.q: What operating activity involves contacting as many stations as possible during a specified period?
questions.x: Contesting is working as many stations as possible inside a set time. Contacts are brief and formulaic because the goal is volume, which is also why contest operating sounds so different from ordinary conversation.

questions.q: Which of the following is good practice when contacting another station in a contest?
a: Signing only the last two letters of your call if there are many other stations calling
Contacting the station twice to be sure that you are in his log
Sending only the minimum information needed for proper identification and the contest exchange
questions.x: Send your call sign and the required exchange, nothing more. Everyone on the band is trying to maximize contacts, so extra conversation costs both operators rate. Brevity is courtesy in a contest.

questions.q: What is a grid locator?
a: A letter-number designator assigned to a geographic location
A letter-number designator assigned to an azimuth and elevation
An instrument for locating faults in power amplifiers
An instrument for radio direction finding
questions.x: A grid locator, or Maidenhead locator, compresses latitude and longitude into a short string such as FN31pr. Two letters, two digits and often two more letters narrow your position to a few kilometers, which is enough for VHF work and awards.

questions.q: How is over the air access to Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP) nodes accomplished?
a: By obtaining a password that is sent via voice to the node
By entering the proper internet password
By using Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System (CTCSS) tone codes
questions.x: You send DTMF tones, the same touch-tone digits a telephone keypad produces. The node decodes them as commands to connect to or disconnect from another node, so your radio's keypad becomes the dialing interface.

questions.q: What is Voice Over Internet Protocol (VoIP)?
a: A set of rules specifying how to identify your station when linked over the internet to another station
A technique employed to “spot” DX stations via the internet
A technique for measuring the modulation quality of a transmitter using remote sites monitored via the internet
A method of delivering voice communications over the internet using digital techniques
questions.x: Voice over Internet Protocol digitizes speech and carries it as data packets across the internet. Amateur linking systems use it to join distant repeaters, so the RF hop is local at each end and the internet covers the middle.

questions.q: What is the Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP)?
a: A technique to connect amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, via the internet
A system for providing access to websites via amateur radio
A system for informing amateurs in real time of the frequency of active DX stations
A technique for measuring signal strength of an amateur transmitter via the internet
questions.x: IRLP links repeaters and other amateur systems over the internet. Every user is on real RF at their end; the internet only carries audio between nodes, which is why IRLP requires a radio to participate.

questions.q: Which of the following protocols enables an amateur station to transmit through a repeater without using a radio to initiate the transmission?
questions.x: EchoLink allows a computer or smartphone to connect directly into the system without RF at that end. That is the distinction from IRLP, where every participant must be on the air.

questions.q: What is required before using the EchoLink system?
a: Purchase a license to use the EchoLink software
Register your call sign and provide proof of license
At least a General Class license
questions.x: You register your call sign and provide proof of license before the system will admit you. Since EchoLink can key transmitters, it has to verify that everyone connecting is actually licensed.

questions.q: What is an amateur radio station that connects other amateur stations to the internet?
questions.x: A gateway is the station bridging amateur radio and the internet, passing traffic between the two. Winlink gateways and IRLP nodes are both examples of the same idea.

questions.q: Which of the following is a digital communications mode?
questions.x: Packet, PSK31, FT8, RTTY and the rest are all digital modes, so the inclusive answer is right. What they share is encoding information as discrete symbols rather than as a continuously varying analog waveform.

questions.q: What is FT8?
a: A digital mode capable of low signal-to-noise operation
An eight-channel multiplex mode for FM repeaters
A digital slow-scan TV mode with forward error correction and automatic color compensation
