questions.x: FT8 is built for signals buried in noise, decoding reliably well below what an ear can hear. It trades speed and flexibility for sensitivity: fixed 15-second transmissions carrying a very small, highly structured message.

questions.q: What kind of data can be transmitted by APRS?
questions.x: APRS carries position, weather data, short text messages and telemetry. All the listed types are genuine, so the inclusive answer applies. It is a general-purpose data channel that happens to be used mostly for position reporting.

questions.q: What is meant by the term "NTSC?"
a: A digital transmission standard for encrypting data
A special mode for satellite uplink
An analog fast-scan color TV signal
A frame compression scheme for TV signals
questions.x: NTSC is the analog color television standard used in North America before digital broadcasting, and amateurs use it for fast-scan TV. It is analog and full motion, which is what separates it from slow-scan TV.

questions.q: Which of the following is an application of APRS?
a: Providing real-time tactical digital communications in conjunction with a map showing the locations of stations
Automatically showing the number of packets transmitted via PACTOR during a specific time interval
Providing voice over internet connection between repeaters
Providing information on the number of stations signed into a repeater
questions.x: APRS plots station positions on a live map, which makes it valuable for public service events where net control needs to see where everyone actually is. Real time and tactical are the words to match.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation "PSK" mean?
questions.x: Phase Shift Keying. Information is encoded by shifting the carrier's phase rather than its amplitude or frequency. PSK31 uses it to fit a keyboard conversation into about 31 Hz of bandwidth.

questions.q: Which of the following describes DMR?
a: A technique for time-multiplexing two digital voice signals on a single 12.5 kHz repeater channel
An automatic position tracking mode for FM mobiles communicating through repeaters
An automatic computer logging technique for hands-off logging when communicating while operating a vehicle
A digital technique for transmitting on two repeater inputs simultaneously for automatic error correction
questions.x: DMR uses two-slot TDMA, interleaving two conversations in alternating time slots on one 12.5 kHz channel. Two independent contacts share the same frequency without hearing each other, which effectively doubles repeater capacity.

questions.q: Which of the following is included in packet radio transmissions?
a: A checksum that permits error detection
A header that contains the call sign of the station to which the information is being sent
Automatic repeat request in case of error
questions.x: A packet frame carries the sender and destination call signs, the data payload, and a checksum for error detection. All the listed elements are part of the frame, so the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: What is CW?
a: A digital mode used primarily on 2-meter FM
Error correction for digital transmission using code words
Another name for a Morse code transmission
questions.x: CW stands for continuous wave, and Part 97 defines it as international Morse code telegraphy. In practice it means keying a carrier on and off. It remains the narrowest and most power-efficient way to get a message through a bad path.

questions.q: Which of the following operating activities is supported by digital mode software in the WSJT-X software suite?
questions.x: WSJT-X supports FT8, FT4, meteor scatter, EME and other weak-signal work, so the inclusive answer is right. The common thread is decoding signals well below the noise floor using known message structure.

questions.q: What is the role of ARQ in a transmission system?
a: A special transmission format limited to video signals
A system used to encrypt command signals to an amateur radio satellite
An error correction method in which the receiving station detects errors and sends a request for retransmission
A method of compressing data using autonomous reiterative Q codes prior to final encoding
questions.x: ARQ means Automatic Repeat reQuest. The receiver checks each block for errors and asks for a resend when one fails, so the data arriving is correct rather than merely approximate. The cost is throughput on a poor path.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes an amateur radio mesh network?
a: An amateur-radio data network using commercial Wi-Fi equipment with modified firmware
A wide-bandwidth digital voice mode employing DMR protocols
An amateur-radio satellite communications network using modified commercial satellite TV hardware
An internet linking protocol allowing communication through repeaters around the world
questions.x: Mesh networking runs commercial Wi-Fi hardware on modified firmware, moving it onto amateur frequencies that overlap the Part 15 bands and allowing amateur power levels. It is still an amateur station, so encryption to obscure meaning stays prohibited.

questions.q: What is a beam antenna?
a: An antenna built from square aluminum beams
An omnidirectional antenna invented by Clarence Beam
An antenna that concentrates signals in one direction
An antenna that focuses the signal into two intense rays
questions.x: A beam antenna concentrates radiation in one direction instead of spreading it everywhere. The energy has to come from somewhere, so what it adds in front it takes from the sides and back. Yagis and quads are the common examples.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a type of antenna loading?
a: Electrically lengthening by inserting inductors in radiating elements
Inserting a resistor in the radiating portion of the antenna to make it resonant
Installing a spring in the base of a mobile vertical antenna to make it more flexible
Strengthening the radiating elements of a beam antenna to better resist wind damage
questions.x: Loading inserts an inductor into a radiating element so a physically short antenna behaves electrically like a longer one. It is how a 2-meter-long mobile whip works on 40 meters. The coil buys resonance, not efficiency.

questions.q: How is the polarization of an antenna described?
a: By the shape of the driven element
By the orientation of the electric field
By the orientation of the magnetic field
questions.x: Antenna polarization is named for the orientation of the electric field it radiates. A vertical element produces a vertical electric field, so it is vertically polarized. Same definition used for the wave itself in T3B02.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of a handheld radio transceiver’s short flexible antenna compared to a full-sized quarter-wave antenna?
a: It transmits only circularly polarized signals
It is more susceptible to receiver desensitization
It only works on analog signals, not digital ones
questions.x: That short rubber antenna is heavily loaded to resonate in a fraction of the length it needs, and loading raises losses while lowering radiation resistance. Much of your power warms the antenna instead of leaving it. It works, just inefficiently.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; antenna efficiency theory

questions.q: Which of the following increases the resonant frequency of a dipole antenna?
a: Inserting coils in series with radiating wires
Adding capacitive loading to the ends of the radiating wires
questions.x: Resonant length and frequency are inversely related, so a shorter dipole resonates higher. Trimming a dipole raises its resonant frequency, which is why you cut antennas long and shorten them in steps.

questions.q: Which of the following types of antennas offers the greatest gain?
questions.x: Of the usual choices, the Yagi has the most gain. Its driven element plus reflector and directors form an array that reinforces radiation forward and cancels it elsewhere. Adding more directors buys more gain and a narrower beam.

questions.q: What is a potential drawback of using a handheld VHF transceiver inside a vehicle that lacks an externally mounted antenna?
a: Signal strength is reduced due to the shielding effect of the vehicle
The bandwidth of the antenna will decrease, increasing SWR
The SWR might decrease, decreasing the signal strength
The handheld will overheat due to reflected power in the vehicle
questions.x: A vehicle body is a metal box that behaves like a Faraday shield, attenuating signals passing through it. Your handheld inside the car is partly enclosed by that shield, so both transmit and receive suffer. An external antenna solves it.

questions.q: Why is a 19-inch-long vertical antenna often used on 2 meters?
a: It has low RF radiation exposure
questions.x: At 146 MHz a wavelength is about 2.05 meters, so a quarter wave is near 20 inches. Trim slightly for end effect and you land at 19. You can rebuild that number any time from 300 divided by frequency.

questions.q: What is an advantage of a 5/8-wavelength whip antenna for VHF or UHF mobile service compared to a 1/4-wave antenna?
a: It radiates at a higher angle
questions.x: A 5/8-wave whip concentrates radiation at a lower angle toward the horizon, which is exactly where distant stations are. That lower takeoff angle is the gain, and it matters more for mobile work than raw height ever will.

questions.q: In which direction does a half-wave dipole antenna radiate the strongest signal?
a: Off the ends of the antenna
In the direction of the feed line
questions.x: A dipole radiates strongest broadside, at right angles to the wire, and puts nulls off the ends. Point the wire across the path you want rather than at it. The pattern is a doughnut with the antenna through the hole.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; dipole radiation pattern

questions.q: What is antenna gain?
a: The additional power that is added to the transmitter power
The additional power that is required in the antenna when transmitting on a higher frequency
The increase in signal strength in a specified direction compared to a reference antenna
The increase in impedance on receive or transmit compared to a reference antenna
questions.x: Gain is the increase in signal in a chosen direction compared with a reference antenna, usually a dipole or an isotropic radiator. No antenna creates power. Gain is redistribution, taking from directions you do not need.

questions.q: Which of the following connectors should be carefully taped for weather protection when used outdoors?
questions.x: Every outdoor connector needs sealing, whichever type it is, so the inclusive answer is right. Water entering a connector wicks into the coax and ruins it well beyond the joint, and that damage is invisible until performance falls off.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; connector weatherproofing practice

questions.q: What is the most common impedance of coaxial cables used in amateur radio?
questions.x: Fifty ohms is the amateur standard, and it is what transceivers, meters and dummy loads are built around. The figure is an engineering compromise between the impedances that minimize loss and maximize power handling in coax.
questions.xs: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: Why is coaxial cable the most common feed line for amateur radio antenna systems?
a: It is easy to use and requires few special installation considerations
It has less loss than any other type of feed line
It can handle more power than any other type of feed line
It is less expensive than any other type of feed line
questions.x: Coax is popular because it is forgiving. The shield confines the field inside the cable, so you can run it along metal, bury it, or coil it without upsetting the impedance. Open-wire line has lower loss but demands spacing from everything.

questions.q: What is the major function of an antenna tuner (antenna coupler)?
a: It matches the antenna system impedance to the transceiver's output impedance
It helps a receiver automatically tune in weak stations
It allows an antenna to be used on both transmit and receive
It automatically selects the proper antenna for the frequency band being used
questions.x: A tuner matches the impedance the antenna system presents to what the transmitter wants to see, usually 50 ohms. Note what it does not do: it changes nothing at the antenna itself, so SWR on the feed line stays exactly where it was.
questions.xs: Impedance matching theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: What happens as the frequency of a signal in coaxial cable is increased?
questions.x: Loss rises with frequency. Skin effect crowds current into an ever thinner surface layer as frequency climbs, raising effective resistance, and dielectric losses grow too. A cable that is fine on 40 meters may be wasteful at 440 MHz.

questions.q: Which of the following connector types is most suitable as an RF connector for frequencies above 400 MHz?
questions.x: Type N maintains a constant 50-ohm impedance through the connector and seals well, so it performs properly above 400 MHz. UHF connectors have no controlled impedance, which becomes a real loss at those frequencies despite the name.

questions.q: Which of the following is true of PL-259 type coax connectors?
a: They are preferred for microwave operation
They are commonly used at HF and VHF frequencies
questions.x: The PL-259, also called the UHF connector, is the familiar screw-on fitting on HF and VHF gear. Its name is historical rather than descriptive: it does not hold a constant impedance, so it is a poor choice at true UHF.

questions.q: Which of the following is a source of loss in coaxial feed line?
questions.x: Loss comes from conductor resistance, dielectric absorption, and radiation or leakage through an imperfect shield. All the listed mechanisms are genuine contributors, so the inclusive answer applies.

questions.q: What can cause erratic changes in SWR?
a: Loose connection in the antenna or feed line
Overload from a strong local station
questions.x: Readings that jump around, especially when the wind blows or you flex the cable, point at a loose or corroded connection rather than a design problem. A steady mismatch reads steady. Intermittent readings mean intermittent contact.

questions.q: What is the electrical difference between RG-58 and RG-213 coaxial cable?
a: There is no significant difference between the two types
RG-213 cable has less loss at a given frequency
RG-58 cable can handle higher power levels
questions.x: Both are 50-ohm cable, but RG-213 is much larger, so its bigger conductor and thicker dielectric mean lower loss at any given frequency. That is the electrical difference; the physical one is that RG-58 is far easier to route.

questions.q: Which of the following types of feed line has the lowest loss?
questions.x: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss, because air absorbs almost nothing compared with solid dielectric and the large center conductor has very little resistance. The tradeoffs are cost, weight, and the fact that it barely bends.
questions.xs: Transmission line theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: What is standing wave ratio (SWR)?
a: A measure of how well a load is matched to a transmission line
The ratio of amplifier power output to input
An indication of the quality of your station’s ground connection
questions.x: SWR expresses how well the load matches the line, derived from the ratio of forward to reflected power. A perfect match reflects nothing and reads 1:1. The number describes the relationship between line and load, not the quality of either alone.

questions.q: What is one way that RF energy can affect human body tissue?
a: It causes the blood count to reach a dangerously low level
questions.x: RF heats tissue. That thermal effect is the established hazard and the entire basis of the exposure limits. RF is non-ionizing, so it cannot break chemical bonds the way X-rays do; what it can do is deposit enough energy to raise temperature.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to determine RF exposure from a transmitted signal?
questions.x: Power at the antenna, antenna gain and pattern, frequency, distance to people and duty cycle all feed the calculation. Every listed factor genuinely matters, so the inclusive answer applies. Exposure is a system property, not a power rating.

questions.q: How can you determine that your station complies with FCC RF exposure regulations?
a: By calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65
By calculation based on computer modeling
By measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment
questions.x: Three routes are acceptable: use the FCC's exemption calculations, run the equations from OET Bulletin 65, or measure with calibrated equipment. All are valid, so the inclusive answer is right. The rule requires an evaluation, not a particular method.

questions.q: What does “time averaging” mean when evaluating RF radiation exposure?
a: The average amount of power developed by the transmitter over a specific 24-hour period
The average time it takes RF radiation to have any long-term effect on the body
The total time of the exposure
The total RF exposure averaged over a certain period
questions.x: Time averaging means exposure is assessed over a defined period rather than instant by instant. A transmitter that is idle most of the time delivers less average energy, which is why duty cycle enters the calculation at all.

questions.q: What must you do if an evaluation of your station shows that the RF energy radiated by your station exceeds permissible limits for possible human absorption?
a: Take action to prevent human exposure to the excessive RF fields
File an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS-97) with the FCC
Secure written permission from your neighbors to operate above the controlled MPE limits
questions.x: Take action to prevent the exposure. The rule requires it: if the evaluation shows fields could exceed the limits in accessible areas, you must fix the situation. Move the antenna, restrict access, reduce power or cut duty cycle.

questions.q: What must you do if your station fails to meet the FCC RF exposure exemption criteria?
a: Perform an RF exposure evaluation in accordance with FCC OET Bulletin 65
Contact the FCC for permission to transmit
Perform an RF exposure evaluation in accordance with World Meteorological Organization guidelines
questions.x: If you cannot claim an exemption, you must perform an actual exposure evaluation following OET Bulletin 65. The exemption is the shortcut; failing it does not forbid operating, it obliges you to do the arithmetic.

questions.q: What is the effect of modulation duty cycle on RF exposure?
a: A lower duty cycle permits greater power levels to be transmitted
A higher duty cycle permits greater power levels to be transmitted
Low duty cycle transmitters are exempt from RF exposure evaluation requirements
High duty cycle transmitters are exempt from RF exposure requirements
questions.x: Lower duty cycle permits higher power, because the limits are averaged over time. Transmit half as often and you may run twice the power for the same average exposure. That is why SSB and CW are treated more leniently than FM or digital modes.

questions.q: Which of the following steps must an amateur operator take to ensure compliance with RF safety regulations?
a: Post a copy of FCC Part 97.13 in the station
Notify neighbors within a 100-foot radius of the antenna of the existence of the station and power levels
Perform a routine RF exposure evaluation and prevent access to any identified high exposure areas
questions.x: Two obligations, and the answer names both: perform the routine evaluation, then keep people out of any area it identifies as over the limit. Doing the evaluation and ignoring the result satisfies nothing.

questions.q: What type of instrument can be used to accurately measure an RF field strength?
a: A receiver with digital signal processing (DSP) noise reduction
A calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna
An SWR meter with a peak-reading function
An oscilloscope with a high-stability crystal marker generator
questions.x: A calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna. Both halves matter. An uncalibrated antenna makes the meter's calibration meaningless, since you cannot convert its reading to a field strength you can trust.

questions.q: What should be done if evaluation shows that a neighbor might experience more than the allowable limit of RF exposure from the main lobe of a directional antenna?
a: Change to a non-polarized antenna with higher gain
Use an antenna with a higher front-to-back ratio
Take precautions to ensure that the antenna cannot be pointed in their direction when they are present
questions.x: Prevent the antenna from pointing at them while they are there. A beam concentrates its energy in the main lobe, so the exposure problem exists in one direction only. Restricting rotation solves it without touching power or antenna height.

questions.q: What precaution should be taken if you install an indoor transmitting antenna?
a: Locate the antenna close to your operating position to minimize feed-line radiation
Position the antenna along the edge of a wall to reduce parasitic radiation
Make sure that MPE limits are not exceeded in occupied areas
Make sure the antenna is properly shielded
questions.x: Confirm that maximum permissible exposure limits are not exceeded where people actually are. An indoor antenna puts the highest field strength in an occupied room, so the evaluation matters far more than it does for a tower-mounted antenna.

questions.q: What stations are subject to the FCC rules on RF exposure?
a: All commercial stations; amateur radio stations are exempt
Only stations with antennas lower than one wavelength above the ground
Only stations transmitting more than 500 watts PEP
All stations with a time-averaged transmission of more than one milliwatt
questions.x: Every station transmitting more than one milliwatt time-averaged. The old blanket exemption for amateurs below certain power levels is gone; the rules now reach essentially all of us, with exemption decided by calculation rather than by license class.

questions.q: Which wire or wires in a four-conductor 240 VAC circuit should be attached to fuses or circuit breakers?
questions.x: Only the hot wires. Interrupting them stops the current and leaves the equipment at ground potential. Fusing the neutral or the ground could open the return path while a hot conductor stays live, which is worse than having no protection.

questions.q: According to the National Electrical Code, what is the minimum wire size that may be used safely for wiring with a 20-ampere circuit breaker?
questions.x: AWG 12 for a 20-amp breaker. The breaker protects the wire, so the wire must safely carry whatever the breaker allows. Pair the two numbers: 14 gauge with 15 amps, 12 gauge with 20.

questions.q: Which size of fuse or circuit breaker would be appropriate to use with a circuit that uses AWG number 14 wiring?
questions.x: 15 amperes for AWG 14. Same rule as G0B02 asked from the other direction. Fit a 20-amp breaker to 14-gauge wire and the wire becomes the fuse, which is how electrical fires start.

questions.q: Where should the station’s lightning protection ground system be located?
a: As close to the station equipment as possible
Next to the closest power pole
Parallel to the water supply line
questions.x: Outside the building. The point is to divert the surge to earth before it gets indoors. A ground system inside means the strike has already travelled past everything you were trying to protect.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions will cause a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) to disconnect AC power?
a: Current flowing from one or more of the hot wires to the neutral wire
Current flowing from one or more of the hot wires directly to ground
questions.x: A GFCI compares current leaving on the hot with current returning on the neutral. Any imbalance means current is finding another path to ground, possibly through a person, so it trips in milliseconds. It protects people, not equipment.

questions.q: Which of the following is covered by the National Electrical Code?
a: RF exposure limits of the human body
questions.x: The electrical safety of your station: wiring, grounding, bonding and overcurrent protection. The NEC is adopted into law by most localities, so it governs your shack even though the FCC has nothing to say about wiring.

questions.q: Which of these choices should be observed when climbing a tower using a safety harness?
a: Always hold on to the tower with one hand
Confirm that the harness is rated for the weight of the climber and that it is within its allowable service life
Ensure that all heavy tools are securely fastened to the harness
questions.x: Check both the weight rating and the service life. Harness webbing degrades from ultraviolet light and age even when it looks fine, so a harness found in the garage may be well past its date. Inspect before every climb.

questions.q: What should be done before climbing a tower that supports electrically powered devices?
a: Notify the electric company that a person will be working on the tower
Make sure all circuits that supply power to the tower are locked out and tagged
Unground the base of the tower
questions.x: Lock out and tag every circuit feeding the tower. Rotators, lights and amplifiers can be energized remotely by someone who has no idea you are up there. Locking the breaker and tagging it is what guarantees they cannot.

questions.q: Which of the following is true of an emergency generator installation?
a: The generator should be operated in a well-ventilated area
The generator must be insulated from ground
Fuel should be stored near the generator for rapid refueling in case of an emergency
questions.x: Run it in a well-ventilated area. Engine exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which is colourless, odourless and kills without warning. Generators must never run in a garage or basement, even with a door open.

questions.q: Which of the following is a danger from lead-tin solder?
a: Lead can contaminate food if hands are not washed carefully after handling the solder
High voltages can cause lead-tin solder to disintegrate suddenly
Tin in the solder can “cold flow,” causing shorts in the circuit
RF energy can convert the lead into a poisonous gas
questions.x: Lead transfers to your hands and then to whatever you eat. Wash before eating, and do not eat at the bench. The solder fumes are mostly flux rather than lead, since lead does not vaporize much at soldering temperatures.

questions.q: Which of the following is required for lightning protection ground rods?
a: They must be bonded to all buried water and gas lines
Bends in ground wires must be made as close as possible to a right angle
Lightning grounds must be connected to all ungrounded wiring
They must be bonded together with all other grounds
questions.x: All ground rods must be bonded together with every other ground at the site. Separate grounds sit at different potentials during a surge, and the difference drives current through your equipment as it equalizes. One bonded system, not several.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a power supply interlock?
a: To prevent unauthorized changes to the circuit that would void the manufacturer’s warranty
To shut down the unit if it becomes too hot
To ensure that dangerous voltages are removed if the cabinet is opened
To shut off the power supply if too much voltage is produced
questions.x: An interlock removes dangerous voltages when the cabinet is opened, usually by cutting the high-voltage supply as the cover comes off. It protects whoever opens the equipment from a supply they forgot was live. Never defeat one to work on a running amplifier.

questions.q: Where should lightning arrestors be located?
a: Where the feed lines enter the building
On the antenna, opposite the feed point
In series with each ground lead
At the closest power pole ground electrode
questions.x: Where the feed lines enter the building, on a grounded panel. Catching the surge at the entry point keeps it out of the shack. An arrestor further inside has already let the energy reach your equipment.

questions.q: On which HF and/or MF amateur bands are there portions where General class licensees cannot transmit?
questions.x: Four HF bands hold Extra-only segments at the bottom end: 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters. A General may not transmit there. Learn those four together, because G1A08 asks the same thing from the Extra side.

questions.q: On which of the following bands is phone operation prohibited?
questions.x: Thirty meters is CW and data only, for everyone. No phone, no image, no exceptions by license class. It is also a narrow band shared with other services, which is why the FCC keeps voice off it entirely.

questions.q: On which of the following bands is image transmission prohibited?
questions.x: Same band, same reason as G1A02. Thirty meters allows only CW and data emissions, so image transmission is out along with phone. If a question about 30 meters offers a mode other than CW or data, that mode is prohibited.

questions.q: On which of the following frequencies are General class licensees prohibited from operating as control operator?
questions.x: On 40 meters the General phone privileges begin at 7.175 MHz. Everything from 7.125 to 7.175 is reserved for Extra. Remember 7.175 as your lower edge on 40 meter voice.

questions.q: Which of the following applies when the FCC rules designate the amateur service as a secondary user on a band?
a: Amateur stations must record the call sign of the primary service station before operating on a frequency assigned to that station
Amateur stations may use the band only during emergencies
Amateur stations must not cause harmful interference to primary users and must accept interference from primary users
Amateur stations may only operate during specific hours of the day, while primary users are permitted 24-hour use of the band
questions.x: Secondary status cuts both ways. You must not cause harmful interference to the primary service, and you have to accept whatever interference it sends your way. You still get to operate there. You just have no standing to complain.

questions.q: On which amateur frequencies in the 10-meter band may stations with a General class control operator transmit CW emissions?
questions.x: CW is authorized "on any frequency authorized to the control operator," and a General holds the whole 10-meter band, 28.0 to 29.7 MHz. So CW is legal across all of it. That §97.305(a) principle answers a lot of CW questions.

questions.q: Which HF bands have segments exclusively allocated to Amateur Extra licensees?
a: All HF bands except 160 meters and 10 meters
questions.x: The bands with Extra-exclusive segments are 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters. Same four as G1A01, viewed from the other direction. No exclusive Extra spectrum exists on 30, 17, 12 or 10 meters.

questions.q: Which of the following frequencies is within the General class portion of the 15-meter band?
questions.x: General phone on 15 meters runs 21.275 to 21.450 MHz, so 21300 kHz sits comfortably inside. Watch the units when a question mixes kHz and MHz: 21300 kHz is 21.300 MHz.

questions.q: What portion of the 10-meter band is available for repeater use?
a: The portion between 28.1 MHz and 28.2 MHz
The portion between 28.3 MHz and 28.5 MHz
questions.x: Section 97.205(b) excludes 28.0 to 29.5 MHz from repeater use, which leaves the top of the band. Repeaters on 10 meters live above 29.5 MHz, and 29.6 MHz is the common simplex-repeater output.

questions.q: When General class licensees are not permitted to use the entire voice portion of a band, which portion of the voice segment is available to them?
a: The lower frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the upper portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
The upper frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the lower portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
questions.x: Where a General does not get the whole voice segment, the missing piece is always at the bottom, reserved for Extra. Generals work the upper portion. That pattern holds on every band, so the answer is the upper part of the segment.

questions.q: What is the maximum height above ground for an antenna structure not near a public use airport without requiring notification to the FAA and registration with the FCC?
questions.x: Structures over 200 feet above ground require FAA notification and FCC registration, and so do shorter ones near a public use airport. Two hundred feet is the number, and note it is measured above ground level at the site, not above sea level.

questions.q: With which of the following conditions must beacon stations comply?
a: No more than one beacon station may transmit in the same band from the same station location
The frequency must be coordinated with the National Beacon Organization
The frequency must be posted on the internet or published in a national periodical
questions.x: A beacon "must not concurrently transmit on more than 1 channel in the same amateur service frequency band, from the same station location." One beacon per band per site. Nothing stops you running beacons on several different bands.

questions.q: Which of the following is a purpose of a beacon station as identified in the FCC rules?
a: Transmission of bulletins of general interest to amateur radio licensees
questions.x: The definition gives the purpose directly: a beacon transmits "for the purposes of observation of propagation and reception or other related experimental activities." Propagation observation is the phrase to match.

questions.q: Which of the following transmissions is permitted for all amateur stations?
a: Unidentified transmissions of less than 10 seconds duration for test purposes only
Automatic retransmission of other amateur signals by any amateur station
Occasional retransmission of weather and propagation forecast information from US government stations
Encrypted messages, if not intended to facilitate a criminal act
questions.x: You generally may not retransmit non-amateur signals, but §97.113(c) carves out propagation and weather forecast information originating from US Government stations. It must be occasional rather than routine, which the rule states plainly.

questions.q: Which of the following one-way transmissions are permitted?
a: Unidentified test transmissions of less than 10 seconds in duration
Transmissions to assist with learning the International Morse code
Regular transmissions offering equipment for sale, if intended for amateur radio use
questions.x: Section 97.111(b) lists the permitted one-way transmissions, and paragraph (5) covers "transmissions necessary to assisting persons learning, or improving proficiency in, the international Morse code." Code practice made the list; general broadcasting never does.

questions.q: Under what conditions are state and local governments permitted to regulate amateur radio antenna structures?
a: Under no circumstances, FCC rules take priority
At any time and to any extent necessary to accomplish a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity, provided that proper filings are made with the FCC
Only when such structures exceed 50 feet in height and are clearly visible 1,000 feet from the structure
Amateur Service communications must be reasonably accommodated, and regulations must constitute the minimum practical to accommodate a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity
questions.x: This is the PRB-1 standard, written into §97.15(b). Local regulation of amateur antenna structures "must have a reasonable and clearly defined objective" and constitute the minimum practical regulation, and it must reasonably accommodate amateur communications. Reasonable accommodation and minimum practical are the two phrases.

questions.q: What are the restrictions on the use of abbreviations or procedural signals in the amateur service?
a: They may be used if they do not obscure the meaning of a message
They are limited to those expressly listed in Part 97 of the FCC rules
questions.x: Q signals, prosigns and the usual on-air shorthand are fine. What the rule forbids is "messages encoded for the purpose of obscuring their meaning." Standard abbreviations aid communication rather than hide it, so intent is the dividing line.

questions.q: When is it permissible to communicate with amateur stations in countries outside the areas administered by the Federal Communications Commission?
a: Only when the foreign country has a formal third-party agreement filed with the FCC
When the contact is with amateurs in any country except those whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object to such communications
Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the United Nations, or by a territory possessed by such a country
Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the International Amateur Radio Union, or by a territory possessed by such a country
questions.x: You may work amateurs anywhere except in countries whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object. The objection must be filed with the ITU. Same rule tested in T1D01 on the Technician exam.

questions.q: On what HF frequencies are automatically controlled beacons permitted?
a: On any frequency if power is less than 1 watt
On any frequency if transmissions are in Morse code
questions.x: On HF the only segment where a beacon may run under automatic control is 28.20 to 28.30 MHz. Ten meters again, and the same range the Technician exam asks about.

questions.q: What is the power limit for beacon stations?
questions.x: Section 97.203(c) is one line: beacon transmitter power "must not exceed 100 W." A beacon exists to report whether a path is open, and more power would only distort that picture.

questions.q: Who or what determines “good engineering and good amateur practice,” as applied to the operation of an amateur station in all respects not covered by the Part 97 rules?
questions.x: Where Part 97 is silent, stations must operate "in accordance with good engineering and good amateur practice," and the FCC decides what that means. Not the ARRL, not your club, not the frequency coordinator. The Commission is the arbiter.

questions.q: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on 10.140 MHz?
questions.x: 10.140 MHz sits in the 30-meter band, 10.100 to 10.150 MHz, and §97.313(c)(1) caps that whole segment at 200 watts PEP for everyone. Thirty meters is the low-power band, so the answer is 200 watts.

questions.q: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on the 12-meter band?
a: An effective radiated power equivalent to 100 watts from a half-wave dipole
questions.x: Twelve meters carries no special restriction, so the general ceiling applies: 1.5 kW PEP, or 1500 watts. Only a short list of segments deviates from that, and 30 meters is the one most likely to appear on your exam.

questions.q: What is the maximum bandwidth permitted by FCC rules for amateur radio stations transmitting on USB frequencies in the 60-meter band?
questions.x: The rule requires that on all 60-meter spectrum, "amateur operators shall ensure that their emissions do not occupy more than 2.8 kHz." That figure matches a normal SSB signal, which is why standard voice gear works there unmodified.

questions.q: Which of the following is required by the FCC rules when operating in the 60-meter band?
a: If you are using an antenna other than a dipole, you must keep a record of the gain of your antenna
You must keep a record of the date, time, frequency, power level, and stations worked
You must keep a record of all third-party traffic
You must keep a record of the manufacturer of your equipment and the antenna used
questions.x: Sixty-meter power is specified as ERP referenced to a dipole, so the FCC needs to know your antenna gain to police it. If you use anything other than a dipole, keep the manufacturer's gain data or your own calculations in your station records.

questions.q: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 28 MHz band for a General Class control operator?
questions.x: A General on 10 meters gets the full 1500 watts PEP. The 200-watt cap that applies to Technicians on 28.0 to 28.5 MHz is tied to the operator class, not the band, so it does not follow you after you upgrade.

questions.q: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 1.8 MHz band?
questions.x: The 1.8 MHz band is 160 meters, and it carries no special power restriction. The general limit applies: 1500 watts PEP. When a power question names a band with no listed exception, 1500 watts is the default.

questions.q: What must be done before using a new digital protocol on the air?
a: Obtain an experimental license from the FCC
Publicly document the technical characteristics of the protocol
Submit a rule-making proposal to the FCC describing the codes and methods of the technique
questions.x: An amateur station may use any digital technique "whose technical characteristics have been documented publicly." Public documentation is what keeps a mode from counting as an obscuring code. No FCC approval or certification is needed, only publication.

questions.q: What measurement is specified by FCC rules that regulate maximum power?
questions.x: All amateur power limits are written as PEP output measured at the transmitter, not input power and not what the amplifier draws from the wall. Section 97.3 defines PEP as the average power supplied to the antenna transmission line at the crest of the modulation envelope.

questions.q: Who may receive partial credit for the elements represented by an expired amateur radio license?
a: Any person who can demonstrate that they once held an FCC-issued General, Advanced, or Amateur Extra class license that was not revoked by the FCC
Anyone who held an FCC-issued amateur radio license that expired not less than 5 and not more than 15 years ago
Any person who previously held an amateur license issued by another country, but only if that country has a current reciprocal licensing agreement with the FCC
Only persons who once held an FCC issued Novice, Technician, or Technician Plus license
questions.x: Element credit for an expired license survives indefinitely, as long as the license was General, Advanced or Extra and was not revoked. You show proof of the old grant and the VEs give credit for the written element it represented. Revocation is the one thing that kills it.

questions.q: What license examinations may you administer as an accredited Volunteer Examiner holding a General class operator license?
a: None, only Amateur Extra class licensees may be accredited
questions.x: A VE may administer exams one full class below their own license. General class VEs administer Technician exams only. Extra or Advanced is needed for General exams, and Extra alone for Extra exams.

questions.q: On which of the following band segments may you operate if you are a Technician class operator and have an unexpired Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE) for General class privileges?
a: Only the Technician band segments until your upgrade is posted in the FCC database
Only on the Technician band segments until you have a receipt for the FCC application fee payment
On any General or Technician class band segment
On any General or Technician class band segment except 30 meters and 60 meters
questions.x: An unexpired CSCE gives you the new privileges immediately, before the FCC database catches up. With a General CSCE in hand a Technician may work any General or Technician segment. Identify with the AG indicator while doing it, per §97.119(f)(2).

questions.q: Who must observe the administration of a Technician class license examination?
a: At least three Volunteer Examiners of General class or higher
At least two Volunteer Examiners of General class or higher
At least two Volunteer Examiners of Technician class or higher
At least three Volunteer Examiners of Technician class
questions.x: Every amateur exam session takes a team of at least three accredited VEs, and for a Technician exam each must hold General or higher. Three is the number, and all three observe the entire examination.

questions.q: When operating a US station by remote control from outside the country, what license is required of the control operator?
a: Only an appropriate US operator/primary license and a special remote station permit from the FCC
Only a license from the foreign country, as long as the call sign includes identification of portable operation in the US
A license from the foreign country and a special remote station permit from the FCC
questions.x: The station is a US station, so US rules follow it regardless of where the operator is sitting. Section 97.7 requires a control operator holding an FCC operator/primary station license. Your physical location does not change what the station needs.

questions.q: Until an upgrade to General class is shown in the FCC database, when must a Technician licensee identify with “AG” after their call sign?
a: Whenever they operate using General class frequency privileges
Whenever they operate on any amateur frequency
Whenever they operate using Technician frequency privileges
A special identifier is not required if their General class license application has been filed with the FCC
questions.x: The AG indicator is required whenever you use the General privileges you have not yet been granted on paper. Operating inside Technician limits needs no indicator. Once the upgrade appears in the FCC database, you stop using AG entirely.

questions.q: Volunteer Examiners are accredited by what organization?
questions.x: Volunteer Examiners are accredited by a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator, the VEC. The FCC certifies VECs and the VECs accredit individual VEs. The Commission never accredits a VE directly.

questions.q: Which of the following criteria must be met for a non-US citizen to be an accredited Volunteer Examiner?
a: The person must be a resident of the US for a minimum of 5 years
The person must hold an FCC granted amateur radio license of General class or above
The person’s home citizenship must be in ITU region 2
None of these choices is correct; a non-US citizen cannot be a Volunteer Examiner
questions.x: Citizenship is not a requirement anywhere in §97.509. What matters is holding an FCC-granted license of General class or above, being at least 18, and never having had a license revoked or suspended.

questions.q: How long is a Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE) valid for exam element credit?
a: For as long as your current license is valid
questions.x: A CSCE is good for 365 days of element credit. One year, and then the credit is gone and the element must be passed again. Note that it gives operating privileges too, under §97.9(b), until the upgrade posts.

questions.q: What is the minimum age that one must be to qualify as an accredited Volunteer Examiner?
questions.x: A VE must be at least 18 years of age. There is no upper age limit and no minimum time licensed, just 18 and the required license class.

questions.q: What action is required to obtain a new General class license after a previously held license has expired and the two-year grace period has passed?
a: They must have a letter from the FCC showing they once held an amateur or commercial license
There are no requirements other than being able to show a copy of the expired license
Contact the FCC to have the license reinstated
The applicant must show proof of the appropriate expired license grant and pass the current Element 2 exam
questions.x: Once the two-year grace period lapses the license is gone, but the element credit is not. Show proof of the expired General grant and you keep Element 3 credit. You still have to sit the current Element 2 exam, because that credit does not carry.

questions.q: When operating a station in South America by remote control over the internet from the US, what regulations apply?
a: Those of both the remote station’s country and the FCC
Those of the remote station’s country and the FCC’s third-party regulations
Only those of the remote station’s country
questions.x: A remotely controlled station is operating where the transmitter is, not where you are. Point the radio at South America and that country's regulations govern the transmission. Your US license does not extend its rules abroad.

questions.q: Which of the following would disqualify a third party from participating in sending a message via an amateur station?
a: The third party’s amateur license has been revoked and not reinstated
The third party is not a US citizen
The third party is speaking in a language other than English
questions.x: A third party is disqualified if they were previously licensed and that license was revoked or suspended and not reinstated. Ordinary unlicensed people are welcome to speak. The bar is aimed at someone the FCC has already sanctioned.

questions.q: When may a 10-meter repeater retransmit the 2-meter signal from a station that has a Technician class control operator?
a: Only if the station on 10-meters is operating under a Special Temporary Authorization allowing such retransmission
Only during an FCC-declared general state of communications emergency
Only if the 10-meter repeater control operator holds at least a General class license
questions.x: The repeater's control operator sets what the repeater may transmit, and 10-meter privileges require General or higher. A Technician may feed the input on 2 meters, but the General class control operator is what makes the 10-meter output legal.

questions.q: What is required to conduct communications with a digital station operating under automatic control outside the automatic control band segments?
a: The station initiating the contact must be under local or remote control
The interrogating transmission must be made by another automatically controlled station
No third-party traffic may be transmitted
The control operator of the interrogating station must hold an Amateur Extra class license
questions.x: Outside the automatic control segments, an automatically controlled digital station may only respond. Section 97.221(c) requires that it be "responding to interrogation by a station under local or remote control," and that its transmissions stay within 500 Hz.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions require a licensed amateur radio operator to take specific steps to avoid harmful interference to other users or facilities?
a: When operating within one mile of an FCC Monitoring Station
When using a band where the Amateur Service is secondary
When a station is transmitting spread spectrum emissions
questions.x: Three separate rules each impose a duty to avoid interference: proximity to an FCC monitoring station, operating on a secondary allocation, and running spread spectrum. Since every listed condition carries that obligation, the inclusive answer is correct.

questions.q: What are the restrictions on messages sent to a third party in a country with which there is a Third-Party Agreement?
a: They must relate to emergencies or disaster relief
They must be for other licensed amateurs
They must relate to amateur radio, or remarks of a personal character, or messages relating to emergencies or disaster relief
The message must be limited to no longer than 1 minute in duration and the name of the third party must be recorded in the station log
questions.x: Even with a third-party agreement in place, the content limits of §97.117 still apply: matters incidental to amateur radio and remarks of a personal character, plus emergency and disaster relief traffic. An agreement opens the door, it does not remove the content rules.

questions.q: The frequency allocations of which ITU region apply to radio amateurs operating in North and South America?
questions.x: The ITU divides the world into three regions. Region 1 is Europe, Africa and northern Asia, Region 3 is the rest of Asia and Oceania, and Region 2 is the Americas. North and South America are Region 2.

questions.q: In what part of the 2.4 GHz band may an amateur station communicate with non-licensed Wi-Fi stations?
questions.x: Section 97.111 lists who an amateur station may communicate with, and unlicensed Part 15 devices are not on that list. Sharing spectrum with Wi-Fi in the 2.4 GHz band does not create permission to work those stations. No part of the band.

questions.q: What is the maximum PEP output allowed for spread spectrum transmissions?
questions.x: Spread spectrum is capped hard: "No station may transmit with a transmitter output exceeding 10 W PEP when the station is transmitting a SS emission type." Ten watts, because SS energy spreads across spectrum other users occupy.

questions.q: Why should an amateur operator normally avoid transmitting on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz?
a: A system of propagation beacon stations operates on those frequencies
A system of automatic digital stations operates on those frequencies
These frequencies are set aside for emergency operations
These frequencies are set aside for bulletins from the FCC
questions.x: Those five frequencies carry the International Beacon Project network, where synchronized beacons around the world transmit in rotation so operators can gauge propagation. Transmitting there breaks a shared resource, which §97.101(a) treats as poor amateur practice.

questions.q: On what bands may automatically controlled stations transmitting RTTY or data emissions communicate with other automatically controlled digital stations?
a: On any band segment where digital operation is permitted
Anywhere in the non-phone segments of the 10-meter or shorter wavelength bands
Only in the non-phone Extra Class segments of the bands
Anywhere in the 6-meter or shorter wavelength bands, and in limited segments of some of the HF bands
questions.x: Automatic control for digital stations is wide open on 6 meters and everything shorter. On HF it is confined to narrow slices such as 28.120 to 28.189 MHz and 21.090 to 21.100 MHz. Above 50 MHz anywhere, below it only in listed segments.

questions.q: When may third-party messages be transmitted via remote control?
a: Under any circumstances in which third party messages are permitted by FCC rules
Under no circumstances except for emergencies
Only when the message is intended for licensed radio amateurs
Only when the message is intended for third parties in areas where licensing is controlled by the FCC
questions.x: Section 97.115 sets conditions on third-party traffic but says nothing about how the station is controlled. Remote control neither adds restrictions nor removes them. If the message would be legal at the radio, it is legal from a distance.

questions.q: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on frequencies of 14 MHz or higher?
questions.x: One convention covers all the sideband questions: 20 meters and up is upper sideband, 40 meters and down is lower. At 14 MHz and above you use USB. Learn the dividing line once and G2A01 through G2A04 all fall out of it.
questions.xs: ARRL band plans; ARRL Operating Manual

questions.q: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
questions.x: The three lowest phone bands use lower sideband: 160, 75 and 40 meters. Everything from 20 meters upward uses upper. The break sits between 40 and 20, with no phone on 30 meters in between.

questions.q: Which mode is most commonly used for SSB voice communications in the VHF and UHF bands?
questions.x: SSB above 50 MHz is upper sideband, following the same rule as 20 meters and up. VHF and UHF weak-signal work is also horizontally polarized by convention, which is worth remembering alongside it.

questions.q: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 17- and 12-meter bands?
questions.x: Seventeen and 12 meters are both above 14 MHz, so both use upper sideband. Any band higher in frequency than 20 meters follows the USB convention.

questions.q: Which mode of voice communication is most commonly used on the HF amateur bands?
questions.x: Single sideband dominates HF voice. It fits roughly 3 kHz where AM needs 6, and it puts all the transmitter's power into the one sideband that carries the intelligence rather than into a carrier that carries none.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of using single sideband, as compared to other analog voice modes on the HF amateur bands?
a: Less subject to interference from atmospheric static crashes
Ease of tuning on receive and immunity to impulse noise
Less bandwidth used and greater power efficiency
questions.x: Two advantages at once, and the answer names both: half the bandwidth of AM and far better power efficiency, since nothing is wasted on a carrier or a redundant second sideband. That combination is why SSB displaced AM on HF.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true of single sideband (SSB)?
a: Only one sideband and the carrier are transmitted; the other sideband is suppressed
Only one sideband is transmitted; the other sideband and carrier are suppressed
SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 20-, 15-, and 10-meter amateur bands
SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter amateur bands
questions.x: SSB starts as double-sideband AM, then the carrier and one sideband are suppressed. Both sidebands carry identical information, so discarding one loses nothing while halving the bandwidth.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to break into a phone contact?
a: Say “QRZ” several times, followed by your call sign
Say “CQ” followed by the call sign of either station
questions.x: Say your call sign once, during a pause between transmissions. Not "break," not "contact," and not repeatedly. Your call sign identifies you and requests entry in one step, which is why it is the accepted practice.

questions.q: Why do most amateur stations use lower sideband on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
a: Lower sideband is more efficient than upper sideband at these frequencies
Lower sideband is the only sideband legal on these frequency bands
Because it is fully compatible with an AM detector
It is commonly accepted amateur practice
questions.x: There is no rule requiring it and no technical reason for it. The LSB convention on the low bands is simply what equipment manufacturers and operators settled on decades ago. Custom, not regulation.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true of VOX operation versus PTT operation?
a: The received signal is more natural sounding
questions.x: VOX keys the transmitter from your voice, so your hands stay free. The tradeoff is that room noise can trip it and pauses can drop you mid-sentence, which is why many operators still prefer a foot switch.

questions.q: Generally, who should respond to a station in the contiguous 48 states calling “CQ DX”?
a: Any caller is welcome to respond
Any stations outside the lower 48 states
questions.x: CQ DX means the caller wants contacts outside their own country. From the contiguous 48 states that means stations outside the lower 48, so Alaska and Hawaii count. If you are inside the 48 and hear it, the call is not for you.

questions.q: What control is typically adjusted for proper ALC setting on a single sideband transceiver?
questions.x: ALC responds to how hard your audio drives the transmitter, so microphone or transmit audio gain is the control that sets it. Adjust until ALC just registers on peaks. Beyond that you are only adding distortion and splatter.

questions.q: Which of the following is true concerning access to frequencies?
a: Except during emergencies, no amateur station has priority access to any frequency
Contest operations should yield to non-contest use of frequencies
questions.x: Part 97 settles it: "no frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station." Nobody owns a frequency, not nets, not repeater groups, not contesters. The one exception in §97.101(c) is emergency traffic, which gets priority.

questions.q: What is the first thing you should do if you are communicating with another amateur station and hear a station in distress break in?
a: Acknowledge the station in distress and determine what assistance may be needed
Immediately decrease power to avoid interfering with the station in distress
questions.x: Acknowledge them and find out what they need. Distress traffic outranks whatever you were doing, and §97.403 lets you use any means at your disposal to help. Do not simply move aside and hope somebody else takes it.

questions.q: What is good amateur practice if propagation changes during a contact creating interference from other stations using the frequency?
a: Advise the interfering stations that you are on the frequency and that you have priority
Decrease power and continue to transmit
Attempt to resolve the interference problem with the other stations in a mutually acceptable manner
questions.x: Work it out with the other stations in a way everyone can accept. Propagation shifts constantly and nobody involved did anything wrong. Since no station holds a frequency exclusively, cooperation is the only mechanism available.

questions.q: When selecting a CW transmitting frequency, what minimum separation from other stations should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
questions.x: Leave 150 to 500 Hz between CW signals. A CW signal is only about 150 Hz wide, so that spacing keeps you clear of the other operator's receive filter without wasting band space.

questions.q: When selecting an SSB transmitting frequency, what minimum separation should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
questions.x: Two to 3 kHz for SSB, because the signal itself occupies about 3 kHz. Space them closer and your sidebands land inside the neighbouring station's passband. Compare with the 150 to 500 Hz needed for far narrower CW.

questions.q: How can you avoid harmful interference on an apparently clear frequency before calling CQ on CW or phone?
a: Send “QRL?” on CW, followed by your call sign; or, if using phone, ask if the frequency is in use, followed by your call sign
Listen for 2 minutes before calling CQ
Send the letter “V” in Morse code several times and listen for a response, or say “test” several times and listen for a response
Send “QSY” on CW or if using phone, announce “the frequency is in use,” then give your call sign and listen for a response
questions.x: Ask before you call. Send "QRL?" with your call sign on CW, or ask whether the frequency is in use on phone. A frequency can sound clear when one end of an existing contact is simply out of your propagation path.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual

questions.q: Which of the following complies with commonly accepted amateur practice when choosing a frequency on which to initiate a call?
a: Listen on the frequency for at least two minutes to be sure it is clear
Identify your station by transmitting your call sign at least 3 times
questions.x: Follow the voluntary band plan. It is not FCC-enforced, but it keeps CW, digital, SSB and beacons out of each other's way, and ignoring it counts against good amateur practice under §97.101(a).

questions.q: What is the voluntary band plan restriction for US stations transmitting within the 48 contiguous states in the 50.1 MHz to 50.125 MHz band segment?
a: Only contacts with stations not within the 48 contiguous states
Only contacts with other stations within the 48 contiguous states
questions.x: That segment is the 6-meter DX window. Stations inside the 48 contiguous states use it only for contacts with stations outside the 48, keeping it clear for the rare openings that make long-haul 6-meter work possible.

questions.q: Who may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES to assist relief operations during a disaster?
a: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license
Only a RACES net control operator
A person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license or an appropriate government official
Any control operator when normal communication systems are operational
questions.x: Only a licensed amateur. RACES runs on amateur frequencies under Part 97, so the control operator needs an FCC amateur license plus certification by the civil defense organization. An emergency does not waive the license requirement.

questions.q: Which of the following is good amateur practice for net management?
a: Always use multiple sets of phonetics during check-in
Have a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions
Transmit the full net roster at the beginning of every session
questions.x: Agree on a backup frequency in advance. Nets get stepped on and propagation fails, and negotiating a new frequency while the net is falling apart does not work. Announce the alternate before you need it.

questions.q: How often may RACES training drills and tests be routinely conducted without special authorization?
a: No more than 1 hour per month
No more than 2 hours per month
No more than 1 hour per week
No more than 2 hours per week
questions.x: One hour per week. The rule permits RACES drills and tests "not to exceed a total time of 1 hour per week" without special authorization. More than that requires approval from the state emergency planning officer.

questions.q: Which of the following describes full break-in CW operation (QSK)?
a: Breaking stations send the Morse code prosign “BK”
Automatic keyers, instead of hand keys, are used to send Morse code
An operator must activate a manual send/receive switch before and after every transmission
Transmitting stations can receive between code characters and elements
questions.x: QSK means your receiver is live between the elements of your own characters, so you hear another station the instant they start sending. It makes CW feel like a conversation rather than an exchange of speeches, since anyone can break in mid-word.

questions.q: What should you do if a CW station sends “QRS?”
questions.x: QRS means send more slowly. Its opposite is QRQ, send faster. If someone sends QRS they are struggling to copy you, so slow down rather than repeating at the same speed.

questions.q: What does it mean when a CW operator sends “KN” at the end of a transmission?
a: Listening only for a specific station or stations
questions.x: KN closes the transmission to everyone except the station you are working. Plain K invites anyone to call; adding the N narrows it. Use KN when you are in a contact and do not want new callers joining.

questions.q: What does the Q signal “QRL?” mean?
a: “Are you operating full break-in?” or “Can you operate full break-in?”
“Are you listening only for a specific station?”
“Are you busy?” or “Is this frequency in use?”
questions.x: QRL? asks whether the frequency is in use, literally "are you busy?" Send it before calling CQ on a frequency that sounds clear. A bare QRL as a statement means the frequency is busy.

questions.q: What is the best speed to use when answering a CQ in Morse code?
a: The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no slower than the CQ
The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no faster than the CQ
At the standard calling speed of 10 wpm
At the standard calling speed of 5 wpm
questions.x: Answer at a speed you can copy comfortably, and never faster than the CQ was sent. Replying faster than someone can receive gets you nowhere, and matching their speed signals that the contact will work.

questions.q: What does the term “zero beat” mean in CW operation?
a: Matching the speed of the transmitting station
Operating split to avoid interference on frequency
Matching the transmit frequency to the frequency of a received signal
questions.x: Zero beat means tuning your transmit frequency onto the other station's, so the audio tone difference between you drops toward zero. Being exactly on frequency puts you in the middle of their filter, where you are loudest.

questions.q: When sending CW, what does a “C” mean when added to the RST report?
a: Report was read from an S meter rather than estimated
questions.x: A trailing C reports a chirpy signal, meaning the frequency shifts slightly each time the key closes. It usually points at a power supply sagging under keying load. The RST report also uses X for a steady signal and K for key clicks.

questions.q: What prosign is sent to indicate the end of a formal message when using CW?
questions.x: AR, sent as one run-together character, marks the end of a formal message. Do not confuse it with SK, which ends the entire contact, or with K, which simply invites a reply.
questions.xs: ARRL Operating Manual; ITU-R Rec. M.1677

questions.q: What does the Q signal “QSL” mean?
a: We have already confirmed the contact
questions.x: QSL means I have received and understood. As a question it asks whether you were copied. The paper QSL card takes its name from this signal, since the card is written confirmation of the same thing.

questions.q: What does the Q signal “QRN” mean?
questions.x: QRN is natural static, the crash of distant lightning. Keep it apart from QRM, which is interference from other stations. QRN is nature, QRM is people.

questions.q: What does the Q signal “QRV” mean?
a: There is interference on the frequency
I am quitting for the day
questions.x: QRV means I am ready. It reports that you are standing by and able to receive, which is why net operators use it to check in.

questions.q: What is the Volunteer Monitor Program?
a: Amateur volunteers who are formally enlisted to monitor the airwaves for rules violations
Amateur volunteers who conduct amateur licensing examinations
Amateur volunteers who conduct frequency coordination for amateur VHF repeaters
Amateur volunteers who use their station equipment to help civil defense organizations in times of emergency
questions.x: The Volunteer Monitor Program is licensed amateurs formally enlisted, under an agreement between the ARRL and the FCC, to monitor the bands for rules violations. It replaced the older Official Observer program in 2019.
questions.xs: ARRL Volunteer Monitor Program; FCC agreement

questions.q: Which of the following are objectives of the Volunteer Monitor Program?
a: To conduct efficient and orderly amateur licensing examinations
To provide emergency and public safety communications
To coordinate repeaters for efficient and orderly spectrum usage
To encourage amateur radio operators to self-regulate and comply with the rules
questions.x: The aim is self-regulation: encourage amateurs to comply voluntarily and document the cases that genuinely need FCC attention. Monitors have no enforcement power of their own. They gather evidence and educate.

questions.q: What procedure may be used by Volunteer Monitors to localize a station whose continuous carrier is holding a repeater on in their area?
a: Compare vertical and horizontal signal strengths on the input frequency
Compare beam headings on the repeater input from their home locations with that of other Volunteer Monitors
Compare signal strengths between the input and output of the repeater
questions.x: Several monitors take beam headings on the repeater input from their own locations and compare them. Where the bearings intersect is the transmitter. One bearing gives a line, and it takes two or more to fix a position.

questions.q: Which of the following describes an azimuthal projection map?
a: A map that shows accurate land masses
A map that shows true bearings and distances from a specific location
A map that shows the angle at which an amateur satellite crosses the equator
A map that shows the number of degrees longitude that an amateur satellite appears to move westward at the equator with each orbit
questions.x: An azimuthal projection centred on your station shows true bearings and distances from that one point. Straight lines out from the centre are great-circle paths, so you read the beam heading to anywhere directly off the map.
questions.xs: Map projection theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: Which of the following indicates that you are looking for an HF contact with any station?
a: Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call” -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
Say “QTC” followed by “this is” and your call sign -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” then your call sign a few times, then pause to listen, repeat as necessary
Transmit an unmodulated carried for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen -- repeat as necessary
questions.x: Repeat CQ a few times, say "this is," give your call sign a few times, then stop and listen. The rhythm matters more than the words: calling too long means transmitting over the people trying to answer you.

questions.q: How is a directional antenna pointed when making a “long-path” contact with another station?
a: 180 degrees from the station’s short-path heading
questions.x: Long path is 180 degrees from the short-path heading, going the other way around the Earth. It is a longer route so it needs better conditions, but sometimes the long way is open when the direct path is not.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of the NATO Phonetic Alphabet?
questions.x: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta opens the standard phonetic alphabet, used internationally by aviation, the military and amateur radio alike. Sticking to the standard words matters because improvised substitutes are exactly what gets misheard.

questions.q: Why do many amateurs keep a station log?
a: The FCC requires a log of all international contacts
The FCC requires a log of all international third-party traffic
The log provides evidence of operation needed to renew a license without retest
To help with a reply if the FCC requests information about your station
questions.x: Logs are no longer required by the FCC, but they help you answer if the Commission asks about your station's operation. They also serve awards and QSL work, which is why most operators keep one anyway.

questions.q: Which of the following is required when participating in a contest on HF frequencies?
a: Submit a log to the contest sponsor
Send a QSL card to the stations worked, or QSL via Logbook of The World
Identify your station according to normal FCC regulations
questions.x: Nothing special. Contest rules do not change FCC requirements, so you still identify at least every 10 minutes and at the end of each contact. Contest exchanges are brief, but the identification rule is unchanged.

questions.q: What is QRP operation?
questions.x: QRP means low power, conventionally 5 watts output or less on CW and 10 watts on phone. It comes from the Q signal QRP, which means reduce power.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. M.1172; ARRL Operating Manual

questions.q: Why are signal reports typically exchanged at the beginning of an HF contact?
a: To allow each station to operate according to conditions
To be sure the contact will count for award programs
To allow each station to calibrate their frequency display
questions.x: An early signal report tells each operator what the path will support, so you can decide whether to slow down, repeat more, or switch modes. It is practical information at the start of a contact rather than a courtesy.

questions.q: Which mode is normally used when sending RTTY signals via AFSK with an SSB transmitter?
questions.x: RTTY sent as AFSK through an SSB transmitter uses lower sideband, which puts the mark and space tones in the same relationship as a direct FSK transmitter. Note this is the exception: the newer WSJT modes use USB instead.

questions.q: What is VARA?
a: A low signal-to-noise digital mode used for EME (moonbounce)
A digital protocol used with Winlink
A radio direction finding system used on VHF and UHF
A DX spotting system using a network of software defined radios
questions.x: VARA is a high-throughput digital protocol used with Winlink, adapting its speed to conditions on the path. It moves email and files considerably faster than the older PACTOR modes it competes with.

questions.q: What symptoms may result from other signals interfering with a PACTOR or VARA transmission?
a: Failure to establish a connection between stations
questions.x: Interference on an ARQ link shows up as repeated retries, slower throughput, and eventually a dropped connection. All the listed symptoms are genuine, so the inclusive answer applies. The protocol is protecting your data by resending it.

questions.q: Which of the following is good practice when choosing a transmitting frequency to answer a station calling CQ using FT8?
a: Always call on the station’s frequency
Call on any frequency in the waterfall except the station’s frequency
Find a clear frequency during the same time slot as the calling station
Find a clear frequency during the alternate time slot to the calling station
questions.x: FT8 alternates 15-second slots, so answer in the slot the caller is not using and pick a clear audio frequency. Transmitting in their slot means neither of you hears the other.

questions.q: What is the standard sideband for JT65, JT9, FT4, or FT8 digital signal when using AFSK?
questions.x: JT65, JT9, FT4 and FT8 all use upper sideband. This is where the WSJT family departs from RTTY, which uses LSB. If you set the wrong sideband nothing decodes, since the tones land inverted.

questions.q: What is the most common frequency shift for RTTY emissions in the amateur HF bands?
questions.x: A 170 Hz shift between mark and space is the amateur HF standard, paired with 45 baud. Commercial and military RTTY used wider shifts; amateurs settled on 170 Hz to keep the signal narrow.

questions.q: Which of the following is required when using FT8?
a: Computer time accurate to within approximately 1 second
questions.x: Your computer clock must be right to within about a second. FT8 slices time into fixed 15-second windows and decodes on that schedule, so a clock off by a few seconds means the software looks for signals in the wrong interval.

questions.q: In what segment of the 20-meter band are most digital mode operations commonly found?
a: At the bottom of the slow-scan TV segment, near 14.230 MHz
At the top of the SSB phone segment, near 14.325 MHz
In the middle of the CW segment, near 14.100 MHz
questions.x: Digital modes on 20 meters cluster between 14.070 and 14.100 MHz. That 30 kHz window holds RTTY, PSK and the WSJT modes, which is why FT8 at 14.074 sits inside it.

questions.q: How do you join a contact between two stations using the PACTOR protocol?
a: Send broadcast packets containing your call sign while in MONITOR mode
Transmit a steady carrier until the PACTOR protocol times out and disconnects
Joining an existing contact is not possible, PACTOR connections are limited to two stations
questions.x: You cannot join. PACTOR is a point-to-point ARQ link between exactly two stations, with each end acknowledging the other's blocks. There is no provision for a third participant, unlike a plain conversational mode.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way to establish contact with a digital messaging system gateway station?
a: Send an email to the system control operator
Respond when the station broadcasts its SSID
Transmit a connect message on the station’s published frequency
