questions.x: Send a connect message on the gateway's published frequency. Gateways advertise their frequencies and operating hours, and your software then negotiates the link automatically.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of an Amateur Radio Emergency Data Network (AREDN) mesh network?
a: To provide FM repeater coverage in remote areas
To provide real time propagation data by monitoring amateur radio transmissions worldwide
To provide high-speed data services during an emergency or community event
To provide DX spotting reports to aid contesters and DXers
questions.x: AREDN builds a high-speed data network from repurposed Wi-Fi hardware, carrying services that ordinary HF data rates cannot: video, file transfer, voice over IP. It is designed for emergencies and community events where normal infrastructure is unavailable.

questions.q: Which of the following describes Winlink?
a: An amateur radio wireless network to send and receive email on the internet
A wireless network capable of both VHF and HF band operation
questions.x: Winlink is all of these: a radio email system, a network of gateway stations, and a service usable over both HF and VHF. Since every listed description is accurate, the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: What is another name for a Winlink Remote Message Server?
questions.x: A Remote Message Server is a gateway, the station bridging radio and the internet so your message reaches ordinary email. Same idea as an IRLP node bridging repeaters.

questions.q: What could be wrong if you cannot decode an RTTY or other FSK signal even though it is apparently tuned in properly?
a: The mark and space frequencies may be reversed
You may have selected the wrong baud rate
You may be listening on the wrong sideband
questions.x: An FSK signal that looks tuned but will not decode usually means inverted mark and space, the wrong baud rate or shift, or the wrong sideband. All the listed faults produce exactly this symptom, so the inclusive answer applies.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common location for FT8?
a: Anywhere in the voice portion of the band
Anywhere in the CW portion of the band
questions.x: FT8 on 20 meters lives around 14.074 to 14.077 MHz, inside the wider digital segment that starts at 14.070. It is the busiest few kilohertz in amateur radio most days.
questions.xs: WSJT-X documentation; ARRL 20 m band plan

questions.q: How does a higher sunspot number affect HF propagation?
a: Higher sunspot numbers generally indicate a greater probability of good propagation at higher frequencies
Lower sunspot numbers generally indicate greater probability of sporadic E propagation
A zero sunspot number indicates that radio propagation is not possible on any band
A zero sunspot number indicates undisturbed conditions
questions.x: More sunspots means more solar ultraviolet, which ionizes the F region more heavily. A denser F region bends higher frequencies back to Earth, so 15, 12 and 10 meters come alive. High sunspot numbers open the high bands.
questions.xs: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center; ITU-R Rec. P.533

questions.q: What effect does a sudden ionospheric disturbance have on the daytime ionospheric propagation?
a: It enhances propagation on all HF frequencies
It disrupts signals on lower frequencies more than those on higher frequencies
It disrupts communications via satellite more than direct communications
None, because only areas on the night side of the Earth are affected
questions.x: A sudden ionospheric disturbance floods the D region with ionization, and the D region absorbs rather than refracts. Absorption falls as frequency rises, so the low bands go out first while the higher frequencies survive longer.

questions.q: Approximately how long does it take the increased ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from a solar flare to affect radio propagation on Earth?
questions.x: Ultraviolet and X-rays travel at the speed of light, and the Sun is about 93 million miles away, so they arrive in roughly 8 minutes. Keep it apart from a coronal mass ejection, which is matter rather than light and takes far longer.

questions.q: Which of the following are the least reliable bands for long-distance communications during periods of low solar activity?
questions.x: At solar minimum the F region never ionizes enough to return the highest bands, so 15, 12 and 10 meters are the first to close and the least dependable. They are also the bands that reward solar maximum most.

questions.q: What is the solar flux index?
a: A measure of the highest frequency that is useful for ionospheric propagation between two points on Earth
A count of sunspots that is adjusted for solar emissions
Another name for the American sunspot number
A measure of solar radiation with a wavelength of 10.7 centimeters
questions.x: Solar flux index is the Sun's radio noise measured at a wavelength of 10.7 centimeters, about 2800 MHz. It tracks solar activity more directly than counting sunspots, and it updates daily rather than being smoothed over a month.

questions.q: What is a geomagnetic storm?
a: A sudden drop in the solar flux index
A thunderstorm that affects radio propagation
A temporary disturbance in Earth’s geomagnetic field
questions.x: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, usually triggered by charged particles arriving from the Sun. It is a magnetic event rather than an ionizing one, which is why its effects differ from a flare's.

questions.q: At what point in the solar cycle does the 20-meter band usually support worldwide propagation during daylight hours?
questions.x: Twenty meters works worldwide in daylight at any point in the solar cycle. It sits low enough that even a weakly ionized F region returns it, and high enough to escape most D region absorption. That balance is why it is the reliable DX band.

questions.q: How can a geomagnetic storm affect HF propagation?
questions.x: Geomagnetic storms hit high latitudes hardest, because Earth's field funnels the incoming particles toward the poles. Paths crossing auroral regions degrade or disappear while equatorial paths often stay usable.

questions.q: How can high geomagnetic activity benefit radio communications?
a: Creates auroras that can reflect VHF signals
Increases signal strength for HF signals passing through the polar regions
questions.x: The same activity that wrecks HF at high latitudes creates auroras, and auroral curtains reflect VHF signals. Six meters and 2 meters open to contacts that would otherwise be impossible, though the signals come back distorted and raspy.

questions.q: What causes HF propagation conditions to vary periodically in a 26- to 28-day cycle?
a: Long term oscillations in the upper atmosphere
Cyclic variation in Earth’s radiation belts
Rotation of the Sun’s surface layers around its axis
The position of the Moon in its orbit
questions.x: The Sun rotates about once every 27 days as seen from Earth, so an active region faces us, turns away, and comes back around. Conditions repeat on that rhythm because you are seeing the same region again.

questions.q: How long does it take a coronal mass ejection to affect radio propagation on Earth?
questions.x: A coronal mass ejection is a cloud of matter, not light, so it crawls compared with a flare's radiation: 15 hours to several days. The flare arrives in 8 minutes, the CME days later, which is why the two effects are separated in time.

questions.q: What does the K-index measure?
a: The relative position of sunspots on the surface of the Sun
The short-term stability of Earth’s geomagnetic field
The short-term stability of the Sun’s magnetic field
The solar radio flux at Boulder, Colorado
questions.x: The K-index reports short-term geomagnetic stability, measured over three-hour intervals on a 0 to 9 scale. Low is quiet and above about 4 means a storm. Pair it with the A-index, which is the longer-term view.

questions.q: What does the A-index measure?
a: The relative position of sunspots on the surface of the Sun
The amount of polarization of the Sun’s electric field
The long-term stability of Earth’s geomagnetic field
The solar radio flux at Boulder, Colorado
questions.x: The A-index is the long-term measure, a daily figure derived from the day's K readings. K tells you what the field is doing now; A tells you what it has been doing. Short-term is K, long-term is A.

questions.q: How is long distance radio communication usually affected by the charged particles that reach Earth from solar coronal holes?
questions.x: Coronal holes emit fast solar wind streams, and the charged particles they send disturb Earth's magnetic field. The result on HF is much like a geomagnetic storm: degraded paths, worst at high latitudes.

questions.q: What is a characteristic of skywave signals arriving at your location by both short-path and long-path propagation?
a: The signal might be cancelled causing severe attenuation
A slightly delayed echo might be heard
questions.x: The same signal reaching you both the short way and the long way around the Earth travels very different distances, so the long-path copy arrives measurably later. You hear it as a faint echo just behind the direct signal.

questions.q: What factors affect the MUF?
questions.x: MUF depends on the path, the time of day, the season and the current state of solar activity. Every listed factor genuinely moves it, so the inclusive answer applies. That is also why MUF is predicted rather than simply looked up.

questions.q: Which frequency will have the least attenuation for long-distance skip propagation?
questions.x: Work just below the MUF. The higher the frequency, the less D region absorption you suffer, so the least attenuated path is the highest one the ionosphere will still bend back. Go above the MUF and the signal leaves for space.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way to determine current propagation on a desired band from your station?
a: Use a network of automated receiving stations on the internet to see where your transmissions are being received
Send a series of dots and listen for echoes
questions.x: Automated receiver networks such as the Reverse Beacon Network and PSK Reporter log who is hearing whom and post it on the web. Transmit briefly, then look up where you were decoded. It is real measurement of your own signal rather than a prediction.

questions.q: How does the ionosphere affect radio waves with frequencies below the MUF and above the LUF?
a: They are refracted back to Earth
They are amplified by interaction with the ionosphere
They are refracted and trapped in the ionosphere to circle Earth
questions.x: Between the LUF and the MUF is the usable window: the ionosphere refracts those signals back to Earth. Above the MUF they punch through into space; below the LUF the D region absorbs them before they get anywhere.

questions.q: What usually happens to radio waves with frequencies below the LUF?
a: They are refracted back to Earth
They are attenuated before reaching the destination
They are refracted and trapped in the ionosphere to circle Earth
questions.x: Below the lowest usable frequency the signal is absorbed before it reaches the far end. The energy does not go to space, it goes into heat in the D region. Absorption rises as frequency falls, which is what sets the LUF.

questions.q: What does LUF stand for?
a: The Lowest Usable Frequency for communications between two specific points
The Lowest Usable Frequency for communications to any point outside a 100-mile radius
The Lowest Usable Frequency during a 24-hour period
The Lowest Usable Frequency during the past 60 minutes
questions.x: Lowest Usable Frequency, and the definition is specific to one path between two points. Below it, absorption kills the signal. LUF is the floor, MUF the ceiling, and both are path-dependent.

questions.q: What does MUF stand for?
a: The Minimum Usable Frequency for communications between two points
The Maximum Usable Frequency for communications between two points
The Minimum Usable Frequency during a 24-hour period
The Maximum Usable Frequency during a 24-hour period
questions.x: Maximum Usable Frequency for a given path between two points. Above it the ionosphere no longer bends the wave enough to return it. Since it depends on the path, two stations can have very different MUFs at the same moment.

questions.q: What is the approximate maximum distance along the Earth’s surface normally covered in one hop using the F2 region?
questions.x: About 2,500 miles per hop off the F2 region, which sits roughly 200 to 400 km up. The higher the reflecting layer, the longer the geometry allows each hop to reach.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. P.533; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: What is the approximate maximum distance along the Earth’s surface normally covered in one hop using the E region?
questions.x: About 1,200 miles per E region hop, from a layer near 110 km. Half the F2 distance because the layer is roughly a third the height. Learn the pair together: E gives 1,200, F2 gives 2,500.
questions.xs: ITU-R Rec. P.533; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: What happens to HF propagation when the LUF exceeds the MUF?
a: Propagation via ordinary skywave communications is not possible over that path
HF communications over the path are enhanced
Double-hop propagation along the path is more common
Propagation over the path on all HF frequencies is enhanced
questions.x: If the LUF climbs above the MUF the usable window closes entirely and no ordinary skywave path exists. The floor has risen above the ceiling, so every frequency is either absorbed or lost to space.

questions.q: Which of the following is typical of the lower HF frequencies during the summer?
a: Poor propagation at any time of day
Heavy distortion on signals due to photon absorption
High levels of atmospheric noise or static
questions.x: Summer means thunderstorms, and lightning is a broadband noise source that propagates efficiently on the low bands. Eighty and 160 meters can be buried in static in July while staying quiet and workable in January.

questions.q: Which ionospheric region is closest to the surface of Earth?
questions.x: The D region is lowest, roughly 50 to 90 km up. Going outward the order is D, E, then F. Being deepest in the atmosphere is exactly why it absorbs instead of refracting: collisions there are frequent.

questions.q: What is meant by the term “critical frequency” at a given incidence angle?
a: The highest frequency which is refracted back to Earth
The lowest frequency which is refracted back to Earth
The frequency at which the signal-to-noise ratio approaches unity
The frequency at which the signal-to-noise ratio is 6 dB
questions.x: At a given angle of incidence, the critical frequency is the highest one still refracted back to Earth. Above it the wave escapes. It is the physical basis for the MUF, which applies the same idea to a specific path.

questions.q: Why is skip propagation via the F2 region longer than that via the other ionospheric regions?
questions.x: F2 is the highest region, so the geometry of a bounce off it covers more ground. Higher reflection point means a shallower angle can still come back down, and that stretches each hop to about 2,500 miles.

questions.q: What does the term “critical angle” mean, as applied to radio wave propagation?
a: The long path azimuth of a distant station
The short path azimuth of a distant station
The lowest takeoff angle that will return a radio wave to Earth under specific ionospheric conditions
The highest takeoff angle that will return a radio wave to Earth under specific ionospheric conditions
questions.x: Critical angle is the highest takeoff angle that still returns a wave to Earth for the conditions of the moment. Steeper than that and the signal goes through the layer rather than being bent back. It moves with ionization, so it is not a fixed number.

questions.q: Why is long-distance communication on the 40-, 60-, 80-, and 160-meter bands more difficult during the day?
a: The F region absorbs signals at these frequencies during daylight hours
The F region is unstable during daylight hours
The D region absorbs signals at these frequencies during daylight hours
The E region is unstable during daylight hours
questions.x: Sunlight creates the D region, and the D region absorbs the low bands. That is why 160 through 40 meters shrink to local coverage by day and open up for long distance after dark, once the D region has recombined away.

questions.q: What is a characteristic of HF scatter?
a: There are very large, sudden swings in signal strength
Scatter propagation occurs only at night
questions.x: Scatter signals flutter. The energy arrives from many small scattering points that move and change, so the sum rises and falls rapidly. Weak and fluttery together is the signature.

questions.q: What makes HF scatter signals often sound distorted?
a: The ionospheric region involved is unstable
Ground waves are absorbing much of the signal
The E region is not present
Energy is scattered into the skip zone through several different paths
questions.x: Scattered energy takes many paths of slightly different length, so copies arrive spread out in time and out of phase. That smearing is heard as distortion, the same mechanism as multipath on VHF but with far more paths involved.

questions.q: Why are HF scatter signals in the skip zone usually weak?
a: Only a small part of the signal energy is scattered into the skip zone
Signals are scattered from the magnetosphere, which is not a good reflector
Propagation is via ground waves, which absorb most of the signal energy
Propagation is via ducts in the F region, which absorb most of the energy
questions.x: Scattering redirects only a small fraction of your signal into the skip zone. Most of the energy continues on its intended path, so what fills the gap is the leftovers. Weak is expected.

questions.q: What type of propagation allows signals to be heard in the transmitting station’s skip zone?
questions.x: Scatter is what fills the skip zone, the dead ring that is too far for ground wave and too near for the first hop. Irregularities in the ionosphere and terrain deflect a little energy down into it.

questions.q: What is near vertical incidence skywave (NVIS) propagation?
a: Short distance MF or HF propagation at high elevation angles
Long path HF propagation at sunrise and sunset
Double hop propagation near the LUF
questions.x: NVIS fires almost straight up on MF or HF and lets the ionosphere drop the signal back over a radius of a few hundred miles. It fills the skip zone deliberately, which is why emergency communicators use it for regional coverage.

questions.q: Which ionospheric region is the most absorbent of signals below 10 MHz during daylight hours?
questions.x: The D region absorbs most strongly below 10 MHz during daylight. It exists only while the Sun is up, and its effect falls off as frequency rises, which is why the low bands suffer and 20 meters does not.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the notch filter found on many HF transceivers?
a: To restrict the transmitter voice bandwidth
To reduce interference from carriers in the receiver passband
To eliminate receiver interference from impulse noise sources
To remove interfering splatter generated by signals on adjacent frequencies
questions.x: A notch filter puts a deep, very narrow null at one frequency, which is exactly the shape needed to kill a steady carrier sitting inside your passband. It removes the heterodyne while leaving the voice around it intact.

questions.q: What is the benefit of using the opposite or “reverse” sideband when receiving CW?
a: Interference from impulse noise will be eliminated
More stations can be accommodated within a given signal passband
It may be possible to reduce or eliminate interference from other signals
Accidental out-of-band operation can be prevented
questions.x: Switching sidebands flips your receiver's passband to the other side of the carrier. An interfering signal that fell inside the filter may now fall outside it. The CW note you want stays the same pitch, so nothing is lost by trying.

questions.q: How does a noise blanker work?
a: By redirecting noise pulses into a filter capacitor
By reducing receiver gain during a noise pulse
questions.x: A noise blanker watches for the sharp leading edge of an impulse and drops receiver gain for the microseconds it lasts. Ignition noise and power line arcing are pulses, so blanking them costs almost no audio. It does nothing for steady hiss.

questions.q: What is the effect on plate current of the correct setting of a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier’s TUNE control?
questions.x: Tuning the plate circuit through resonance produces a pronounced dip in plate current. The dip is the indicator you tune for, because at resonance the tube's load looks resistive and it draws least current.

questions.q: Why is automatic level control (ALC) used with an RF power amplifier?
a: To balance the transmitter audio frequency response
questions.x: ALC feeds a control voltage back to the exciter so the amplifier cannot be driven past its linear range. Without it, cranking up the transceiver simply produces distortion and splatter rather than more clean output.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an antenna tuner?
a: Reduce the SWR in the feed line to the antenna
Reduce the power dissipation in the feedline to the antenna
Increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line
questions.x: A tuner presents the transmitter the load it wants to see, so it delivers full power into the feed line instead of folding back. Note what it does not do: nothing changes at the antenna, so feed line SWR beyond the tuner is unaffected.
questions.xs: Impedance matching theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: What happens as a receiver’s noise reduction control level is increased?
a: CW signals may become severely attenuated
Received frequency may shift several kHz
questions.x: Noise reduction guesses which parts of the audio are signal and which are noise, and the aggressive settings guess wrong. Push it too far and voices go hollow and watery. Use the least amount that makes copy comfortable.

questions.q: What is the correct adjustment for the LOAD or COUPLING control of a vacuum tube RF power amplifier?
a: Minimum plate current without exceeding maximum allowable grid current
Highest plate voltage while minimizing grid current
Desired power output without exceeding maximum allowable plate current
questions.x: Adjust LOAD for the output you want while keeping plate current within the tube's rating. TUNE finds resonance, LOAD sets how hard the tube works. The two interact, so you go back and forth between them.

questions.q: What is the purpose of delaying RF output after activating a transmitter’s keying line to an external amplifier?
a: To prevent key clicks on CW
To allow time for the amplifier to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output
To allow time for the amplifier power supply to reach operating level
questions.x: The amplifier's relays need a few milliseconds to move the antenna from the transceiver to the amplifier output. Sending RF before they settle arcs the contacts and can destroy them. The delay simply lets the mechanics finish first.

questions.q: What is the function of an electronic keyer?
a: Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation
To allow time for switching the antenna from the receiver to the transmitter
Computer interface for PSK and RTTY operation
questions.x: A keyer turns paddle closures into correctly timed dots and dashes at a set speed. You still form the characters; the keyer handles the element lengths and spacing so your fist stays even.

questions.q: Why should the ALC system be inactive when transmitting AFSK data signals?
a: ALC will invert the modulation of the AFSK mode
The ALC action distorts the signal
When using digital modes, too much ALC activity can cause the transmitter to overheat
questions.x: ALC is designed for the varying envelope of speech. AFSK data has constant amplitude, so any ALC action modulates it and smears the signal. Set drive so ALC never activates, then leave the level alone.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common use of the dual-VFO feature on a transceiver?
a: To allow transmitting on two frequencies at once
To permit full duplex operation -- that is, transmitting and receiving at the same time
To transmit on one frequency and listen on another
To improve frequency accuracy by allowing variable frequency output (VFO) operation
questions.x: Two VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another, which is split operation. DX stations use it to keep their transmit frequency clear of the pileup calling them.

questions.q: What is the purpose of using a receive attenuator?
a: To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals
To reduce the transmitter power when driving a linear amplifier
To reduce power consumption when operating from batteries
To reduce excessive audio level on strong signals
questions.x: An attenuator cuts everything ahead of the first mixer, keeping a very strong signal from overloading the front end. You lose sensitivity you did not need, and in exchange the distortion products that were burying weaker signals disappear.

questions.q: What item of test equipment contains horizontal and vertical channel amplifiers?
questions.x: Horizontal and vertical channel amplifiers belong to an oscilloscope. The vertical channel carries the signal you are looking at, the horizontal drives the time base that sweeps it across the screen.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of an oscilloscope versus a digital voltmeter?
a: Complex impedances can be easily measured
questions.x: A voltmeter reduces a signal to a single number. A scope shows the waveform against time, so you can see shape, distortion, ringing and timing. For anything more complex than a steady level, the picture is the point.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best instrument to use for checking the keying waveform of a CW transmitter?
questions.x: Keying waveform is about shape over time: how fast the envelope rises and falls. Only a scope shows that. Rise times that are too abrupt generate key clicks, and you cannot see the problem on a meter.

questions.q: What signal source is connected to the vertical input of an oscilloscope when checking the RF envelope pattern of a transmitted signal?
a: The local oscillator of the transmitter
The attenuated RF output of the transmitter
questions.x: Feed the vertical input from an attenuated sample of the transmitter's RF output. Attenuated matters. Full transmitter output into a scope input will destroy it, so the sample comes through a suitable pad or coupler.

questions.q: Why do voltmeters have high input impedance?
a: It allows for higher voltages to be safely measured
It improves the resolution of the readings
It decreases the loading on circuits being measured
questions.x: A voltmeter in parallel with the circuit draws some current of its own, which changes the very voltage you are measuring. High input impedance keeps that current negligible, so the reading reflects the circuit rather than the meter.

questions.q: What is an advantage of a digital multimeter as compared to an analog multimeter?
questions.x: A digital meter resolves more digits and removes the guesswork of reading a needle against a scale. Note the flip side, tested in G4B09: for peaking or nulling an adjustment, a moving needle beats a jittering number.

questions.q: What signals are used to conduct a two-tone test?
a: Two audio signals of the same frequency shifted 90 degrees
Two audio frequency range square wave signals of equal amplitude
questions.x: Two audio tones that are not harmonically related. Non-harmonic matters, because any intermodulation products the amplifier creates then land on frequencies no legitimate harmonic could occupy, which makes them unmistakable.

questions.q: What transmitter performance parameter does a two-tone test analyze?
a: Percentage of suppression of the carrier and undesired sideband for SSB
questions.x: A two-tone test measures linearity. A perfectly linear amplifier reproduces both tones and nothing else; a nonlinear one manufactures intermodulation products between them. Those extra products are the measurement.

questions.q: When is an analog multimeter preferred to a digital multimeter?
a: When measuring the frequency of an oscillator
When adjusting circuits for maximum or minimum values
questions.x: When you are peaking or nulling something, a needle shows the direction and rate of change at a glance. A digital display flickers through unrelated digits and you lose the trend. Analog wins for adjusting, digital for reading.

questions.q: Which of the following can be determined with a directional wattmeter?
questions.x: A directional wattmeter reads forward and reflected power separately, and SWR follows from their ratio. Many meters compute it for you and show it directly on the scale.

questions.q: Which of the following must be connected to an antenna analyzer when it is being used for SWR measurements?
questions.x: The analyzer needs to see the whole system it is measuring, so connect the antenna with its feed line. What you get is the SWR at the shack end, which is what your transmitter actually sees.

questions.q: What effect can strong signals from nearby transmitters have on an antenna analyzer?
a: Desensitization which can cause intermodulation products which interfere with impedance readings
Received power that interferes with SWR readings
Generation of harmonics which interfere with frequency readings
questions.x: An analyzer measures its own weak test signal, so a strong nearby transmitter arriving on the same antenna swamps that measurement and the readings go wrong. If a neighbouring station is active, wait rather than trusting the numbers.

questions.q: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?
questions.x: An antenna analyzer measures complex impedance, so it can characterize a length of coax as well as an antenna: its impedance, electrical length and velocity factor. Useful for finding a cable's actual quarter-wave frequency.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; transmission line theory

questions.q: Which of the following might be useful in reducing RF interference to audio frequency circuits?
questions.x: A bypass capacitor gives RF a low-impedance path to ground before it reaches the audio stages, while leaving the audio frequencies untouched. It works because reactance falls as frequency rises, so the capacitor is nearly a short at RF.

questions.q: Which of the following could be a cause of interference covering a wide range of frequencies?
a: Not using a balun or line isolator to feed balanced antennas
Lack of rectification of the transmitter’s signal in power conductors
Arcing at a poor electrical connection
Using a balun to feed an unbalanced antenna
questions.x: An arc is a broadband noise generator. Each spark is a fast pulse, and fast pulses contain energy across an enormous span of frequencies. That is why arcing shows up as a buzz right across the bands rather than on one frequency.

questions.q: What sound is heard from an audio device experiencing RF interference from a single sideband phone transmitter?
a: A steady hum whenever the transmitter is on the air
questions.x: Distorted, unintelligible speech. RF from an SSB transmitter gets rectified in an audio stage that was never meant to demodulate anything, so the result is a rough approximation of your voice rather than a clean copy.

questions.q: What sound is heard from an audio device experiencing RF interference from a CW transmitter?
a: A CW signal at a nearly pure audio frequency
questions.x: On-and-off humming or clicking, following your keying. CW is a carrier switched on and off, so the interference switches with it. The rhythm of the sound matches your fist, which makes the source easy to identify.

questions.q: What is a possible cause of high voltages that produce RF burns?
a: Flat braid rather than round wire has been used for the ground wire
Insulated wire has been used for the ground wire
The ground wire has high impedance on that frequency
questions.x: A ground wire is only a ground at DC. At RF its inductance can make it look like a high impedance, or even resonate, so the chassis it was supposed to hold at zero volts floats at high RF potential instead. Touch it and you get burned.

questions.q: What is a possible effect of a resonant ground connection?
a: High RF voltages on the enclosures of station equipment
questions.x: A ground conductor about a quarter wavelength long behaves as a resonant element rather than a short, presenting high impedance at its far end. The result is high RF voltage on equipment enclosures, which is the same mechanism as G4C05.

questions.q: Why should soldered joints not be used in lightning protection ground connections?
a: A soldered joint will likely be destroyed by the heat of a lightning strike
Solder flux will prevent a low conductivity connection
Solder has too high a dielectric constant to provide adequate lightning protection
questions.x: A lightning strike carries enough current to melt solder, so a soldered joint can simply vanish at the moment you most need it intact. Lightning grounds use mechanical connections: clamps, exothermic welds, crimps.

questions.q: Which of the following would reduce RF interference caused by common-mode current on an audio cable?
a: Place a ferrite choke on the cable
Connect the center conductor to the shield of all cables to short circuit the RFI signal
Ground the center conductor of the audio cable causing the interference
Add an additional insulating jacket to the cable
questions.x: A ferrite choke adds impedance to common-mode current, the component flowing the same direction on every conductor in the cable. The signal you want is differential and passes unaffected, so the choke removes interference without touching the audio.

questions.q: How can the effects of ground loops be minimized?
a: Connect all ground conductors in series
Connect the AC neutral conductor to the ground wire
Avoid using lock washers and star washers when making ground connections
questions.x: Bond the enclosures together so there is no potential difference to drive current between them. A ground loop exists because two grounded points sit at slightly different voltages; bonding removes the difference rather than the loop.

questions.q: What could be a symptom caused by a ground loop in your station’s audio connections?
a: You receive reports of “hum” on your station’s transmitted signal
The SWR reading for one or more antennas is suddenly very high
An item of station equipment starts to draw excessive amounts of current
You receive reports of harmonic interference from your station
questions.x: Hum reports. A ground loop lets AC line current circulate through your audio grounds, and that current appears as 60 Hz hum riding on your modulation. Everyone hears it except you.

questions.q: What technique helps to minimize RF “hot spots” in an amateur station?
a: Building all equipment in a metal enclosure
Placing low-pass filters on all feed lines
questions.x: Bond every enclosure together. Hot spots appear where two pieces of equipment sit at different RF potentials, so tying them to a common bonded system removes the difference that makes a spot hot.

questions.q: Why must all metal enclosures of station equipment be grounded?
a: It prevents a blown fuse in the event of an internal short circuit
It ensures that the neutral wire is grounded
It ensures that hazardous voltages cannot appear on the chassis
questions.x: Grounding the chassis means a fault inside the equipment goes to ground and trips the breaker instead of leaving the case live. Without it, an insulation failure can put line voltage on the metal you are touching.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a speech processor in a transceiver?
a: Increase the apparent loudness of transmitted voice signals
Increase transmitter bass response for more natural-sounding SSB signals
Decrease high-frequency voice output to prevent out-of-band operation
questions.x: A speech processor raises the average level of your voice relative to its peaks, so the signal sounds louder without exceeding the same peak limit. It buys apparent loudness rather than more peak power.

questions.q: How does a speech processor affect a single sideband phone signal?
questions.x: Average power goes up while peak envelope power stays where it was. Speech is mostly quiet punctuated by peaks, so compressing that range puts more energy on the air within the same PEP limit. That is why processing helps readability.

questions.q: What is the effect of an incorrectly adjusted speech processor?
questions.x: Overdone processing brings distortion, splatter into adjacent frequencies, and a harsh unnatural sound, and it can pump up background noise along with your voice. All the listed effects are real, so the inclusive answer applies.

questions.q: What does an S meter measure?
questions.x: An S meter reads received signal strength. It says nothing about your transmitter, and its calibration varies between radios, which is why reports from different stations are not directly comparable.

questions.q: How does a signal that reads 20 dB over S9 compare to one that reads S9 on a receiver, assuming a properly calibrated S meter?
questions.x: Twenty dB is a factor of 100 in power, since 10 to the power of 20 over 10 is 100. So 20 dB over S9 is a hundred times the power of S9. The two dB rules cover it: 10 dB is ten times, and 20 dB is ten times ten.

questions.q: How much change in signal strength is typically represented by one S unit?
questions.x: One S unit is 6 dB by the standard, which is a factor of about four in power. Real receivers rarely match that exactly below S9, but 6 dB is the figure the exam wants and the basis for G4D07.

questions.q: How much must the power output of a transmitter be raised to change the S meter reading on a distant receiver from S8 to S9?
questions.x: One S unit is 6 dB, and 6 dB in power is 10 to the power of 0.6, which is 3.98. So roughly four times the power to move S8 to S9. Quadrupling your output to gain one S unit is why chasing S units with power rarely pays.

questions.q: What frequency range is occupied by a 3 kHz LSB signal when the displayed carrier frequency is set to 7.178 MHz?
questions.x: Lower sideband puts your energy below the displayed carrier, so a 3 kHz signal runs from 7.175 up to 7.178 MHz. Subtract the bandwidth from the dial reading and you have the lower edge.

questions.q: What frequency range is occupied by a 3 kHz USB signal with the displayed carrier frequency set to 14.347 MHz?
questions.x: Upper sideband puts energy above the displayed carrier, so 14.347 plus 3 kHz reaches 14.350 MHz, exactly the top of the band. One kilohertz higher on the dial and you would be transmitting outside it.

questions.q: How close to the lower edge of a band’s phone segment should your displayed carrier frequency be when using 3 kHz wide LSB?
a: At least 3 kHz above the edge of the segment
At least 3 kHz below the edge of the segment
At least 1 kHz below the edge of the segment
At least 1 kHz above the edge of the segment
questions.x: Stay at least 3 kHz above the lower edge, because LSB energy extends downward by the full bandwidth. Sitting on the edge itself puts your sidebands outside the segment even though the dial looks legal.

questions.q: How close to the upper edge of a band’s phone segment should your displayed carrier frequency be when using 3 kHz wide USB?
a: At least 3 kHz above the edge of the band
At least 3 kHz below the edge of the band
At least 1 kHz above the edge of the segment
At least 1 kHz below the edge of the segment
questions.x: Stay at least 3 kHz below the upper edge, the mirror image of G4D10. USB extends upward, so the dial reading has to leave room for the whole signal. Same rule, opposite direction.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a capacitance hat on a mobile antenna?
a: To increase the power handling capacity of a whip antenna
To electrically lengthen a physically short antenna
questions.x: A capacitance hat adds capacitance near the top of a short antenna, which raises the current in the radiating section and makes the antenna behave electrically longer. It lets you resonate without adding more loading coil.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a corona ball on an HF mobile antenna?
a: To narrow the operating bandwidth of the antenna
To increase the “Q” of the antenna
To reduce the chance of damage if the antenna should strike an object
To reduce RF voltage discharge from the tip of the antenna while transmitting
questions.x: Voltage is highest at the tip of a mobile whip, and a sharp point concentrates the field enough to ionize the air. A rounded ball spreads the field over a larger radius, keeping the gradient below the level where corona forms.

questions.q: Which of the following direct, fused power connections would be the best for a 100-watt HF mobile installation?
a: To the battery using heavy-gauge wire
To the alternator or generator using heavy-gauge wire
To the battery using insulated heavy duty balanced transmission line
To the alternator or generator using insulated heavy duty balanced transmission line
questions.x: Run heavy-gauge fused wire directly to the battery, both leads. A 100-watt radio draws around 20 amps on peaks, and any lighter or longer path drops enough voltage to make the radio misbehave when you need it most.

questions.q: Why should DC power for a 100-watt HF transceiver not be supplied by a vehicle’s auxiliary power socket?
a: The socket is not wired with an RF-shielded power cable
The socket’s wiring may be inadequate for the current drawn by the transceiver
The DC polarity of the socket is reversed from the polarity of modern HF transceivers
Drawing more than 50 watts from this socket could cause the engine to overheat
questions.x: Accessory sockets are wired for small loads, often fused at 10 or 15 amps through thin wire. A 100-watt HF radio asks for roughly 20 amps, so the socket wiring becomes the weak point and can overheat.

questions.q: Which of the following most limits an HF mobile installation?
a: The wire gauge of the DC power line to the transceiver
Efficiency of the electrically short antenna
FCC rules limiting mobile output power on the 75-meter band
questions.x: The antenna is the limitation. A whip a few feet long on 40 meters is a tiny fraction of a wavelength, heavily loaded, with low radiation resistance and real losses. Most of your power warms the loading coil rather than leaving the vehicle.

questions.q: What is one disadvantage of using a shortened mobile antenna as opposed to a full-size antenna?
a: Short antennas are more likely to cause distortion of transmitted signals
Q of the antenna will be very low
Operating bandwidth may be very limited
questions.x: Shortening an antenna raises its Q, and high Q means narrow bandwidth. You may retune every few tens of kilohertz. That sharpness is the same property that makes a short antenna hard to match in the first place.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; Q and bandwidth

questions.q: Which of the following may cause receive interference to an HF transceiver installed in a vehicle?
questions.x: A modern vehicle is full of noise sources: the ignition system, the alternator, and dozens of electronic control modules and switching supplies. All the listed sources are genuine contributors, so the inclusive answer applies.

questions.q: In what configuration are the individual cells in a solar panel connected together?
questions.x: Cells are wired in series to build voltage and those strings are paralleled to build current, so the panel is series-parallel. Series alone would give the right voltage at too little current for charging.

questions.q: What is the approximate open-circuit voltage from a fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell?
questions.x: About 0.5 volts open circuit for a silicon cell, set by the physics of the silicon junction rather than by the cell's size. Area determines current, not voltage, which is why a 12-volt panel needs roughly 36 cells in series.

questions.q: Why should a series diode be connected between a solar panel and a storage battery that is being charged by the panel?
a: To prevent overload by regulating the charging voltage
To prevent discharge of the battery through the panel during times of low or no illumination
To limit the current flowing from the panel to a safe value
To prevent damage to the battery due to excessive voltage at high illumination levels
questions.x: In darkness the panel becomes a load rather than a source, and the battery would quietly discharge back through it overnight. A series diode conducts only the charging direction and blocks the reverse.

questions.q: What precaution should be taken when connecting a solar panel to a lithium iron phosphate battery?
a: Ground the solar panel outer metal framework
Ensure the battery is placed terminals-up
A series resistor must be in place
The solar panel must have a charge controller
questions.x: Lithium iron phosphate cells need a controlled charge profile and a hard voltage ceiling, and a bare panel provides neither. A charge controller enforces the limits. Overcharging lithium chemistry is a fire risk, not merely bad for capacity.

questions.q: What happens when inductive and capacitive reactance are equal in a series LC circuit?
a: Resonance causes impedance to be very high
Impedance is equal to the geometric mean of the inductance and capacitance
Resonance causes impedance to be very low
Impedance is equal to the arithmetic mean of the inductance and capacitance
questions.x: At resonance the two reactances are equal and opposite, so they cancel and only the resistance remains. In a series circuit that leaves a very low impedance, which is why series resonance is used to pass one frequency. Parallel resonance does the opposite.

questions.q: What is reactance?
a: Opposition to the flow of direct current caused by resistance
Opposition to the flow of alternating current caused by capacitance or inductance
Reinforcement of the flow of direct current caused by resistance
Reinforcement of the flow of alternating current caused by capacitance or inductance
questions.x: Reactance is opposition to alternating current from capacitance or inductance. Unlike resistance it dissipates nothing: energy is stored and returned each cycle. That is also why it varies with frequency while resistance does not.

questions.q: Which of the following is opposition to the flow of alternating current in an inductor?
questions.x: Reactance, specifically inductive reactance. An inductor opposes a change in current by generating a back EMF, and the faster the change the stronger the opposition.

questions.q: Which of the following is opposition to the flow of alternating current in a capacitor?
questions.x: Reactance, in this case capacitive. Both capacitors and inductors oppose AC through reactance; what differs is the direction the opposition moves as frequency changes.

questions.q: How does an inductor react to AC?
a: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
questions.x: Inductive reactance rises with frequency. The formula says it directly: XL equals 2πfL, so doubling frequency doubles reactance. An inductor passes DC easily and chokes off high frequencies, which is exactly how an RF choke works.

questions.q: How does a capacitor react to AC?
a: As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
As the frequency of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance increases
As the amplitude of the applied AC increases, the reactance decreases
questions.x: Capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises, since frequency sits in the denominator of 1 over 2πfC. A capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies, the mirror image of an inductor. That is why bypass capacitors work.

questions.q: What is the term for the inverse of impedance?
questions.x: Admittance, measured in siemens. It is the reciprocal of impedance, the way conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. Useful when analysing parallel circuits, where admittances simply add.

questions.q: What is impedance?
a: The ratio of current to voltage
The product of current and voltage
The ratio of voltage to current
The product of current and reactance
questions.x: Impedance is the ratio of voltage to current, the AC generalization of resistance. It bundles resistance and reactance into one quantity, which is why it is expressed in ohms and why Ohm's law still applies.
questions.xs: Ohm's law for AC; IEEE Std 270

questions.q: What unit is used to measure reactance?
questions.x: Ohms, the same unit as resistance and impedance. All three describe opposition to current, so they share a unit even though the underlying mechanisms differ.

questions.q: Which of the following devices can be used for impedance matching at radio frequencies?
questions.x: Transformers, LC networks and quarter-wave transmission line sections all transform impedance, so the inclusive answer is right. Which one you use depends on frequency, power and how wide a range you need to cover.

questions.q: What letter is used to represent reactance?
questions.x: X denotes reactance, written XL for inductive and XC for capacitive. R is resistance, Z is impedance, and Z combines R and X.

questions.q: What occurs in an LC circuit at resonance?
a: The circuit radiates all its energy in the form of radio waves
Inductive reactance and capacitive reactance cancel
questions.x: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so they cancel and the circuit looks purely resistive. Whether that leaves low or high impedance depends on whether the components are in series or parallel.

questions.q: What dB change represents a factor of two increase or decrease in power?
questions.x: Doubling or halving power is 3 dB, up or down. The exact figure is 3.01, and 3 dB is the single most useful number in radio. Its partner: 10 dB is a factor of ten.

questions.q: How does the total current relate to the individual currents in a circuit of parallel resistors?
a: It equals the average of the branch currents
It decreases as more parallel branches are added to the circuit
It equals the sum of the currents through each branch
It is the sum of the reciprocal of each individual voltage drop
questions.x: Branch currents add up to the total. Each parallel branch sees the same voltage and draws current according to its own resistance, so the source supplies the sum. Adding another branch always increases total current.

questions.q: How many watts of electrical power are consumed if 400 VDC is supplied to an 800-ohm load?
questions.x: With voltage and resistance given, use P equals E squared over R: 400 squared is 160,000, divided by 800 gives 200 watts. Reach for this form whenever the question hands you volts and ohms but no current.

questions.q: How many watts of electrical power are consumed by a 12 VDC light bulb that draws 0.2 amperes?
questions.x: Volts times amps: 12 times 0.2 is 2.4 watts. The simplest form of the power formula, usable whenever both voltage and current are given.

questions.q: How many watts are consumed when a current of 7.0 milliamperes flows through a 1,250-ohm resistance?
questions.x: Current and resistance given, so use P equals I squared R. Seven milliamperes is 0.007 A, squared gives 0.000049, times 1250 gives 0.061 watts, or about 61 milliwatts. Watch the unit conversion; that is where this one is usually lost.

questions.q: What is the PEP produced by 200 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm dummy load?
questions.x: Three steps. Halve 200 peak-to-peak for 100 volts peak, divide by root 2 for 70.7 volts RMS, then square and divide by 50 to get 100 watts. Power always comes from RMS, never from peak.

questions.q: What value of an AC signal produces the same power dissipation in a resistor as a DC voltage of the same value?
a: The reciprocal of the RMS value
questions.x: The RMS value, root mean square. It is defined as the AC value that heats a resistor exactly as much as the same DC voltage would, which is why RMS is the figure used for every power calculation.

questions.q: What is the peak-to-peak voltage of a sine wave with an RMS voltage of 120 volts?
questions.x: Multiply RMS by root 2 for peak, then double it for peak-to-peak: 120 times 1.414 is 169.7, doubled gives 339.4 volts. Household 120 volts really does swing nearly 340 volts across a cycle.

questions.q: What is the RMS voltage of a sine wave with a value of 17 volts peak?
questions.x: Divide peak by root 2: 17 over 1.414 is 12.0 volts RMS. Going from peak to RMS you always divide, so the answer must be smaller than the peak value.

questions.q: What percentage of power loss is equivalent to a loss of 1 dB?
questions.x: One dB down leaves 10 to the power of minus 0.1, which is 0.794, so about 79 percent gets through and 20.6 percent is lost. A single dB sounds trivial and is actually a fifth of your power.

questions.q: What is the ratio of PEP to average power for an unmodulated carrier?
questions.x: Exactly 1.00. An unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, so its peak and average are the same. Ratios above 1 only appear once modulation makes the envelope vary, as with SSB speech.

questions.q: What is the RMS voltage across a 50-ohm dummy load dissipating 1200 watts?
questions.x: Rearrange P equals E squared over R into E equals the square root of P times R: 1200 times 50 is 60,000, and the square root is 245 volts RMS. That is a genuinely dangerous voltage inside a dummy load.

questions.q: What is the output PEP of an unmodulated carrier if the average power is 1060 watts?
questions.x: The same, 1060 watts. Since an unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, PEP equals average power. This is G5B11 asked with numbers instead of a ratio.

questions.q: What is the output PEP of 500 volts peak-to-peak across a 50-ohm load?
questions.x: Same three steps as G5B06: half of 500 is 250 volts peak, divided by root 2 gives 176.8 RMS, squared over 50 gives 625 watts. Peak-to-peak to RMS is a division by 2 root 2, or about 2.83.

questions.q: What causes a voltage to appear across the secondary winding of a transformer when an AC voltage source is connected across its primary winding?
questions.x: Mutual inductance. Alternating current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field, and that changing field induces a voltage in the secondary. Changing is essential, which is why a transformer does nothing with DC.

questions.q: What is the output voltage if an input signal is applied to the secondary winding of a 4:1 voltage step-down transformer instead of the primary winding?
a: The input voltage is multiplied by 4
The input voltage is divided by 4
Additional resistance must be added in series with the primary to prevent overload
Additional resistance must be added in parallel with the secondary to prevent overload
questions.x: Feeding a transformer backwards reverses its ratio, so a 4 to 1 step-down becomes a 4 to 1 step-up and the input is multiplied by four. Transformers are symmetrical; step-up and step-down describe how you wire it, not the part itself.

questions.q: What is the total resistance of a 10-, a 20-, and a 50-ohm resistor connected in parallel?
questions.x: Add the reciprocals and invert: one tenth plus one twentieth plus one fiftieth is 0.17, and one over 0.17 is 5.9 ohms. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest resistor, so 5.9 passing that check is a good sanity test.

questions.q: What is the approximate total resistance of a 100- and a 200-ohm resistor in parallel?
questions.x: For two resistors, product over sum is quicker: 100 times 200 is 20,000, divided by 300 gives 67 ohms. Again below the smaller of the two, as parallel combinations always are.

questions.q: Why is the primary winding wire of a voltage step-up transformer usually a larger size than that of the secondary winding?
a: To improve the coupling between the primary and secondary
To accommodate the higher current of the primary
To prevent parasitic oscillations due to resistive losses in the primary
To ensure that the volume of the primary winding is equal to the volume of the secondary winding
questions.x: Power in equals power out, so stepping voltage up means stepping current down. The primary of a step-up transformer therefore carries the higher current and needs the heavier wire. Follow the current, not the voltage.

questions.q: What is the voltage output of a transformer with a 500-turn primary and a 1500-turn secondary when 120 VAC is applied to the primary?
questions.x: Output equals input times the turns ratio: 1500 over 500 is 3, and 120 times 3 is 360 volts. More turns on the secondary means a step-up, which the answer being larger than 120 confirms.

questions.q: What transformer turns ratio matches an antenna’s 600-ohm feed point impedance to a 50-ohm coaxial cable?
questions.x: Impedance transforms as the square of the turns ratio, so the turns ratio is the square root of the impedance ratio. 600 over 50 is 12, and the square root of 12 is 3.46, so about 3.5 to 1. Forgetting the square root is the classic error here.

questions.q: What is the equivalent capacitance of two 5.0-nanofarad capacitors and one 750-picofarad capacitor connected in parallel?
questions.x: Capacitors in parallel simply add, but the units must match first. 750 picofarads is 0.75 nanofarads, so 5 plus 5 plus 0.75 gives 10.75 nanofarads. Parallel capacitors behave like parallel resistors turned upside down.

questions.q: What is the capacitance of three 100-microfarad capacitors connected in series?
questions.x: Capacitors in series combine like parallel resistors, so three equal 100 microfarad units give 100 divided by 3, or 33.3 microfarads. Series capacitance is always less than the smallest capacitor.

questions.q: What is the inductance of three 10-millihenry inductors connected in parallel?
questions.x: Inductors in parallel behave like resistors in parallel, so three equal 10 millihenry units give 10 divided by 3, about 3.3 millihenries. Inductors follow the resistor rules; capacitors are the ones that flip.

questions.q: What is the inductance of a circuit with a 20-millihenry inductor connected in series with a 50-millihenry inductor?
questions.x: Inductors in series add, exactly like resistors: 20 plus 50 is 70 millihenries. Pair this with G5C10 and the whole inductor family is covered, since inductors always follow the resistance rules.

questions.q: What is the capacitance of a 20-microfarad capacitor connected in series with a 50-microfarad capacitor?
questions.x: Two capacitors in series follow product over sum: 20 times 50 is 1000, divided by 70 gives 14.3 microfarads. Less than the smaller of the two, which is the check on every series capacitance answer.

questions.q: Which of the following components should be added to a capacitor to increase the capacitance?
questions.x: Add a capacitor in parallel, because parallel capacitances add. Putting one in series would reduce the total instead. Capacitors are backwards from resistors in both directions.

questions.q: Which of the following components should be added to an inductor to increase the inductance?
questions.x: Add an inductor in series, since series inductances add. This is the opposite arrangement from capacitors, which is precisely what the pair of questions G5C13 and G5C14 is testing.

questions.q: What is the minimum allowable discharge voltage for maximum life of a standard 12-volt lead-acid battery?
questions.x: Stop at 10.5 volts, about 1.75 volts per cell. Below that the plates begin to sulfate in ways that do not fully reverse on the next charge, so every deep discharge permanently costs you capacity.

questions.q: What is an advantage of batteries with low internal resistance?
questions.x: Low internal resistance means less voltage is lost inside the battery itself, so it can deliver high current without the terminal voltage collapsing. That is what lets a battery run a 100-watt transmitter through modulation peaks.

questions.q: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a germanium diode?
questions.x: About 0.3 volts, roughly half the silicon figure, because germanium has a smaller bandgap. That low drop is why germanium diodes still appear in sensitive detector circuits where 0.7 volts would swallow the signal.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of an electrolytic capacitor?
a: Much less leakage than any other type
High capacitance for a given volume
questions.x: Electrolytics pack far more capacitance into a given volume than other types, thanks to an extremely thin oxide dielectric grown on the plate. The tradeoffs are polarity, leakage and a limited life, which is why they appear in power supplies rather than RF circuits.

questions.q: What is the approximate forward threshold voltage of a silicon junction diode?
questions.x: About 0.7 volts for silicon. Learn it beside germanium's 0.3: silicon is roughly double. Nothing much conducts below the threshold, which is why a couple of diodes in series make a simple voltage reference.

questions.q: Why should wire-wound resistors not be used in RF circuits?
a: The resistor’s tolerance value would not be adequate
The resistor’s inductance could make circuit performance unpredictable
The resistor’s internal capacitance would detune the circuit
questions.x: A wire-wound resistor is a coil, so it has inductance whether you want it or not. At RF that reactance adds to the resistance in ways that shift tuning and make behaviour unpredictable. Use carbon or metal film instead.
questions.xs: ARRL Handbook; inductance of wound components

questions.q: What are the operating points for a bipolar transistor used as a switch?
a: The active region (between cutoff and saturation)
questions.x: A switch has two states, so the transistor is driven to saturation (fully on) or cutoff (fully off). It passes through the linear region only in transit. Staying out of that middle region is what keeps dissipation low.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of low voltage ceramic capacitors?
questions.x: Cheap. Low-voltage ceramics are mass-produced in enormous quantities, which is why they are everywhere. They are also small and non-polarized, but cost is the characteristic this question is after.

questions.q: Which of the following describes MOSFET construction?
a: The gate is formed by a back-biased junction
The gate is separated from the channel by a thin insulating layer
The source is separated from the drain by a thin insulating layer
The source is formed by depositing metal on silicon
questions.x: The gate sits on a thin insulating oxide layer rather than touching the channel, which is what the M-O-S in the name describes: metal, oxide, semiconductor. That insulation gives near-zero gate current and also makes MOSFETs easy to destroy with static.

questions.q: Which element of a vacuum tube regulates the flow of electrons between cathode and plate?
questions.x: The control grid. A small voltage on it steers the electron stream from cathode to plate, which is how a tube amplifies. It plays the same role the base does in a bipolar transistor.

questions.q: What happens when an inductor is operated above its self-resonant frequency?
questions.x: Every inductor has stray capacitance between its turns, and above the frequency where the two resonate the capacitance dominates. The part stops behaving like an inductor and starts behaving like a capacitor, which is why a choke chosen for the wrong band does nothing useful.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a screen grid in a vacuum tube?
a: To increase the control grid resistance
questions.x: The screen grid sits between control grid and plate and shields one from the other, cutting grid-to-plate capacitance. That capacitance is what causes unwanted feedback and oscillation in a triode amplifier.

questions.q: What determines the performance of a ferrite core at different frequencies?
a: The composition, or “mix,” of materials used
The ratio of outer diameter to inner diameter
questions.x: A ferrite's mix, its exact material composition, determines the frequency range where it is lossy and therefore useful. A mix meant for HF does little at VHF. Choosing the right mix matters more than adding more turns.
questions.xs: Ferrite material science; manufacturer mix data

questions.q: What is meant by the term MMIC?
questions.x: Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit: a complete microwave amplifier or mixer built on a single chip. Monolithic means one piece of substrate, which keeps the internal connections short enough to work at those frequencies.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of CMOS integrated circuits compared to TTL integrated circuits?
a: Better suited for power supply regulation
questions.x: CMOS draws almost no current when it is not switching, because its complementary transistors are never both fully on. TTL pulls current continuously. That difference is why battery-powered devices use CMOS.
questions.xs: CMOS logic; IEEE logic family standards

questions.q: What is a typical upper frequency limit for low SWR operation of 50-ohm BNC connectors?
questions.x: About 4 GHz for 50-ohm BNC. Above that the connector's geometry no longer maintains constant impedance and SWR climbs. Keep the connector ladder straight: BNC to 4 GHz, SMA to several GHz, Type N to 10 GHz.

questions.q: What is an advantage of using a ferrite core toroidal inductor?
a: Large values of inductance may be obtained
The magnetic properties of the core may be optimized for a specific range of frequencies
Most of the magnetic field is contained in the core
questions.x: A toroid confines its magnetic field almost entirely within the core, so it needs fewer turns for a given inductance and barely couples to neighbouring components. All the listed advantages are real, so the inclusive answer applies.

questions.q: What kind of device is an integrated circuit operational amplifier?
questions.x: An op-amp is an analog device. It amplifies continuously varying voltages rather than switching between logic levels. Digital circuits deal in discrete states; the op-amp works with everything in between.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a type N connector?
a: A moisture-resistant RF connector useful to 10 GHz
A small bayonet connector used for data circuits
A low noise figure VHF connector
A nickel plated version of the PL-259
questions.x: Type N is the weatherproof one, holding a constant 50-ohm impedance up to about 10 GHz. That combination of sealing and controlled impedance is why it belongs at the top of a tower rather than a PL-259.

questions.q: How is an LED biased when emitting light?
questions.x: Forward biased. Current crossing the junction in the forward direction releases energy as photons. Reverse the polarity and it simply stops, since an LED is a diode first and a light second.

questions.q: How does a ferrite bead or core reduce common-mode RF current on the shield of a coaxial cable?
a: By creating an impedance in the current’s path
It converts common-mode current to differential mode current
By creating an out-of-phase current to cancel the common-mode current
questions.x: The bead adds impedance to common-mode current, the component travelling the same direction on shield and centre conductor together. The differential signal you want sees almost nothing, so the bead removes the problem without touching your transmission.

questions.q: What is an SMA connector?
a: A small threaded connector suitable for signals up to several GHz
A connector designed for serial multiple access signals
A type of push-on connector intended for high-voltage applications
questions.x: SMA is a small threaded connector good for several gigahertz, common on handhelds and test gear. Its size is the point: it fits where a Type N cannot, at the cost of lower power handling and a finite number of matings.

questions.q: Which of these connector types is commonly used for low frequency or dc signal connections to a transceiver?
questions.x: RCA phono connectors handle low-frequency and DC connections on the back of a transceiver: keying lines, ALC, audio. They are cheap and easy but have no controlled impedance, so they never carry RF.

questions.q: What is the function of a power supply bleeder resistor?
a: It acts as a fuse for excess voltage
It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed
It removes shock hazards from the induction coils
questions.x: A bleeder resistor drains the filter capacitors once power is removed, so the supply is not still holding a lethal charge when you open it. It draws a trickle continuously in exchange for making the chassis safe to work on.

questions.q: Which of the following components are used in a power supply filter network?
questions.x: Capacitors and inductors. The capacitor holds voltage up between rectifier pulses while the inductor resists changes in current, and together they smooth pulsating DC into something steady. Resistors would only waste power doing it.

questions.q: Which type of rectifier circuit uses two diodes and a center-tapped transformer?
questions.x: That is the classic full-wave centre-tapped circuit: each diode handles one half of the cycle, using the centre tap as the return. Two diodes and a centre tap means full-wave; four diodes in a bridge is the other way to get there.

questions.q: What is characteristic of a half-wave rectifier in a power supply?
a: The ripple frequency is twice that of a full-wave rectifier
More current can be drawn from the half-wave rectifier
The output voltage is two times the peak input voltage
questions.x: A half-wave rectifier needs just one diode, which is its only real advantage. It throws away half the cycle, so the filtering has to work much harder and the transformer is used less efficiently.

questions.q: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a half-wave rectifier?
questions.x: 180 degrees, half the cycle. The diode conducts on one polarity and blocks the other, so only half the waveform reaches the load. That leaves a long gap the filter capacitor has to cover.

questions.q: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a full-wave rectifier?
questions.x: All 360 degrees. A full-wave circuit flips the negative half up rather than discarding it, so both halves reach the load. Nothing is wasted, which is why full-wave supplies filter more easily.

questions.q: What is the output waveform of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier connected to a resistive load?
a: A series of DC pulses at twice the frequency of the AC input
A series of DC pulses at the same frequency as the AC input
A sine wave at half the frequency of the AC input
questions.x: DC pulses at twice the input frequency. Both halves of each cycle become a positive pulse, so 60 Hz in gives 120 pulses per second out. That doubled ripple frequency is easier to filter, which is a second advantage of full-wave.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of a switchmode power supply as compared to a linear power supply?
a: Faster switching time makes higher output voltage possible
High-frequency operation allows the use of smaller components
questions.x: A switchmode supply chops the input at tens of kilohertz or more, and transformers and filters shrink dramatically as frequency rises. That is why a switching supply weighs a fraction of a linear one at the same power. The cost is switching noise.

questions.q: Which symbol in figure G7-1 represents a field effect transistor?
questions.x: Symbol 1 shows a circle with a vertical bar for the gate and an arrow into the channel, with the gate not touching the channel line. That separation is the FET signature. Compare it with symbol 2, where the leads meet the base bar directly.

questions.q: Which symbol in figure G7-1 represents a Zener diode?
questions.x: Symbol 5 is the diode whose cathode bar is bent at the ends rather than straight, which marks a Zener. The bend is the only difference from the plain diode at symbol 3, so look closely at the bar.

questions.q: Which symbol in figure G7-1 represents an NPN junction transistor?
questions.x: Symbol 2 is the bipolar transistor, and the arrow on the emitter points away from the base, which makes it NPN. An arrow pointing inward would be PNP. Remember it as Not Pointing iN.

questions.q: Which symbol in Figure G7-1 represents a solid core transformer?
questions.x: Symbol 6 shows two coils with solid lines drawn between them, and those lines represent an iron or solid core. Air-core transformers omit them, so the presence of the core lines is what the question is testing.

questions.q: Which symbol in Figure G7-1 represents a tapped inductor?
questions.x: Symbol 7 is the coil with an extra connection partway along its length. A tap lets you take part of the winding, so one inductor offers several values. No arrow means fixed taps rather than a continuously variable inductor.

questions.q: What is the purpose of neutralizing an amplifier?
a: To cut off the final amplifier during standby periods
To keep the carrier on frequency
questions.x: Neutralizing cancels the feedback that internal capacitance couples from output back to input. Left alone that feedback turns an amplifier into an oscillator, so a deliberate out-of-phase path is injected to cancel it.

questions.q: Which of these classes of amplifiers has the highest efficiency?
questions.x: Class C is the most efficient, because the device conducts for well under half the cycle and dissipates very little the rest of the time. Efficiency and linearity trade against each other, so Class C is also the most distorting.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the function of a two-input AND gate?
a: Output is high when either or both inputs are low
Output is high only when both inputs are high
Output is low when either or both inputs are high
Output is low only when both inputs are high
questions.x: AND means both. The output goes high only when every input is high, so with two inputs there is exactly one combination that produces a high output. OR would need only one input high.

questions.q: In a Class A amplifier, what percentage of the time does the amplifying device conduct?
questions.x: 100 percent. A Class A stage conducts through the entire cycle, which is what makes it the most linear and the least efficient. The device dissipates power even with no signal present.

questions.q: How many states does a 3-bit binary counter have?
questions.x: Eight, since 2 to the third power is 8. Each bit doubles the count, so n bits gives 2 to the n states: 3 bits gives 8, 4 bits gives 16. The counter runs 000 through 111.

questions.q: What is a shift register?
a: A clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array
An array of operational amplifiers used for tri-state arithmetic operations
questions.x: A shift register is a chain of clocked stages, each passing its contents to the next on every clock pulse. Data walks along the array one step per clock, which is how serial and parallel formats get converted.

questions.q: Which of the following are basic components of a sine wave oscillator?
a: A frequency multiplier and a mixer
A circulator and a filter operating in a feed-forward loop
A filter and an amplifier operating in a feedback loop
questions.x: An amplifier and a frequency-selective filter connected in a feedback loop. The amplifier supplies gain, the filter decides which frequency survives, and the loop sustains oscillation at that frequency.

questions.q: How is the efficiency of an RF power amplifier determined?
a: Divide the DC input power by the DC output power
Divide the RF output power by the DC input power
Multiply the RF input power by the reciprocal of the RF output power
Add the RF input power to the DC output power
questions.x: RF output power divided by DC input power. A 100-watt output drawing 200 watts from the supply is 50 percent efficient, and the missing 100 watts left as heat. The difference always becomes heat, which is why amplifiers need sinks and fans.

questions.q: What determines the frequency of an LC oscillator?
a: The number of stages in the counter
The number of stages in the divider
The inductance and capacitance in the tank circuit
The time delay of the lag circuit
questions.x: The inductance and capacitance of the tank circuit set the frequency, since resonance occurs where their reactances cancel. Change either component and the frequency moves, which is exactly how a VFO tunes.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a linear amplifier?
a: Any RF power amplifier used in conjunction with an amateur transceiver
An amplifier in which the output preserves the input waveform
A Class C high efficiency amplifier
An amplifier used as a frequency multiplier
questions.x: A linear amplifier reproduces the input waveform's shape at higher amplitude, without adding distortion. That fidelity is essential for SSB, where the envelope carries the information. Class A and AB are linear; Class C is not.

questions.q: For which of the following modes is a Class C power stage appropriate for amplifying a modulated signal?
questions.x: FM, because its envelope is constant. Class C mangles amplitude but FM carries nothing in the amplitude, so nothing is lost and you keep the efficiency. Try it with SSB and the signal is destroyed.

questions.q: What circuit is used to select one of the sidebands from a balanced modulator?
questions.x: A filter. A balanced modulator produces both sidebands with the carrier suppressed, and a sharp filter then passes one sideband and rejects the other. Filter method is the traditional way to generate SSB.

questions.q: What output is produced by a balanced modulator?
a: Audio extracted from the modulation signal
questions.x: Double-sideband RF with the carrier suppressed. The balancing is what kills the carrier; both sidebands survive. Removing one of them is the next stage, which is what G7C01 asks about.

questions.q: What is one reason to use an impedance matching transformer at a transmitter output?
a: To present the desired impedance to the transmitter and feed line
questions.x: To present the impedance both the transmitter and the feed line expect, normally 50 ohms. The transmitter delivers full power into its designed load, and reflections on the line are minimized.

questions.q: How is a product detector used?
a: Used in test gear to detect spurious mixing products
Used in a transmitter to perform frequency multiplication
Used in an FM receiver to filter out unwanted sidebands
Used in a single sideband receiver to extract the modulated signal
questions.x: A product detector mixes the incoming SSB signal with a locally generated carrier to recover the audio. SSB arrives with its carrier removed, so the receiver has to supply a replacement, and that is what the detector multiplies against.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of a direct digital synthesizer (DDS)?
a: Variable output frequency with the stability of a crystal oscillator
