questions.x: A DDS synthesizes any frequency you ask for from a single crystal reference, so you get continuous tuning with crystal stability. Older VFOs gave you one or the other, not both.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of a digital signal processing (DSP) filter compared to an analog filter?
a: A wide range of filter bandwidths and shapes can be created
The DSP filter is much more effective at VHF frequencies
questions.x: A DSP filter is defined in software, so its bandwidth and response shape are just numbers you can change. One radio offers dozens of filters where an analog design would need a physical crystal filter for each.

questions.q: What term specifies a filter’s attenuation inside its passband?
questions.x: Insertion loss is the attenuation a filter adds inside its own passband, the price you pay for the signals you wanted to keep. Ideally near zero, and it is measured by comparing the signal with and without the filter in circuit.

questions.q: Which parameter affects receiver sensitivity?
questions.x: Sensitivity depends on noise figure, gain distribution and bandwidth together, so all the listed parameters matter. Sensitivity is a system property rather than a single stage's specification.

questions.q: What is the phase difference between the I and Q RF signals that software-defined radio (SDR) equipment uses for modulation and demodulation?
questions.x: Ninety degrees, which is what quadrature means. Two signals a quarter cycle apart carry both amplitude and phase, and that pair is enough to describe any modulation completely.

questions.q: What is an advantage of using I-Q modulation with software-defined radios (SDRs)?
a: The need for high resolution analog-to-digital converters is eliminated
All types of modulation can be created with appropriate processing
Minimum detectible signal level is reduced
Automatic conversion of the signal from digital to analog
questions.x: With both I and Q available, any modulation can be created or decoded purely in software, since the pair fully describes amplitude and phase. That is why one SDR handles SSB, FM, digital modes and anything invented next year.

questions.q: Which of these functions is performed by software in a software-defined radio (SDR)?
questions.x: An SDR does filtering, demodulation and modulation in software, so all the listed functions apply. The hardware's job shrinks to converting between RF and digital samples as faithfully as possible.

questions.q: What is the frequency above which a low-pass filter’s output power is less than half the input power?
questions.x: Cutoff frequency, defined at the half-power point, which is 3 dB down. Half power is not zero power: a low-pass filter keeps attenuating above cutoff rather than stopping abruptly there.

questions.q: What term specifies a filter’s maximum ability to reject signals outside its passband?
questions.x: Ultimate rejection is the best attenuation a filter achieves far outside its passband. Insertion loss describes what happens inside the passband, ultimate rejection describes what happens well outside it.

questions.q: The bandwidth of a band-pass filter is measured between what two frequencies?
questions.x: Between the upper and lower half-power points, each 3 dB down from the peak. Same convention as the cutoff frequency in G7C12. Bandwidth is the distance between those two 3 dB points.

questions.q: How is direct binary FSK modulation generated?
a: By keying an FM transmitter with a sub-audible tone
By changing an oscillator’s frequency directly with a digital control signal
By using a transceiver’s computer data interface protocol to change frequencies
By reconfiguring the CW keying input to act as a tone generator
questions.x: Direct FSK shifts the oscillator itself between two frequencies under control of the data bits. No audio tones are involved, which distinguishes it from AFSK, where tones are fed into an SSB transmitter instead.

questions.q: What is the name of the process that changes the phase angle of an RF signal to convey information?
questions.x: Phase modulation, PM. Information rides on where the wave sits in its cycle rather than on how fast or how strong it is. PM and FM are closely related, which is why radios often list the mode as FM/PM together.

questions.q: What is the name of the process that changes the instantaneous frequency of an RF wave to convey information?
questions.x: Frequency modulation. The instantaneous frequency moves with the modulating signal while amplitude stays constant. That constant amplitude is what gives FM its noise immunity and lets Class C amplifiers handle it.

questions.q: What emission is produced by a reactance modulator connected to a transmitter RF amplifier stage?
questions.x: Phase modulation. A reactance modulator applied at an RF amplifier stage varies phase rather than the oscillator's frequency. Applied to the oscillator itself it would produce FM, so where it sits determines which you get.

questions.q: What type of modulation varies the instantaneous power level of the RF signal?
questions.x: Amplitude modulation. The instantaneous power level tracks the modulating signal, which is exactly why AM is vulnerable to noise: anything that changes amplitude along the way corrupts the information.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of QPSK31?
a: Its bandwidth is approximately the same as BPSK31
questions.x: QPSK31 uses four phase states, includes forward error correction, and occupies the same narrow bandwidth as PSK31. All the listed characteristics are accurate, so the inclusive answer applies. The FEC costs throughput but survives worse paths.

questions.q: Which of the following phone emissions uses the narrowest bandwidth?
questions.x: Single sideband, about 3 kHz. AM needs roughly 6 kHz for the same audio because it carries both sidebands plus a carrier, and FM voice needs 10 to 15 kHz. SSB is the narrowest phone mode there is.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effect of overmodulation?
questions.x: Excessive bandwidth. Driving a transmitter past its linear range creates distortion products that spread outside the intended channel, so you splatter onto neighbouring frequencies. It also makes your audio worse, not louder.

questions.q: What type of modulation is used by FT8?
questions.x: FT8 uses 8-tone frequency shift keying, which is where the 8 in the name comes from. Eight tones let each symbol carry three bits, and the whole signal fits in about 50 Hz.

questions.q: What is meant by the term “flat-topping,” when referring to an amplitude-modulated phone signal?
a: Signal distortion caused by insufficient collector current
The transmitter’s automatic level control (ALC) is properly adjusted
Signal distortion caused by excessive drive or speech levels
The transmitter’s carrier is properly suppressed
questions.x: Flat-topping is what you see when the modulation peaks get clipped off square because drive or speech level is too high. The envelope should be a smooth curve; a flattened top means distortion and splatter.

questions.q: What is the modulation envelope of an AM signal?
a: The waveform created by connecting the peak values of the modulated signal
The carrier frequency that contains the signal
Spurious signals that envelop nearby frequencies
The bandwidth of the modulated signal
questions.x: The envelope is the curve you get by joining the peaks of the modulated waveform. It traces out the modulating audio, which is why looking at the envelope on a scope tells you immediately whether the modulation is clean.

questions.q: What is QPSK modulation?
a: Modulation using quasi-parallel to serial conversion to reduce bandwidth
Modulation using quadra-pole sideband keying to generate spread spectrum signals
Modulation using Fast Fourier Transforms to generate frequencies at the first, second, third, and fourth harmonics of the carrier frequency to improve noise immunity
Modulation in which digital data is transmitted using 0-, 90-, 180- and 270-degrees phase shift to represent pairs of bits
questions.x: QPSK uses four phase states at 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, and four states encode two bits each. That doubles the data rate compared with plain PSK without needing more bandwidth.

questions.q: What is a link budget?
a: The financial costs associated with operating a radio link
The sum of antenna gains minus system losses
The sum of transmit power and antenna gains minus system losses as seen at the receiver
The difference between transmit power and receiver sensitivity
questions.x: A link budget adds up transmit power and antenna gains, subtracts every loss along the path, and tells you what arrives at the receiver. It is how you decide whether a path will work before building anything.
questions.xs: Link budget analysis; ITU-R Rec. P.341

questions.q: What is link margin?
a: The difference between received power level and minimum required signal level at the input to the receiver
questions.x: Link margin is the headroom: how much stronger the received signal is than the minimum the receiver needs. Margin is what absorbs fading, so a path with no margin works only under ideal conditions.

questions.q: Which mixer input is varied or tuned to convert signals of different frequencies to an intermediate frequency (IF)?
questions.x: The local oscillator. Tuning it changes which incoming frequency lands on the fixed IF, so the LO is what you move when you turn the dial. The IF stays put, which is what lets its filters be so good.

questions.q: What is the term for interference from a signal at twice the IF frequency from the desired signal?
questions.x: Image response. A signal offset from the desired one by twice the IF mixes down to the same IF, so the receiver cannot tell them apart. Front-end filtering ahead of the mixer is what rejects it.

questions.q: What is another term for the mixing of two RF signals?
questions.x: Heterodyning, from the Greek for other force. Mixing two frequencies in a non-linear device produces their sum and difference, and that principle underlies every superheterodyne receiver.

questions.q: What is the stage in a VHF FM transmitter that generates a harmonic of a lower frequency signal to reach the desired operating frequency?
questions.x: A multiplier stage. It is driven into non-linearity deliberately so it generates harmonics, then one harmonic is filtered out. That is how a stable low-frequency oscillator reaches VHF, and it is why G8B07's deviation gets multiplied too.

questions.q: Which intermodulation products are closest to the original signal frequencies?
questions.x: Odd-order products land closest to the original signals, which is precisely why they cause trouble. Third-order products such as 2F1 minus F2 fall right beside the wanted signals, where no filter can remove them.

questions.q: What is the total bandwidth of an FM phone transmission having 5 kHz deviation and 3 kHz modulating frequency?
questions.x: Carson's rule: bandwidth is twice the sum of deviation and highest modulating frequency. Two times 5 plus 3 gives 16 kHz. Both numbers go inside the parentheses before doubling, which is the step people skip.

questions.q: What is the frequency deviation for a 12.21 MHz reactance modulated oscillator in a 5 kHz deviation, 146.52 MHz FM phone transmitter?
questions.x: 146.52 divided by 12.21 is exactly 12, so the oscillator is multiplied twelvefold. Deviation multiplies by the same factor, so working backwards gives 5000 divided by 12, or 416.7 Hz at the oscillator.

questions.q: Why is it important to know the duty cycle of the mode you are using when transmitting?
a: To aid in tuning your transmitter
Some modes have high duty cycles that could exceed the transmitter’s average power rating
To allow time for the other station to break in during a transmission
questions.x: Modes differ enormously in duty cycle. SSB transmits in bursts, while FT8 and RTTY key at full output for their entire transmission. Run a high duty cycle mode at full power and you can cook a transmitter rated for SSB service.

questions.q: Why is it good to match receiver bandwidth to the bandwidth of the operating mode?
a: It is required by FCC rules
It minimizes power consumption in the receiver
It improves impedance matching of the antenna
It results in the best signal-to-noise ratio
questions.x: Noise arrives across the whole passband while the signal occupies only part of it, so a filter matched to the mode admits the signal and rejects the rest. Matching bandwidth to mode gives the best signal-to-noise ratio available.

questions.q: What is the relationship between transmitted symbol rate and bandwidth?
a: Symbol rate and bandwidth are not related
Higher symbol rates require wider bandwidth
Lower symbol rates require wider bandwidth
Bandwidth is half the symbol rate
questions.x: Higher symbol rates need more bandwidth. Faster transitions mean sidebands spread further from the carrier, which is a hard limit set by information theory rather than by equipment quality.

questions.q: What combination of a mixer’s Local Oscillator (LO) and RF input frequencies is found in the output?
questions.x: Both the sum and the difference appear, along with the two originals. The IF filter then selects whichever you want, which is why the same mixer works for either high-side or low-side injection.

questions.q: What process combines two signals in a non-linear circuit to produce unwanted spurious outputs?
questions.x: Intermodulation. Two signals passing through a non-linear stage mix with each other and produce sums and differences of their multiples. Unlike harmonics, these products involve both signals, which is why they land in awkward places.

questions.q: Which of the following is an odd-order intermodulation product of frequencies F1 and F2?
questions.x: Order is the sum of the coefficients, so 2F1 minus F2 has order 2 plus 1, which is 3 and therefore odd. Third-order products are the troublesome ones because they fall closest to the original frequencies.

questions.q: Which digital mode is used as a low-power beacon for assessing HF propagation?
questions.x: WSPR, the Weak Signal Propagation Reporter, runs a few watts or less and reports decodes to a central database. It is built to map propagation rather than to hold contacts, so you can see which paths are open worldwide.

questions.q: What part of a packet radio frame contains the routing and handling information?
questions.x: The header carries source and destination call signs plus the digipeater path, so every station handling the frame knows where it came from and where it is going. The data payload follows, and a checksum ends the frame.

questions.q: Which of the following describes Baudot code?
a: A 7-bit code with start, stop, and parity bits
A code using error detection and correction
A 5-bit code with additional start and stop bits
A code using SELCAL and LISTEN
questions.x: Baudot is a 5-bit code with start and stop bits added around each character. Five bits give only 32 combinations, so it uses shift characters to switch between letters and figures, which is why RTTY garbles into numbers when a shift is missed.
questions.xs: ITU-T Rec. F.1 (International Telegraph Alphabet No. 2)

questions.q: In an ARQ mode, what is meant by a NAK response to a transmitted packet?
a: Receiving station connected and ready for transmissions
questions.x: NAK is a negative acknowledgment: the block arrived corrupted, so send it again. Its counterpart ACK confirms good receipt. That request-and-resend cycle is what the ARQ in the name describes.

questions.q: What action results from a failure to exchange information due to excessive transmission attempts when using an ARQ mode?
a: Encoding reverts to the default character set
questions.x: After enough failed retries the connection is dropped. The protocol will not corrupt your data by giving up on accuracy, so when the path degrades past usefulness it disconnects instead.

questions.q: Which of the following narrow-band digital modes can receive signals with very low signal-to-noise ratios?
questions.x: FT8 decodes well below the noise floor, roughly to minus 21 dB signal-to-noise. It achieves that with a tightly structured message, a fixed 15-second window and heavy error correction, trading flexibility for sensitivity.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true about PSK31?
a: Upper case letters are sent with more power
Upper case letters use longer Varicode bit sequences and thus slow down transmission
Error correction is used to ensure accurate message reception
Higher power is needed as compared to RTTY for similar error rates
questions.x: Varicode gives common characters short bit sequences and rare ones longer sequences, and upper case letters are among the long ones. Typing in capitals genuinely slows your transmission, which is why PSK31 operators use lower case.

questions.q: Which is true of mesh network microwave nodes?
a: Having more nodes increases signal strengths
If one node fails, a packet may still reach its target station via an alternate node
Links between two nodes in a network may have different frequencies and bandwidths
More nodes reduce overall microwave out of band interference
questions.x: A mesh finds another route when a node fails, because every node relays for its neighbours and the routing adapts. That self-healing property is the reason mesh networks suit emergency work.

questions.q: How does forward error correction (FEC) allow the receiver to correct data errors?
a: By controlling transmitter output power for optimum signal strength
By using the Varicode character set
By transmitting redundant information with the data
By using a parity bit with each character
questions.x: FEC sends extra redundant bits alongside the data, enough that the receiver can reconstruct what was corrupted without asking for a resend. That is the difference from ARQ, which requests retransmission instead.

questions.q: How are the two separate frequencies of a Frequency Shift Keyed (FSK) signal identified?
questions.x: Mark and space, the two frequencies of an FSK signal. The names come from mechanical telegraphy, where one state marked the paper and the other left a space. Swap them and the decode inverts into garbage.

questions.q: Which type of code is used for sending characters in a PSK31 signal?
questions.x: Varicode, a variable-length code designed for PSK31. Assigning the shortest patterns to the most frequent letters keeps the average throughput high at a very low symbol rate, which is what makes PSK31 so narrow.

questions.q: What is indicated on a waterfall display by one or more vertical lines on either side of a data mode or RTTY signal?
questions.x: Extra vertical lines flanking the signal are the sidebands overmodulation creates. A clean data signal shows only its own tones, so those flanking lines mean turn the audio down.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a waterfall display?
a: Frequency is horizontal, signal strength is vertical, time is intensity
Frequency is vertical, signal strength is intensity, time is horizontal
Frequency is horizontal, signal strength is intensity, time is vertical
Frequency is vertical, signal strength is horizontal, time is intensity
questions.x: A waterfall maps frequency across the screen, signal strength as brightness or colour, and time scrolling vertically. That third axis is what makes it a waterfall rather than a plain spectrum display.

questions.q: What does an FT8 signal report of +3 mean?
a: The signal is 3 times the noise level of an equivalent SSB signal
The signal-to-noise ratio is equivalent to +3dB in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth
The signal is 3 dB over S9
questions.x: FT8 reports signal-to-noise ratio referenced to a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, so plus 3 means the signal is 3 dB above the noise in that reference. Negative numbers are the norm; anything positive is genuinely strong for FT8.

questions.q: Which of the following provide digital voice modes?
a: Winlink, PACTOR II, and PACTOR III
questions.x: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are the three digital voice systems in common amateur use, each with its own vocoder and network. They do not interoperate over the air, which is why local repeater choice matters.
questions.xs: ETSI TS 102 361 (DMR); JARL D-STAR; Yaesu System Fusion

questions.q: Which of the following factors determine the characteristic impedance of a parallel conductor feed line?
a: The distance between the centers of the conductors and the radius of the conductors
The distance between the centers of the conductors and the length of the line
The radius of the conductors and the frequency of the signal
The frequency of the signal and the length of the line
questions.x: For parallel conductors, impedance is set by the spacing between conductor centres and the conductor radius. Wider spacing raises it, thicker wire lowers it. Nothing about length or power enters into characteristic impedance.

questions.q: What is the relationship between high standing wave ratio (SWR) and transmission line loss?
a: There is no relationship between transmission line loss and SWR
High SWR increases loss in a lossy transmission line
High SWR makes it difficult to measure transmission line loss
High SWR reduces the relative effect of transmission line loss
questions.x: High SWR only matters in a lossy line. Reflected power travels the line again, so it gets attenuated twice more, and each pass costs whatever that cable loses per hundred feet. On low-loss line at HF the penalty is small; on lossy cable at UHF it is severe.

questions.q: What is the nominal characteristic impedance of “window line” transmission line?
questions.x: 450 ohms. Window line is the flat ladder line with rectangular cutouts, and those windows keep the effective dielectric mostly air, which is why its loss is far lower than coax.

questions.q: What causes reflected power at an antenna’s feed point?
a: Operating an antenna at its resonant frequency
Using more transmitter power than the antenna can handle
A difference between feed line impedance and antenna feed point impedance
Feeding the antenna with unbalanced feed line
questions.x: A mismatch between the line's characteristic impedance and the antenna's feed point impedance. Whatever the line cannot deliver into that load comes back toward the transmitter. Match the two and nothing reflects.

questions.q: How does the attenuation of coaxial cable change with increasing frequency?
a: Attenuation follows Marconi’s Law of Attenuation
questions.x: Attenuation rises with frequency. Skin effect crowds current into an ever thinner surface layer, raising resistance, and dielectric losses climb too. A cable that is fine on 80 meters can waste half your power at 440 MHz.

questions.q: In what units is RF feed line loss usually expressed?
questions.x: Decibels per 100 feet, quoted at a stated frequency. Expressing it per unit length lets you scale to your own run, and it must be per frequency because loss changes with it.

questions.q: What must be done to prevent standing waves on a feed line connected to an antenna?
a: The antenna feed point must be at DC ground potential
The feed line must be an odd number of electrical quarter wavelengths long
The feed line must be an even number of physical half wavelengths long
The antenna feed point impedance must be matched to the characteristic impedance of the feed line
questions.x: Match the antenna feed point impedance to the line's characteristic impedance. Standing waves exist because energy reflects, and only a matched load absorbs it all. A tuner at the shack end does not prevent them.

questions.q: If the SWR on an antenna feed line is 5:1, and a matching network at the transmitter end of the feed line is adjusted to present a 1:1 SWR to the transmitter, what is the resulting SWR on the feed line?
a: Between 1:1 and 5:1 depending on the characteristic impedance of the line
Between 1:1 and 5:1 depending on the reflected power at the transmitter
questions.x: Still 5:1. The tuner makes the transmitter see 1:1, but nothing at the antenna has changed, so the standing waves on the line are exactly where they were. This is the most commonly misunderstood point about tuners.

questions.q: What standing wave ratio results from connecting a 50-ohm feed line to a 200-ohm resistive load?
questions.x: For a purely resistive load, SWR is the ratio of the larger impedance to the smaller: 200 over 50 is 4, so 4:1. Always put the bigger number on top, since SWR can never read below 1:1.

questions.q: What standing wave ratio results from connecting a 50-ohm feed line to a 10-ohm resistive load?
questions.x: 50 over 10 is 5, so 5:1. Note this is a load below the line impedance while G9A09 was above it, and the arithmetic is the same either way. Divide larger by smaller.

questions.q: What is the effect of transmission line loss on SWR measured at the input to the line?
a: Higher loss reduces SWR measured at the input to the line
Higher loss increases SWR measured at the input to the line
Higher loss increases the accuracy of SWR measured at the input to the line
Transmission line loss does not affect the SWR measurement
questions.x: Loss makes the SWR measured at the shack look better than it really is. The reflected wave is attenuated on its way back, so less of it reaches your meter. A very lossy line can read a comfortable SWR while the antenna is badly mismatched.

questions.q: What is a characteristic of a random-wire HF antenna connected directly to the transmitter?
a: It must be longer than 1 wavelength
Station equipment may carry significant RF current
It produces only vertically polarized radiation
It is more effective on the lower HF bands than on the higher bands
questions.x: A random wire fed directly against the station gives the RF current no defined return path, so it flows on your equipment chassis, cables and microphone. That is what causes RF burns and interference in your own shack. A counterpoise or proper ground system is what fixes it.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common way to adjust the feed point impedance of an elevated quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna to be approximately 50 ohms?
a: Lengthen the radials beyond one wavelength
questions.x: Slope the radials downward. A quarter-wave ground plane with horizontal radials feeds near 36 ohms; drooping them raises it toward 50, which matches coax directly. Around 45 degrees gets you there.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the radiation pattern of a quarter-wave ground-plane vertical antenna?
questions.x: Omnidirectional in azimuth, meaning equal in every compass direction. It is not omnidirectional in elevation: the pattern is a doughnut with a null straight up, which is why verticals favour low angles and DX.

questions.q: What is the radiation pattern of a dipole antenna in free space in a plane containing the conductor?
a: It is a figure-eight at right angles to the antenna
It is a figure-eight off both ends of the antenna
It is a circle (equal radiation in all directions)
It has a pair of lobes on one side of the antenna and a single lobe on the other side
questions.x: A figure-eight broadside to the wire, with deep nulls off the ends. Point the wire across the path you want rather than at it. Two lobes at right angles to the conductor is the whole pattern.

questions.q: How does antenna height affect the azimuthal radiation pattern of a horizontal dipole HF antenna at elevation angles higher than about 45 degrees?
a: If the antenna is too high, the pattern becomes unpredictable
Antenna height has no effect on the pattern
If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, the azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional
If the antenna is less than 1/2 wavelength high, radiation off the ends of the wire is eliminated
questions.x: Below half a wavelength up, ground reflection fills in the dipole's nulls at high elevation angles, so the azimuthal pattern goes nearly omnidirectional. The figure-eight only appears once the antenna is high enough to be free of that effect.

questions.q: Where should the radial wires of a ground-mounted vertical antenna system be placed?
a: As high as possible above the ground
On the surface or buried a few inches below the ground
At the center of the antenna
questions.x: On the surface or a few inches under. Radials work as the return path for antenna current, and burying them deeply puts lossy soil between them and the antenna. Shallow is better, and more radials beat longer ones.

questions.q: How does the feed point impedance of a horizontal 1/2 wave dipole antenna change as the antenna height is reduced to 1/10 wavelength above ground?
a: It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength above ground
It is unaffected by the height above ground
questions.x: It steadily decreases. A dipole is near 73 ohms in free space, but bringing it close to ground drops the feed point impedance well below that, sometimes under 50 ohms at a tenth of a wavelength. Ground coupling changes the antenna, not just the pattern.

questions.q: How does the feed point impedance of a 1/2 wave dipole change as the feed point is moved from the center toward the ends?
a: It peaks at about 1/8 wavelength from the end
It is unaffected by the location of the feed point
questions.x: It steadily increases, because current is highest at the centre and voltage is highest at the ends. Impedance is voltage over current, so moving toward the ends raises it, reaching thousands of ohms at the tip. That is why an end-fed half wave needs a matching network.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of using a horizontally polarized as compared to a vertically polarized HF antenna?
questions.x: Lower ground losses. A vertical relies on the ground as part of its return path, so soil conductivity directly costs you efficiency. A horizontal antenna a reasonable height up does not depend on the ground that way.

questions.q: What is the approximate length for a 1/2 wave dipole antenna cut for 14.250 MHz?
questions.x: Use 468 divided by the frequency in MHz: 468 over 14.25 is 32.8, so about 33 feet. The 468 accounts for end effect, which is why it is not the full 492 that free-space geometry would suggest.

questions.q: What is the approximate length for a 1/2 wave dipole antenna cut for 3.550 MHz?
questions.x: 468 divided by 3.55 gives 131.8, so about 132 feet. Same formula as G9B10, and worth noticing that a lower frequency means a much longer antenna. Eighty meters needs real estate.

questions.q: What is the approximate length for a 1/4 wave monopole antenna cut for 28.5 MHz?
questions.x: A quarter wave uses 234, half of the dipole's 468: 234 over 28.5 is 8.2, so about 8 feet. Two formulas cover most antenna length questions, and one is simply half the other.

questions.q: Which of the following would increase the bandwidth of a Yagi antenna?
a: Loading coils in series with the element
questions.x: Larger-diameter elements. Fatter conductors lower the antenna's Q, and lower Q means a broader response. It is the same relationship that makes a physically short, heavily loaded antenna so narrow.

questions.q: What is the approximate length of the driven element of a Yagi antenna?
questions.x: About a half wavelength, since the driven element is essentially a dipole. The reflector and directors are parasitic: they are not fed at all, and they work by re-radiating what the driven element illuminates them with.

questions.q: How do the lengths of a three-element Yagi reflector and director compare to that of the driven element?
a: The reflector is longer, and the director is shorter
The reflector is shorter, and the director is longer
They are all the same length
Relative length depends on the frequency of operation
questions.x: Reflector longer, director shorter. A longer element is inductive and lags, pushing energy forward; a shorter one is capacitive and leads, pulling it forward. Directors always point the way the beam looks.

questions.q: How does antenna gain in dBi compare to gain stated in dBd for the same antenna?
a: Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB lower
Gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher
Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd lower
Gain in dBd is 1.25 dBd higher
questions.x: dBi is 2.15 dB higher for the same antenna, because an isotropic radiator is a weaker reference than a dipole. A dipole already has 2.15 dBi of gain, so quoting against isotropic makes any number look better. Check which reference a manufacturer used.

questions.q: What is the primary effect of increasing boom length and adding directors to a Yagi antenna?
questions.x: Gain increases. A longer boom with more directors concentrates radiation into a narrower beam, and narrowing the beam is what gain means. The cost is a sharper pattern and less bandwidth.

questions.q: What does “front-to-back ratio” mean in reference to a Yagi antenna?
a: The number of directors versus the number of reflectors
The relative position of the driven element with respect to the reflectors and directors
The power radiated in the major lobe compared to that in the opposite direction
The ratio of forward gain to dipole gain
questions.x: Front-to-back ratio compares power in the main lobe with power radiated directly behind. It measures how well the antenna ignores what is behind you, which matters more for rejecting interference than for reaching the station in front.

questions.q: What is meant by the “main lobe” of a directive antenna?
a: The magnitude of the maximum vertical angle of radiation
The point of maximum current in a radiating antenna element
The maximum voltage standing wave point on a radiating element
The direction of maximum radiated field strength from the antenna
questions.x: The main lobe is the direction of maximum radiated field strength, the direction you point the beam. Every other lobe is a side lobe, and gain figures always refer to the main one.

questions.q: In free space, how does the gain of two three-element, horizontally polarized Yagi antennas spaced vertically 1/2 wavelength apart typically compare to the gain of a single three-element Yagi?
questions.x: About 3 dB higher, because doubling the number of identical antennas doubles the effective aperture. Stacking two of anything correctly phased is the classic 3 dB, the same 3 dB that means twice the power.
questions.xs: Antenna stacking theory; ARRL Antenna Book

questions.q: Which of the following can be adjusted to optimize forward gain, front-to-back ratio, or SWR bandwidth of a Yagi antenna?
a: The physical length of the boom
The number of elements on the boom
The spacing of each element along the boom
questions.x: Element lengths, element spacing and the matching arrangement all interact, so any of them can be adjusted to favour gain, front-to-back ratio or bandwidth. Since all the listed items apply, the inclusive answer is right. You cannot maximize all three at once.

questions.q: What is a beta or hairpin match?
a: A shorted transmission line stub placed at the feed point of a Yagi antenna to provide impedance matching
A 1/4 wavelength section of 75-ohm coax in series with the feed point of a Yagi to provide impedance matching
A series capacitor selected to cancel the inductive reactance of a folded dipole antenna
A section of 300-ohm twin-lead transmission line used to match a folded dipole antenna
questions.x: A beta or hairpin match is a shorted stub across the feed point, adding a parallel inductance that transforms a low driven-element impedance up to 50 ohms. It is simple, weatherproof and needs no adjustment once cut.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of using a gamma match with a Yagi antenna?
a: It does not require the driven element to be insulated from the boom
It does not require any inductors or capacitors
It is useful for matching multiband antennas
questions.x: A gamma match feeds the element off-centre through a series capacitor, so the driven element can stay bonded to the boom. That mechanical simplicity is the advantage: no insulators to fail up in the air.

questions.q: Which of the following antenna types will be most effective as a near vertical incidence skywave (NVIS) antenna for short-skip communications on 40 meters during the day?
a: A horizontal dipole placed between 1/10 and 1/4 wavelength above the ground
A vertical antenna placed between 1/4 and 1/2 wavelength above the ground
A horizontal dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
A vertical dipole placed at approximately 1/2 wavelength above the ground
questions.x: A horizontal dipole between a tenth and a quarter wavelength up. That low height sends most of the energy nearly straight upward, which is exactly what NVIS needs to drop signals back down within a few hundred miles.

questions.q: What is the feed point impedance of an end-fed half-wave antenna?
questions.x: Very high, in the thousands of ohms, because voltage peaks and current is minimal at the end of a half wave. That is the same current and voltage distribution behind G9B08, which is why an end fed needs a substantial matching transformer.

questions.q: In which direction is the maximum radiation from a VHF/UHF “halo” antenna?
a: Broadside to the plane of the halo
Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo
On the same side as the feed point
questions.x: Omnidirectional in the plane of the halo. A halo is a dipole bent into a near-circle, which keeps horizontal polarization for weak-signal work while giving coverage in all directions rather than a figure-eight.

questions.q: What is the primary function of antenna traps?
a: To provide balanced feed point impedance
questions.x: Traps enable multiband operation. Each trap is a parallel resonant circuit that goes high-impedance on one band, electrically disconnecting the wire beyond it, so the same antenna presents a different length on each band.

questions.q: What is an advantage of vertically stacking horizontally polarized Yagi antennas?
a: It allows quick selection of vertical or horizontal polarization
It allows simultaneous vertical and horizontal polarization
It narrows the main lobe in azimuth
It narrows the main lobe in elevation
questions.x: It narrows the main lobe in elevation. Vertical stacking compresses the pattern vertically, which lowers the takeoff angle and puts more energy toward the horizon where distant stations are. Horizontal coverage is unchanged.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of a log-periodic antenna?
a: Higher gain per element than a Yagi antenna
questions.x: Wide bandwidth. A log-periodic covers a very broad frequency range with usable gain and pattern, which is why it appears where one antenna must handle many bands. The tradeoff is less gain than a monoband Yagi of similar size.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a log-periodic antenna?
a: Element length and spacing vary logarithmically along the boom
Impedance varies periodically as a function of frequency
Gain varies logarithmically as a function of frequency
SWR varies periodically as a function of boom length
questions.x: Element lengths and spacings scale logarithmically along the boom, so at any frequency a different group of elements is active. That scaling is what produces the wide bandwidth in G9D06.

questions.q: How does a “screwdriver” mobile antenna adjust its feed point impedance?
a: By varying the base loading inductance
By extending and retracting the whip
questions.x: By varying the base loading inductance. A motor drives a threaded core in and out of the coil, which is where the screwdriver nickname comes from. It lets one mobile antenna retune across the bands from the driver's seat.

questions.q: What is the primary use of a Beverage antenna?
a: Directional receiving for MF and low HF bands
Directional transmitting for low HF bands
Portable direction finding at higher HF frequencies
Portable direction finding at lower HF frequencies
questions.x: Directional receiving on MF and low HF. A Beverage is a long wire close to the ground, terminated at the far end, and it is a receiving antenna: very directional, very quiet, and inefficient enough that nobody transmits on one.

questions.q: In which direction or directions does an electrically small loop (less than 1/10 wavelength in circumference) have nulls in its radiation pattern?
a: In the plane of the loop
Broadside and in the plane of the loop
questions.x: Nulls broadside to the loop, with maximum response in the plane of the loop. Those nulls are extremely sharp, which is what makes a small loop the standard tool for direction finding and for notching out a noise source.
questions.xs: ARRL Antenna Book; small loop theory

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of multiband antennas?
a: They present low impedance on all design frequencies
They must be used with an antenna tuner
They must be fed with open wire line
questions.x: Poor harmonic rejection. An antenna resonant on several bands is also happy to radiate on harmonics that fall on those bands, so anything spurious your transmitter produces gets radiated efficiently rather than being attenuated.

questions.q: What is the common name of a dipole with a single central support?
questions.x: An inverted V. One central support with both legs sloping down is cheaper and needs less space than a flat dipole. The sloping legs narrow the pattern slightly and lower the feed point impedance a little.

questions.q: What is the primary function of an external earth connection or ground rod?
a: Prevent static build up on power lines
Reduce RF current flow between pieces of equipment
Protect breaker panel from power surges

questions.q: When evaluating RF exposure levels from your station at a neighbor’s home, what must you do?
a: Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits

questions.q: Over what range of frequencies are the FCC human body RF exposure limits most restrictive?
When evaluating a site with multiple transmitters operating at the same time, the operators and licensees of which transmitters are responsible for mitigating over-exposure situations?
a: Each transmitter that produces 20 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 25 percent
Each transmitter that produces 5 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 50 percent

questions.q: What hazard is created by operating at microwave frequencies?
a: The high gain antennas commonly used can result in high exposure levels
Microwaves are in the frequency range where wave velocity is higher
The extremely high frequency energy can damage the joints of antenna structures

questions.q: Why are there separate electric (E) and magnetic (H) MPE limits at frequencies below 300 MHz?
a: The body reacts to electromagnetic radiation from both the E and H fields
Ground reflections and scattering cause the field strength to vary with location
E field and H field radiation intensity peaks can occur at different locations

questions.q: What is meant by “100% tie-off” regarding tower safety?
a: All loose ropes and guys secured to a fixed structure
At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times
All tools secured to the climber’s harness
All circuit breakers feeding power to the tower must be tied closed with tape, cable, or ties

questions.q: What does SAR measure?
a: The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body
The rate of RF energy reflected from stationary terrain

questions.q: Which of the following types of equipment are exempt from RF exposure evaluations?
a: Transceivers with less than 7 watts of RF output
Antennas that radiate only in the near field
Dish antennas less than one meter in diameter

questions.q: When must an RF exposure evaluation be performed on an amateur station operating on 80 meters?
a: An evaluation must always be performed
When the ERP of the station is less than 10 watts
When the station’s operating mode is CW
When the output power from the transmitter is less than 100 watts

questions.q: To what should lanyards be attached while climbing?
Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground?
a: To the belt of the fall-arrest harness
To the next lowest set of guys

questions.q: Why is it not legal to transmit a 3 kHz bandwidth USB signal with a carrier frequency of 14.348 MHz?
a: USB is not used on 20-meter phone
The lower 1 kHz of the signal is outside the 20-meter band
The upper 1 kHz of the signal is outside the 20-meter band
questions.x: USB puts your energy above the displayed carrier frequency. Add the 3 kHz bandwidth to 14.348 and the signal reaches 14.351 MHz, while 20 meters stops at 14.350. That top 1 kHz falls outside the band, and §97.307(b) requires emissions to stay confined to the segment available to you.

questions.q: When using a transceiver that displays the carrier frequency of phone signals, which of the following displayed frequencies represents the lowest frequency at which a properly adjusted LSB emission will be totally within the band?
a: 300 Hz above the lower band edge
1 kHz above the lower band edge
3 kHz above the lower band edge
questions.x: LSB places energy below the displayed frequency, so a 3 kHz signal extends 3 kHz down. To keep all of it inside, set the carrier at least 3 kHz above the lower edge. USB works the mirror image: stay 3 kHz below the upper edge.

questions.q: What is the highest legal carrier frequency on the 20-meter band for transmitting a 2.8 kHz wide USB data signal?
questions.x: Data on 20 meters must sit below 14.150 MHz, and USB extends upward from the carrier. Subtract the 2.8 kHz bandwidth from 14.150 and you get 14.1472 MHz. Take the segment edge and back off by the bandwidth.

questions.q: May an Extra class operator answer the CQ of a station on 3.601 MHz LSB phone?
a: Yes, the entire signal will be inside the SSB allocation for Extra class operators
Yes, the displayed frequency is within the 75-meter phone band segment
No, the sideband components will extend beyond the edge of the phone band segment
No, US stations are not permitted to use phone emissions below 3.610 MHz
questions.x: The 75-meter phone segment starts at 3.600 MHz. An LSB signal on 3.601 spreads roughly 3 kHz downward, reaching about 3.598, which puts most of it below the edge. Being inside the band with your carrier is not enough when the sidebands are not.

questions.q: Who must be in physical control of the station apparatus of an amateur station aboard any vessel or craft that is documented or registered in the United States?
a: Only a person with an FCC Marine Radio license grant
Only a person named in an amateur station license grant
Any person holding an FCC issued amateur license or who is authorized for alien reciprocal operation
Any person named in an amateur station license grant or a person holding an unrestricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit
questions.x: Section 97.5(a) requires the apparatus to be under the physical control of a person named in an amateur license grant or authorized for alien reciprocal operation. Vessel registry decides which rules apply; the licensing requirement itself does not change.

questions.q: What is the required transmit frequency of a CW signal for channelized 60 meter operation?
a: At the lowest frequency of the channel
At the center frequency of the channel
At the highest frequency of the channel
On any frequency where the signal’s sidebands are within the channel
questions.x: On the four discrete 60-meter channels, phone, data and RTTY are offset 1.5 kHz below center so the suppressed-carrier signal lands centered in the channel. CW carries no sidebands, so it is transmitted right at the center frequency.

questions.q: What is the maximum power permitted on the 2200-meter band?
questions.x: Two limits apply on 2200 meters and the tighter one governs: 1.5 kW PEP at the transmitter, but only 1 watt EIRP radiated. Antennas at 137 kHz are so short compared with a wavelength that they radiate a tiny fraction of what you feed them.

questions.q: If a station in a message forwarding system inadvertently forwards a message that is in violation of FCC rules, who is primarily accountable for the rules violation?
a: The control operator of the packet bulletin board station
The control operator of the originating station
The control operators of all the stations in the system
The control operators of all the stations in the system not authenticating the source from which they accept communications
questions.x: In a message forwarding system the control operator of the originating station is primarily accountable for a violation in the message. Section 97.219(c) protects intermediate forwarding stations that pass it along inadvertently. Accountability sits with whoever wrote it.

questions.q: Except in some parts of Alaska, what is the maximum power permitted on the 630-meter band?
questions.x: On 630 meters the ceiling is 500 W PEP at the transmitter and 5 watts EIRP radiated. Pair it with the 2200-meter figure: 1 watt on 2200, 5 watts on 630, both EIRP.

questions.q: If an amateur station is installed aboard a ship or aircraft, what condition must be met before the station is operated?
a: Its operation must be approved by the master of the ship or the pilot in command of the aircraft
The amateur station operator must agree not to transmit when the main radio of the ship or aircraft is in use
The amateur station must have a power supply that is completely independent of the main ship or aircraft power supply
The amateur station must operate only in specific segments of the amateur service HF and VHF bands
questions.x: Installing and operating an amateur station aboard a ship or aircraft "must be approved by the master of the ship or pilot in command of the aircraft." Their authority over the vessel outranks your license. Section 97.11(b) adds that the station must be independent of the vessel's own radio gear.

questions.q: What licensing is required when operating an amateur station aboard a US-registered vessel in international waters?
a: Any amateur license with an FCC Marine or Aircraft endorsement
Only General class or higher amateur licenses
questions.x: A US-registered vessel carries US jurisdiction with it into international waters, so any FCC-issued amateur license is sufficient. No endorsement, no maritime permit, and no foreign authorization is needed while you are aboard.

questions.q: Which of the following constitutes a spurious emission?
a: An amateur station transmission made without the proper call sign identification
A signal transmitted to prevent its detection by any station other than the intended recipient
Any transmitted signal that unintentionally interferes with another licensed radio station and whose levels exceed 40 dB below the fundamental power level
An emission outside the signal’s necessary bandwidth that can be reduced or eliminated without affecting the information transmitted
questions.x: The definition: "An emission, or frequencies outside the necessary bandwidth of a transmission, the level of which may be reduced without affecting the information being transmitted." That last clause is the test. If removing it costs you nothing, it was spurious.

questions.q: Which of the following is an acceptable bandwidth for digital voice or slow-scan TV transmissions made on the HF amateur bands?
questions.x: No non-phone emission may exceed the bandwidth of a communications quality phone signal of the same modulation type. On HF that benchmark is about 3 kHz, so digital voice and SSTV are held to the same width as an SSB conversation.

questions.q: Within what distance must an amateur station protect an FCC monitoring facility from harmful interference?
questions.x: A station within 1600 meters, which is 1 mile, of an FCC monitoring facility must protect it from harmful interference. Fail to do so and the FCC may impose operating restrictions on your station.

questions.q: What must the control operator of a repeater operating in the 70-centimeter band do if a radiolocation system experiences interference from that repeater?
a: Reduce the repeater antenna HAAT (Height Above Average Terrain)
File an FAA NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) with the repeater system's ERP, call sign, and six-character grid locator
Cease operation or make changes to the repeater that mitigate the interference
questions.x: Amateurs are secondary on 70 centimeters and must not cause harmful interference to the radiolocation service. If your repeater is the source, the obligation is immediate: cease operating or change the repeater so the interference stops.

questions.q: What is the National Radio Quiet Zone?
a: An area surrounding the FCC monitoring station in Laurel, Maryland
An area in New Mexico surrounding the White Sands Test Area
An area surrounding the National Radio Astronomy Observatory
An area in Florida surrounding Cape Canaveral
questions.x: The National Radio Quiet Zone is a rectangle across Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia protecting the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank. Its telescopes listen for signals far weaker than anything a transmitter nearby would leave intact.

questions.q: Which of the following additional rules apply if you are erecting an amateur station antenna structure at a site at or near a public use airport?
a: You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register it with the FCC as required by Part 17 of the FCC rules
You may have to enter the height above ground in meters, and the latitude and longitude in degrees, minutes, and seconds on the FAA website
You must file an Environmental Impact Statement with the EPA before construction begins
You must obtain a construction permit from the airport zoning authority per Part 119 of the FAA regulations
questions.x: The 200-foot threshold is not the only trigger. A structure at or near a public use airport may require FAA notification and FCC registration under Part 17 at heights well below 200 feet, because the limit there follows the airport's glide slope.

questions.q: To what type of regulations does PRB-1 apply?
a: Use of wireless devices in vehicles
questions.x: PRB-1 is the FCC's limited preemption of state and local zoning as it applies to amateur antenna structures. It reaches land use and zoning rules, not private deed restrictions or homeowner association covenants, which are contracts rather than government regulation.

questions.q: What limitations may the FCC place on an amateur station if its signal causes interference to domestic broadcast reception, assuming that the receivers involved are of good engineering design?
a: The amateur station must cease operation
The amateur station must cease operation on all frequencies below 30 MHz
The amateur station must cease operation on all frequencies above 30 MHz
The amateur station must avoid transmitting during certain hours on frequencies that cause the interference
questions.x: When your station interferes with domestic broadcast reception on receivers of good engineering design, the FCC may impose quiet hours: you avoid transmitting on the offending frequencies during specified times. The remedy restricts when and where you operate rather than shutting you down.

questions.q: Which amateur stations may be operated under RACES rules?
a: Only those club stations licensed to Amateur Extra class operators
Any FCC-licensed amateur station except a Technician class
Any FCC-licensed amateur station certified by the responsible civil defense organization for the area served
Only stations meeting the FCC Part 97 technical standards for operation during an emergency
questions.x: Any FCC-licensed amateur station may operate under RACES rules once it is certified by the civil defense organization responsible for the area served. The license alone is not enough, and no separate class of station license exists for RACES.

questions.q: What frequencies are authorized to an amateur station operating under RACES rules?
a: All amateur service frequencies authorized to the control operator
Specific segments in the amateur service MF, HF, VHF, and UHF bands
questions.x: RACES operation uses the ordinary amateur allocations. Every frequency and emission authorized to the control operator by license class remains available, shared with the amateur service. There is no separate block of RACES-only spectrum.

questions.q: What does PRB-1 require of state and local regulations affecting amateur radio antenna size and structures?
a: No limitations may be placed on antenna size or placement
Reasonable accommodations of amateur radio must be made
Such structures must be permitted when use for emergency communications can be demonstrated
Such structures must be permitted if certified by a registered professional engineer
questions.x: Local regulation must reasonably accommodate amateur service communications and represent the minimum practical regulation needed to serve the locality's legitimate purpose. Reasonable accommodation is the operative phrase, and it does not mean a jurisdiction has to permit any structure you want.

questions.q: What is the maximum bandwidth for a data emission on 60 meters?
questions.x: All 60-meter emissions are limited to 2.8 kHz occupied bandwidth, data included. One figure covers every mode on the band, which matches the width of an ordinary SSB signal.

questions.q: Which of the following apply to communications transmitted to amateur stations in foreign countries?
a: Third party traffic must be limited to that intended for the exclusive use of government and non-Government Organization (NGOs) involved in emergency relief activities
All transmissions must be in English
Communications must be limited to those incidental to the purpose of the amateur service and remarks of a personal nature
questions.x: International transmissions are "limited to communications incidental to the purposes of the amateur service and to remarks of a personal character." One sentence covering every DX contact you will ever make, and the answer restates it.

questions.q: How long must an operator wait after filing a notification with the Utilities Technology Council (UTC) before operating on the 2200-meter or 630-meter band?
a: Operators must not operate until approval is received
Operators may operate after 30 days, providing they have not been told that their station is within 1 kilometer of PLC systems using those frequencies
Operators may not operate until a test signal has been transmitted in coordination with the local power company
Operations may commence immediately, and may continue unless interference is reported by the UTC
questions.x: After notifying the UTC you wait 30 days. If nothing comes back saying your station sits within 1 kilometer of a power line carrier system using those frequencies, you may operate. Silence after 30 days is your clearance.

questions.q: What is an IARP?
a: A permit that allows US amateurs to operate in certain countries of the Americas
The internal amateur radio practices policy of the FCC
An indication of increased antenna reflected power
A forecast of intermittent aurora radio propagation
questions.x: The International Amateur Radio Permit comes out of the CITEL convention and lets US amateurs operate in participating countries across the Americas without applying for a separate license in each one. Think of IARP as the Western Hemisphere counterpart to CEPT.
questions.xs: CITEL Inter-American Convention; FCC International Bureau

questions.q: Under what situation may a station transmit third party communications while being automatically controlled?
a: Only when transmitting RTTY or data emissions
Only when transmitting SSB or CW
On any mode approved by the National Telecommunication and Information Administration
questions.x: Section 97.115(c) bars third-party traffic under automatic control, "except a station transmitting a RTTY or data emission." Automated digital forwarding systems keep working; automated phone relay of third-party messages does not.

questions.q: Which of the following is required in order to operate in accordance with CEPT rules in foreign countries where permitted?
a: You must identify in the official language of the country in which you are operating
The US embassy must approve of your operation
You must have a copy of FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048
You must append "/CEPT" to your call sign
questions.x: Operating under CEPT abroad requires you to carry proof of your authority: your FCC license plus a copy of Public Notice DA 16-1048, which is the document establishing that US amateurs may use CEPT privileges. Carry both, because a foreign administration has no other way to verify you.

questions.q: What notifications must be given before transmitting on the 630- or 2200-meter bands?
a: A special endorsement must be requested from the FCC
An environmental impact statement must be filed with the Department of the Interior
Operators must inform the FAA of their intent to operate, giving their call sign and distance to the nearest runway
Operators must inform the Utilities Technology Council (UTC) of their call sign and coordinates of the station
questions.x: Before operating on 2200 or 630 meters you notify the Utilities Technology Council of your call sign, the band or bands you intend to use, and the coordinates of your antenna's fixed location. The point is to check you are clear of power line carrier systems sharing those frequencies.

questions.q: What is the maximum permissible duration of a remotely controlled station’s transmissions if its control link malfunctions?
questions.x: A telecommand station must include provisions limiting transmission to no more than 3 minutes if the control link fails. Without it a stuck transmitter could hold a frequency indefinitely with nobody able to stop it.

questions.q: What is the highest modulation index permitted at the highest modulation frequency for angle modulation below 29.0 MHz?
questions.x: Below 29.0 MHz no angle-modulated emission may have a modulation index greater than 1 at the highest modulation frequency. Holding the index at 1.0 keeps the occupied bandwidth from expanding into neighboring HF signals.

questions.q: What is the maximum mean power level for a spurious emission below 30 MHz with respect to the fundamental emission?
questions.x: For transmitters installed after January 1, 2003, spurious emissions below 30 MHz must be at least 43 dB below the mean power of the fundamental. Above 30 MHz the requirement tightens to 60 dB, so keep the two figures paired.

questions.q: Which of the following operating arrangements allows an FCC-licensed US citizen to operate in many European countries, and amateurs from many European countries to operate in the US?
questions.x: CEPT is the European arrangement that lets a US amateur operate in participating countries, and their amateurs operate here, without a separate license application. IARP does the same job in the Americas.
questions.xs: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01; FCC Public Notice DA 16-1048

questions.q: In what portion of the 630-meter band are phone emissions permitted?
questions.x: The emission table authorizes phone across the whole 630-meter band. Very little voice happens there in practice because the band is 7 kHz wide and power is capped at 5 watts EIRP, but the rules permit it throughout.

questions.q: What is the definition of telemetry?
a: One-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument
Two-way transmissions in excess of 1000 feet
One-way transmission that initiates, modifies, or terminates the functions of a device at a distance
questions.x: Definition, verbatim: "Telemetry. A one-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument." One-way and measurements are the two elements. Telemetry reports data outward; telecommand sends control the other direction.

questions.q: Which of the following may transmit encrypted messages?
a: Telecommand signals from a space telecommand station
Auxiliary relay links carrying repeater audio
questions.x: Section 97.211(b) permits a space telecommand station to "transmit special codes intended to obscure the meaning of telecommand messages." The reason is security: anyone able to decode the commands could take over the spacecraft.

questions.q: What is a space telecommand station?
a: An amateur station located on the surface of the Earth for communication with other Earth stations by means of Earth satellites
An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a space station
An amateur station located in a satellite or a balloon more than 50 kilometers above the surface of the Earth
An amateur station that receives telemetry from a satellite or balloon more than 50 kilometers above the surface of the Earth
questions.x: A space telecommand station is the ground station that commands the satellite, transmitting to "initiate, modify, or terminate functions" of a space station. Telecommand goes up and controls; telemetry comes down and reports.

questions.q: Which of the following is required in the identification transmissions from a balloon-borne telemetry station?
a: The output power of the balloon transmitter
The station's six-character Maidenhead grid locator
questions.x: A balloon telemetry beacon is an amateur station like any other, so §97.119(a) applies in full and the call sign must go out. Nothing in the rules requires altitude, position or speed to be transmitted, however common those are in practice.

questions.q: What must be posted at the location of a station being operated by telecommand on or within 50 kilometers of the Earth’s surface?
a: A photocopy of the station license
A label with the name, address, and telephone number of the station licensee
A label with the name, address, and telephone number of the control operator
questions.x: Section 97.213(d) requires a photocopy of the station license and a label showing the name, address and telephone number of the licensee and at least one designated control operator, posted conspicuously at the station. Since every listed item appears in the rule, the inclusive answer is right.

questions.q: What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power when operating a model craft by telecommand?
questions.x: Model craft telecommand is capped at 1 watt. Section 97.215 also waives on-air identification for those transmissions, provided a label with your call sign and address is affixed to the transmitter.

questions.q: Which of the following HF amateur bands include allocations for space stations?
a: Satellite operation is permitted on all HF bands
questions.x: Space stations get 40, 20, 15 and 10 meters on HF, specifically the 7.0 to 7.1 MHz and 14.00 to 14.25 MHz segments plus the 17, 15, 12 and 10 meter bands. Below 40 meters nothing is allocated, since satellite work needs frequencies that pass through the ionosphere.

questions.q: Which VHF amateur bands have frequencies authorized for space stations?
questions.x: On VHF only 2 meters carries a space station allocation, at 144 to 146 MHz. Note this is the lower half of the band only, not all of 144 to 148, which is why 145.8 to 146.0 shows up as a satellite subband in practice.

questions.q: Which UHF amateur bands have frequencies authorized for space stations?
questions.x: Two UHF bands are authorized: 435 to 438 MHz on 70 centimeters and 2400 to 2450 MHz on 13 centimeters. The 435 MHz segment carries most amateur satellite downlinks you will actually hear.

questions.q: Which amateur stations are eligible to be telecommand stations of space stations, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator of the station?
a: Any amateur station approved by AMSAT
Any amateur station so designated by the space station licensee
Any amateur station so designated by the ITU
questions.x: Eligibility comes from designation, not license class. Any amateur station designated by the space station licensee may act as its telecommand station, and the control operator then works within the privileges of the license held.

questions.q: Which amateur stations are eligible to operate as Earth stations?
a: Any amateur licensee who has successfully completed the AMSAT space communications course
Only those of General, Advanced or Amateur Extra class operators
Only those of Amateur Extra class operators
Any amateur station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator
questions.x: Any amateur station may be an Earth station, and any class of operator may control one, within their own privileges. An Earth station is simply a ground station communicating through a satellite, which is what most operators are doing on the birds.

questions.q: Which of the following amateur stations may transmit one-way communications?
a: A space station, beacon station, or telecommand station
A local repeater or linked repeater station
A message forwarding station or automatically controlled digital station
questions.x: One-way transmission is normally prohibited, but three station types are given explicit permission: space stations, beacons and telecommand stations. Each has a purpose that cannot work as a two-way exchange.

questions.q: For which types of out-of-pocket expenses do the Part 97 rules state that VEs and VECs may be reimbursed?
a: Preparing, processing, administering, and coordinating an examination for an amateur radio operator license
Teaching an amateur operator license examination preparation course
No expenses are authorized for reimbursement
Providing amateur operator license examination preparation training materials
questions.x: Section 97.527 allows reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses incurred "in preparing, processing, administering, or coordinating an examination." Actual costs only. VEs receive no payment for their time, and §97.509(e) makes charging beyond that a serious violation.

questions.q: Who is tasked by Part 97 with maintaining the pools of questions for all US amateur license examinations?
questions.x: All VECs must cooperate in maintaining one question pool per written element, each holding at least ten times the number of questions used on a single exam. The VECs own the pools jointly. The FCC does not write the questions.

questions.q: What is a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator?
a: A person who has volunteered to administer amateur operator license examinations
An organization paid by the volunteer examiner team to publicize and schedule examinations
An organization that has entered into an agreement with the FCC to coordinate, prepare, and administer amateur operator license examinations
The person who has entered into an agreement with the FCC to be the VE session manager
questions.x: A VEC is an organization that has entered into a written agreement with the FCC to coordinate, prepare and administer amateur license examinations. The agreement with the Commission is what makes an organization a VEC.

questions.q: What is required to be accredited as a Volunteer Examiner?
a: Each General, Advanced and Amateur Extra class operator is automatically accredited as a VE when the license is granted
The amateur operator applying must pass a VE examination administered by the FCC Enforcement Bureau
The prospective VE must obtain accreditation from the FCC
A VEC must confirm that the VE applicant meets FCC requirements to serve as an examiner
questions.x: Accreditation is the VEC confirming that a candidate meets the FCC's requirements: correct license class, at least 18 years old, and never revoked or suspended. The VEC may also decline anyone it judges not competent or whose integrity is in question.

questions.q: What must the VE team do with the application form if the examinee does not pass the exam?
a: Maintain the application form with the VEC’s records
Return the application document to the examinee
Send the application form to the FCC and inform the FCC of the grade
questions.x: On a failing grade the VE team returns the application document to the examinee and tells them the grade. Nothing goes to the VEC. The paperwork is theirs to keep, and they may test again the same day if the session allows it.

questions.q: Who is responsible for the proper conduct and necessary supervision during an amateur operator license examination session?
questions.x: Responsibility is individual, not collective. The rule states that the administering VEs are responsible for the proper conduct and necessary supervision of each examination, and each VE must observe the examinee throughout. No one gets to defer to the team lead.

questions.q: What should a VE do if a candidate fails to comply with the examiner’s instructions during an amateur operator license examination?
a: Warn the candidate that continued failure to comply will result in termination of the examination
Allow the candidate to complete the examination, but invalidate the results
Immediately terminate everyone’s examination and close the session
questions.x: Section 97.511 requires each examinee to comply with the instructions given by the administering VEs. If a candidate will not, the VE terminates that examination immediately. There is no warning step written into the rules.

questions.q: To which of the following examinees may a VE not administer an examination?
a: Relatives of the VE as listed in the FCC rules
questions.x: A VE may not examine a spouse, child, grandchild, stepchild, parent, grandparent, stepparent, sibling, stepsibling, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew, or in-law. The list is long and specific, and the point is avoiding any appearance of favoritism.

questions.q: What may be the penalty for a VE who fraudulently administers or certifies an examination?
a: Revocation of the VE’s amateur station license grant and the suspension of the VE’s amateur operator license grant
A fine of up to $1,000 per occurrence
A sentence of up to one year in prison
questions.x: Fraudulent administration or certification may result in revocation of the VE's station license grant and suspension of the operator license grant. The penalty falls on the examiner's own license, which is what gives the volunteer system its teeth.
